Hard-Constraint DC Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for globally bounding DC problems with constraints that cannot be relaxed by unsafe penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constraints \(c_i(x)=g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\), a node \(R\) is hard-constraint safe when its relaxation uses functions \(\underline c_{i,R}\) satisfying
\[
\underline c_{i,R}(x)\le c_i(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in R,
\]
and declares node infeasibility only after certifying that no \(x\in R\) satisfies all relaxed inequalities \(\underline c_{i,R}(x)\le0\). Consequently, the relaxed feasible set contains the original feasible set within \(R\). A finite penalty substitution is not equivalent unless an independently justified exact-penalty threshold is available; otherwise pruning must retain the explicit hard constraints through valid outer relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard DC constraints require outer-feasible node relaxations. An arbitrary finite penalty cannot replace them without a proven exact-penalty threshold.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) and \(h_i\) is convex on the node domain.
Node rejection is based on certified relaxation infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible point of the original constrained problem remains feasible for the node relaxation and therefore cannot be removed solely by relaxed infeasibility.

notation.meaning: nodewise lower relaxation of the constraint function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Paired-Inequality Representation of a DC Equality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact treatment of a DC equality and the failure boundaries of one-sided or tolerance-based replacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q,r:X\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions. Then
\[q(x)-r(x)=0\iff q(x)-r(x)\le0\ \text{and}\ r(x)-q(x)\le0.\]
Thus an inequality-based DC global method handles the equality exactly only when it retains both orientations. Retaining one orientation is generally a strict relaxation: for \(q(x)=0\), \(r(x)=x\), and \(X=[0,1]\), the inequality \(q-r\le0\) admits every \(x\in X\), whereas the equality admits only \(x=0\). Replacing equality by \(|q-r|\le\tau\) with \(\tau>0\) defines tolerance feasibility and need not preserve the exact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC equality is exactly two opposing DC inequalities; one-sided enforcement or a positive residual tolerance generally enlarges the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) and \(r\) are finite convex functions on \(X\).
All relations are interpreted pointwise on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact equality enforcement requires both inequality orientations and zero residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Paired-Inequality Representation of a DC Equality
DC Equality-Constraint Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of a DC equality into two DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q,r:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex on a convex domain \(X\). The DC equality
\[
q(x)-r(x)=0
\]
is equivalent to the pair
\[
q(x)-r(x)\le0,\qquad r(x)-q(x)\le0.
\]
Both inequalities are DC constraints. Hence a global method for DC inequalities may enforce the equality by retaining both directions and constructing valid outer relaxations for each. Enforcing only one direction yields a strict relaxation in general. Likewise, replacing the pair by \(\lvert q(x)-r(x)\rvert\le\tau\) changes the feasible set unless \(\tau=0\), although positive \(\tau\) may define an explicit feasibility tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC equality is exactly two opposing DC inequalities. Both must be retained; one direction or a positive residual tolerance changes the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) and \(r\) are finite convex functions on \(X\).
Equality and inequalities are interpreted pointwise over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \(q(x)-r(x)=0\) if and only if both displayed DC inequalities hold.

children.title: DC Decomposition Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of valid DC decompositions for the same model.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Decomposition Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic nonuniqueness of convex-minus-convex representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f=g-h\) on a convex set \(X\), where \(g\) and \(h\) are convex. For every convex function \(\psi:X\to\mathbb R\),
\[
f=(g+\psi)-(h+\psi),
\]
and both new components are convex. Thus, whenever one DC decomposition exists, infinitely many generally distinct decompositions exist, for example by taking \(\psi(x)=\alpha\lVert x\rVert^2\) with any \(\alpha\ge0\) in a Euclidean space. The represented objective and its minimizers are unchanged, but relaxations that approximate the subtracted component may change because they act on \(h+\psi\), not directly on \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex function to both DC components preserves the objective, creating infinitely many decompositions whose induced global relaxations may differ.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex.
\(g\), \(h\), and \(\psi\) are finite convex functions on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((g+\psi,h+\psi)\) is another DC decomposition of exactly the same function \(f\).

children.title: DC Decomposition Quality Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria used to compare alternative decompositions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Dominance Is Sufficient but Not Necessary for Better Optimized Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between pointwise error ranking and solved cell-bound ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a common objective \(f\) on a cell \(R\), models \(m_i=f-e_i\) with \(e_i\ge0\) satisfy \(e_1\le e_2\Rightarrow m_1\ge m_2\Rightarrow\inf_Rm_1\ge\inf_Rm_2\). The converse fails. For \(f\equiv0\) on \([0,1]\), take \(e_1(x)=x\) and \(e_2(x)=2(1-x)\). The errors cross, so neither model dominates pointwise, but \[\inf_{[0,1]}(-e_1)=-1>-2=\inf_{[0,1]}(-e_2).\] Thus pointwise error dominance is a strong sufficient criterion, while optimized lower-bound value is a weaker comparison criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise smaller error guarantees a better bound, but crossing errors can still yield a strict ordering of optimized lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: Both models underestimate the same objective on the same nonempty cell.
The displayed example uses nonnegative bounded errors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise error dominance implies bound dominance but is not necessary for it.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Dominance Is Sufficient but Not Necessary for Better Optimized Bounds
DC Decomposition Quality Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cellwise dominance criterion for decomposition quality in outer lower bounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a decomposition \(f=g-h\) and a partition cell \(R\), let \(\overline h_R\ge h\) be the overestimator used by the lower model and define its error by
\[
e_R(x):=\overline h_R(x)-h(x)\ge0.
\]
The induced model equals \(g(x)-\overline h_R(x)=f(x)-e_R(x)\). Given two decompositions and their prescribed overestimator constructions, decomposition \(1\) dominates decomposition \(2\) on \(R\) when \(e_R^{(1)}(x)\le e_R^{(2)}(x)\) for every \(x\in R\). Useful secondary criteria are inexpensive construction, tractable lower-model minimization, and errors converging uniformly to zero as \(\operatorname{diam}(R)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition is bound-superior on a cell when its overestimation error is pointwise smaller, subject also to tractable construction and vanishing error under refinement.
assumptions_latex: Both decompositions represent the same objective on \(R\).
Each selected overestimator is valid throughout \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise error dominance implies a pointwise tighter lower model and hence a no-worse node lower bound.

notation.meaning: cellwise overestimation error of the subtracted convex component

children.title: Bound Sensitivity to Decomposition Choice
children.top_down_role: Effects of decomposition choice on relaxation strength and global bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent DC Decompositions Can Give Unequal Cell Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete realization of decomposition-sensitive lower bounds under affine majorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=[0,1]\) and \(f\equiv0\). The decomposition \(f=0-0\), with exact overestimator \(0\), gives lower model \(m_1=0\) and bound \(L_1=0\). The equivalent decomposition \(f=x^2-x^2\), with the affine chord \(\overline h(x)=x\ge x^2\) on \(R\), gives \[m_2(x)=x^2-x\quad\text{and}\quad L_2=\min_{x\in R}(x^2-x)=-\tfrac14.\] Thus the represented objective is unchanged while the rigorous cell lower bound changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equivalent decompositions of the zero function yield lower bounds zero and minus one quarter under their specified valid majorants.
assumptions_latex: Each overestimator is valid on \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_1=0>-\tfrac14=L_2\) although both decompositions represent \(f\equiv0\).

notation.meaning: affine upper estimator of the subtracted convex component
cell lower bound from decomposition i

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent DC Decompositions Can Give Unequal Cell Bounds
Bound Sensitivity to Decomposition Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative dependence of cell lower bounds on DC decomposition error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let two DC decompositions of the same objective induce valid cell models \(m_i(x)=f(x)-e_i(x)\) on a nonempty cell \(R\), where \(e_i(x)\ge0\), and let \(L_i=\inf_{x\in R}m_i(x)\). Then
\[
|L_1-L_2|\le \sup_{x\in R}|e_1(x)-e_2(x)|.
\]
Moreover, if \(e_1(x)\le e_2(x)\) throughout \(R\), then \(m_1(x)\ge m_2(x)\) throughout \(R\) and consequently \(L_1\ge L_2\). Thus algebraically equivalent DC decompositions can produce unequal rigorous lower bounds solely through unequal approximation errors in their subtracted convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower bounds from equivalent DC decompositions can differ by at most the uniform difference of their relaxation errors; pointwise smaller error always gives a stronger bound.
assumptions_latex: The two decompositions represent the same finite objective \(f\) on \(R\).
Both error functions are bounded and nonnegative on \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed sensitivity inequality and the stated monotonic ordering of \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) hold.

notation.meaning: relaxation error induced by decomposition i
lower model induced by decomposition i
infimum of the i-th lower model on R

children.title: Search Sensitivity to Decomposition Choice
children.top_down_role: Effects of decomposition choice on exact-search behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Crossing Node Bounds Give No Pruning Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of search-effort ordering without uniform dominance on a common potential tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a common potential partition tree with two unresolved nodes \(A,B\), incumbent \(U=0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon=0\), and regional optima equal to \(0\). Suppose two valid decomposition-induced bound systems satisfy \[(L_A^{(1)},L_B^{(1)})=(0,-1),\qquad (L_A^{(2)},L_B^{(2)})=(-1,0).\] Under the bound test \(L_R^{(i)}\ge U\), method \(1\) prunes \(A\) but not \(B\), whereas method \(2\) prunes \(B\) but not \(A\). Thus crossing valid bounds imply neither inclusion of pruned-node sets nor a decomposition-independent ordering of generated descendants or search effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When decomposition-induced bounds cross across nodes, each decomposition can prune a node that the other cannot, so neither search dominates.
assumptions_latex: The comparison uses one common potential tree and common incumbent and tolerance.
All displayed bounds are valid for their regional optima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither method's bound-pruned node set contains the other's.

notation.meaning: bound on potential node R under decomposition i

knowledge_statements.title: Crossing Node Bounds Give No Pruning Dominance
Search Sensitivity to Decomposition Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of decomposition-induced bound dominance on a fixed branching search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run two branch-and-bound searches on the same partition tree, with the same incumbent \(U\), tolerance \(\varepsilon\), and node-selection rules, but with lower bounds \(L_R^{(1)}\) and \(L_R^{(2)}\) induced by different DC decompositions. If \(L_R^{(1)}\ge L_R^{(2)}\) for every generated node \(R\), then every node pruned by \(L_R^{(2)}\ge U-\varepsilon\) is also pruned by method \(1\). Hence method \(1\) explores no additional node solely because of the bound test. Without uniform bound dominance, errors may cross between cells, so neither decomposition has a decomposition-independent ordering in explored-node count or search effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly stronger bounds cannot worsen pruning on a fixed tree, but crossing cellwise errors can reverse which decomposition searches fewer nodes.
assumptions_latex: Both searches use the same tree, incumbents, tolerance, and non-bound decisions.
All compared node lower bounds are rigorous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform nodewise dominance transfers directly to pruning dominance; absent it, no general search-effort ordering follows.

notation.meaning: lower bound on node R from decomposition i

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Global Minimization Versus Local Minimization p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\), where \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and noncompact, and \(f=g-h\) on \(C\) for finite convex functions \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). These assumptions alone imply neither a finite optimal value nor attainment: for \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the affine DC function \(f(x)=-x\), one has \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=-\infty\). A sufficient additional condition is that \(f\) be level-bounded on \(C\), meaning that for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the sublevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact. Because \(f\) is continuous and \(C\) is nonempty, this condition yields a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness of a noncompact DC feasible region does not prevent escape to infinity. If the finite DC objective is level-bounded on the region, its minimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact DC Feasible Regions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Infimum Without Attainment on a Noncompact DC Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates boundedness below from attainment on a closed noncompact feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=e^{-x}\). The function is finite, convex, and therefore DC, with \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex DC objective exp(-x) on the real line has finite infimum zero but no minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_C f=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{argmin}_C f=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Boundedness Is Not Necessary for Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness boundary for the seed's sufficient existence condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(f\equiv0\), the finite convex objective attains its minimum at every point, but \(\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}=\mathbb R\) for every \(\alpha\ge0\). Thus level-boundedness is sufficient but not necessary for finite attainment on a closed noncompact region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant DC objective attains its minimum everywhere on a noncompact region although it is not level-bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\mathbb R\).
\(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{argmin}_C f=C\neq\varnothing,\qquad f\text{ is not level-bounded on }C.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Boundedness Is Not Necessary for Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent sequential formulation of level-boundedness on a closed noncompact feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then all sublevel sets \(\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) are compact if and only if every sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) with \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) satisfies \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a closed finite-dimensional region, level-boundedness is equivalent to coercivity along every feasible sequence escaping to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is level-bounded on }C\iff\bigl(\|x_k\|\to\infty,\ x_k\in C\bigr)\Rightarrow f(x_k)\to+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Coercivity Characterization of Level-Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative definition of weakness for a valid regional minorant used in DC optimization.

source_refs.locator: 4.7 Convex Minorants of a DC Function p. 117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(m_D:D\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) satisfy \(m_D(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). Write \(f_D^*=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\) and \(\beta_D=\inf_{x\in D}m_D(x)\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), the minorant is called \(\varepsilon\)-weak on \(D\) when \(f_D^*\) is finite and \(f_D^*-\beta_D\geq\varepsilon\), with the difference interpreted as \(+\infty\) if \(\beta_D=-\infty\). It remains valid but provides a lower bound separated from the true regional optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid regional minorant is called epsilon-weak when its infimum lies at least epsilon below the finite true regional optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak DC Minorants

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large Pointwise Error Need Not Produce a Weak Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse from large uniform model error to a poor optimized lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(M>0\), let \(D=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=Mx\), and \(m_D(x)=0\). Then \(m_D\le f\), \[\sup_{x\in D}(f(x)-m_D(x))=M,\] but \(f_D^*=\beta_D=0\). Thus arbitrarily large error away from all minimizers need not create a positive regional lower-bound gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minorant can have arbitrarily large error away from the optimum while still giving the exact regional lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_D(f-m_D)=M\) while \(f_D^*-\beta_D=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Large Pointwise Error Need Not Produce a Weak Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minorant Error Bounds for Regional Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between pointwise minorant error and the optimized regional bound gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\ne\varnothing\), let \(m_D\le f\) on \(D\), and define \(e=f-m_D\ge0\), \(f_D^*=\inf_Df\), and \(\beta_D=\inf_Dm_D\). If \(f_D^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(E:=\sup_De<\infty\), then \[0\le f_D^*-\beta_D\le E.\] If \(f\) attains its minimum at \(x^*\in D\), then \[f_D^*-\beta_D\ge e(x^*).\] Thus uniform error below \(\varepsilon\) rules out \(\varepsilon\)-weakness, while error at least \(\varepsilon\) at a regional minimizer guarantees it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regional bound gap is at most the worst pointwise minorant error and, when a minimizer exists, at least the error at that minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(D\ne\varnothing\) and \(m_D\le f\) on \(D\).
\(f_D^*\in\mathbb R\).
For the upper estimate, \(\sup_D(f-m_D)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f_D^*-\beta_D\le\sup_D(f-m_D)\), and \(f_D^*-\beta_D\ge f(x^*)-m_D(x^*)\) at an attained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Minorant Error Bounds for Regional Weakness

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent DC decompositions can make separate-term bounds arbitrarily poor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M>0\), minimize \(f_M(x)=0\) over \(D=[-1,1]\) using the DC decomposition \(f_M=g_M-h_M\), where \(g_M(x)=Mx^2\) and \(h_M(x)=Mx^2\). The separate-term lower bound is valid and equals \[B_M=\inf_{x\in D}g_M(x)-\sup_{x\in D}h_M(x)=0-M=-M.\] Nevertheless, \(f_M^*=0\) for every \(M\). Hence \(f_M^*-B_M=M\to\infty\), although the represented objective and feasible region do not change. A lower-bounding rule that ignores cancellation between DC components can therefore degenerate solely because of decomposition scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling two cancelling convex components leaves the objective unchanged but drives a separate-term lower bound to negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_M^*-B_M=M\to\infty\) as \(M\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: scaled convex components of the DC decomposition

children.title: Persistent Bound Gaps

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Bound Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonvanishing global relaxation error under repeated refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\). At iteration \(k\), let \(\mathcal P_k\) be a finite cover of \(C\), and let each \(B_k(D)\) satisfy \(B_k(D)\leq\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\). Define \(L_k=\min_{D\in\mathcal P_k}B_k(D)\). The bounding scheme has a persistent bound gap when \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}(f^*-L_k)>0.\] This condition may hold even when the maximum diameter of regions in \(\mathcal P_k\) tends to zero; geometric refinement alone does not ensure convergence unless the regional minorants are asymptotically exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound gap is persistent when valid global lower bounds remain uniformly below the optimum despite indefinitely fine regional refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(f^*\in\mathbb{R}\).
\(B_k(D)\leq\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\) for every \(D\in\mathcal P_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}(f^*-L_k)>0\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound on region D
global lower bound at iteration k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Limsup Characterization of a Persistent Bound Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent asymptotic formulations for valid global lower-bound sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(L_k\le f^*\) for every \(k\). Then \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}(f^*-L_k)=f^*-\limsup_{k\to\infty}L_k.\] Hence the gap is persistent exactly when \(\limsup_k L_k<f^*\). If \((L_k)\) is nondecreasing, then \(L_k\to L_\infty:=\sup_kL_k\le f^*\), and persistence is equivalent to \(L_\infty<f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistence means that the upper asymptotic limit of the lower bounds stays strictly below the optimum; for monotone bounds this is strict separation of their limit from the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f^*\in\mathbb R\).
\(L_k\le f^*\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_k(f^*-L_k)>0\iff\limsup_kL_k<f^*\), with the stated monotone specialization.

notation.meaning: limit of a nondecreasing lower-bound sequence

children.title: Bound-Driven Search Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Failure modes caused by repeatedly uninformative regional bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Driven Search Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagnation caused by repeatedly selecting a spuriously promising region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization search that at iteration \(k\) selects a region \(D_k\) attaining the smallest valid bound \(L_k=B_k(D_k)\), while \(U_k\) is the best feasible objective value found. If some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \(L_k\leq f^*-\delta\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), then the certified gap obeys \(U_k-L_k\geq\delta\) because \(U_k\geq f^*\). Consequently, no stopping rule requiring \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon<\delta\) can terminate, even if \(U_k\to f^*\). Persistent underestimation therefore causes bound-driven certification stagnation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the selected lower bound stays falsely low, the certified gap cannot close, even when incumbent values converge to the true optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(U_k\geq f^*\) and \(L_k\leq f^*\).
\(L_k\leq f^*-\delta\) eventually for some \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k-L_k\geq\delta\) eventually, so tolerance \(\varepsilon<\delta\) cannot be certified.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-Bound Starvation from a Persistently Low Valid Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid but nonconvergent bound can make pure best-bound selection ignore a region containing the global optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the feasible set be \(D=A\cup B\) with \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), let \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\in A\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\in B\), and suppose an incumbent of value \(U_0=1\) is available. Assign \(B\) the exact bound \(L(B)=0\). Suppose refinement of the selected region in \(A\) always leaves at least one descendant \(A_k\) with valid bound \(L(A_k)=-1\), and processing such descendants produces only feasible values equal to \(1\). A pure best-bound rule always has an \(A_k\) with bound below \(L(B)\), so \(B\) need never be processed and \(U_k=1>f^*=0\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistently lower valid bounds on one branch can starve an unprocessed branch containing the global optimizer.

After each selected refinement in \(A\), at least one live descendant has valid bound \(-1\).

knowledge_statements.title: DC Representation Universality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic DC representation for smooth functions on compact convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and suppose \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(C\). Set \(\mu=\min_{x\in C}\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x))\), which is finite, and choose \(\rho\geq\max\{0,-\mu\}\). Then \[f(x)=\left(f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\right)-\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\quad(x\in C).\] Both displayed components are convex on \(C\). Thus every such smooth objective admits a DC representation on the compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every twice continuously differentiable function on a compact convex set becomes DC after adding and subtracting a sufficiently curved quadratic.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f\in C^2(U)\) for an open neighborhood \(U\supseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), where \(g=f+\rho\lVert\cdot\rVert^2/2\) and \(h=\rho\lVert\cdot\rVert^2/2\) are convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Lipschitz Boundary of Finite DC Representability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary interior regularity of finite convex-minus-convex representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and suppose \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), where \(g,h:C\to\mathbb R\) are finite convex functions. Then \(g\), \(h\), and hence \(f\), are locally Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{ri}C\). Therefore not every finite continuous function on a compact convex set is DC. In particular, \[f(x)=\sqrt{|x|}\quad(x\in[-1,1])\] is continuous but not locally Lipschitz at the relative-interior point \(0\), so it is not the difference of two finite convex functions on that interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite DC functions are locally Lipschitz in the relative interior; square-root of absolute value is therefore not DC on an interval.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex.
\(g\) and \(h\) are finite convex functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) is locally Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(x\mapsto\sqrt{|x|}\) is not DC on \([-1,1]\).

children.title: Worst-Case DC Complexity
children.top_down_role: Worst-case computational difficulty within broadly expressive DC families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case hardness already present in rational concave-quadratic minimization over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph with nonnegative integer edge weights and weighted Laplacian \(L\), \(x^{\mathsf T}Lx=4w(\delta(S_x))\) at every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\), where \(S_x=\{i:x_i=1\}\). Since the convex function \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Lx\) attains a maximum over \([-1,1]^n\) at a vertex, deciding whether \[\min_{x\in[-1,1]^n}-x^{\mathsf T}Lx\le -4K\] is equivalent to deciding whether the graph has a cut of weight at least \(K\). The decision problem is therefore NP-complete under binary encoding, and exact minimization is NP-hard. Its objective is concave quadratic and hence DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Max-Cut is equivalent to minimizing a rational concave quadratic over a box, making this restricted DC decision problem NP-complete and exact DC minimization NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights and \(K\) are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
Complexity is measured in the deterministic Turing model.
The standard Laplacian convention \(x^{\mathsf T}Lx=\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Concave-quadratic box minimization is NP-hard, and its threshold decision form is NP-complete.}

notation.meaning: cut shore encoded by a sign vector

knowledge_statements.title: NP-Completeness of Concave-Quadratic Box Minimization
Worst-Case DC Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-hardness already within concave quadratic box minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph with nonnegative rational edge weights, let \(L\) be its weighted Laplacian. The convex quadratic \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Lx\) attains its maximum over \([-1,1]^n\) at a vertex in \(\{-1,1\}^n\), and its vertex values encode weighted cuts up to a fixed factor. Therefore deciding whether \[\min_{x\in[-1,1]^n}-x^{\mathsf T}Lx\leq-T\] is NP-hard under the standard binary encoding. The objective is concave quadratic and hence DC. Consequently, general rationally encoded DC minimization admits no polynomial-time exact algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact DC minimization is NP-hard even for a concave quadratic objective over a box, by reduction from weighted Max-Cut.
assumptions_latex: Graph weights and threshold \(T\) are rational and binary encoded.
Computation is measured in the deterministic Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Exact box-constrained DC minimization is NP-hard.}\)

children.title: Expressiveness–Tractability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural boundary between representational generality and exploitable tractability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Hard Concave-Quadratic Subclass of DC Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete hardness witness showing that DC syntax alone does not imply tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a weighted graph with nonnegative rational edge weights and Laplacian \(L\succeq0\). The quadratic \(q(x)=-x^TLx\) is concave and therefore DC, for example \(q=0-x^TLx\). A concave function attains a minimum over the box \([0,1]^n\) at a vertex, so \[\min_{x\in[0,1]^n}-x^TLx=-\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}x^TLx.\] The right-hand maximization is the weighted Max-Cut problem up to its conventional constant factor. Consequently, exact minimization of a concave quadratic over a rational box, and hence unrestricted exact DC minimization, is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concave quadratic box minimization contains weighted Max-Cut, so unrestricted exact DC minimization is NP-hard despite the compact DC representation.
assumptions_latex: The graph has nonnegative rational edge weights encoded in binary.
Complexity concerns exact global optimization in the deterministic Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact minimization of DC functions over rational boxes is NP-hard, already for concave quadratics.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hard Concave-Quadratic Subclass of DC Minimization
Expressiveness–Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC representability does not imply global computational tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The DC class contains the convex subclass obtained by taking \(h=0\), but it also contains every concave quadratic \(f=-h\) with convex quadratic \(h\). Convex minimization admits polynomial-time methods under standard rational-data or oracle assumptions, whereas exact minimization of concave quadratics over rational boxes is NP-hard. Hence the syntactic property \(f=g-h\) does not identify a tractable global-optimization class. Tractability requires additional restrictions on the decomposition, feasible geometry, dimension, or available bounding structure; unrestricted DC expressiveness crosses the NP-hardness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC form spans both tractable convex minimization and NP-hard concave quadratic minimization, so representation alone gives no tractability guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Problems use rational data or standard polynomial-time evaluation and separation oracles.
Exact global optimization is measured in the deterministic Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) alone does not imply polynomial-time global minimizability unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Minimization over Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point reduction for compact polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope and let \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and concave. Then \(f\) attains its minimum on \(P\), and at least one minimizing point is a vertex of \(P\). Equivalently, \[\min_{x\in P}f(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(P)}f(v).\] The assertion guarantees an optimal vertex but does not assert that every minimizer is a vertex; for example, a constant concave function is minimized throughout \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous concave function on a compact polytope has an optimal vertex, so its minimum equals the minimum over all vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in P}f(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(P)}f(v)\).

Concave Minimization over Unbounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finite attainment when a recession direction decreases the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty unbounded polyhedron. Concavity and continuity of \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) do not ensure a finite minimum. If there exist \(x_0\in P\), a nonzero recession direction \(d\) with \(x_0+td\in P\) for all \(t\geq0\), and constants \(a\in\mathbb{R}\), \(b>0\) such that \(f(x_0+td)\leq a-bt\), then \(\inf_{x\in P}f(x)=-\infty\). In particular, \(P=[0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=-x\) satisfy this condition. Thus the compact-polytope extreme-point theorem cannot be transferred without recession analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an unbounded polyhedron, a decreasing recession ray can drive a continuous concave objective to negative infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty unbounded polyhedron.
\(x_0+td\in P\) and \(f(x_0+td)\leq a-bt\) for all \(t\geq0\), with \(b>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P}f(x)=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Feasibility Does Not Imply an Unbounded Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse failure showing that feasible-set unboundedness alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\in P\). Then \(P\) is an unbounded polyhedron and \(f\) is continuous and concave, but \[\min_{x\in P}f(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)=P.\] Thus an unbounded feasible polyhedron need not produce an unbounded-below or unattained concave-minimization problem.

Compact Convex Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point attainment beyond polyhedral feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and concave. Then \(f\) attains its minimum on \(C\), and some minimizer is an extreme point of \(C\). Consequently, \[\min_{x\in C}f(x)=\min_{e\in\operatorname{ext}(C)}f(e).\] The extreme-point set need not be finite, so this equality is a structural reduction rather than a finite enumeration algorithm for general compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous concave function on a compact convex set attains its minimum at some extreme point, though there may be infinitely many extreme points.

\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and concave.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point optimality persists, but finite vertex enumeration fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compact nonpolyhedral convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), continuous concave minimization still admits an extreme-point minimizer, but \(\operatorname{ext}(C)\) may be infinite. For example, when \(n\geq2\), the Euclidean unit ball \(C=\{x:\lVert x\rVert_2\leq1\}\) is nonpolyhedral and every boundary point is extreme. For any \(c\neq0\), the linear, hence concave, objective \(f(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x\) has the unique minimizer \(x^*=-c/\lVert c\rVert_2\). Thus polytope-style finite vertex enumeration has no direct analogue on general nonpolyhedral convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Concave Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separable concave objectives over nonempty polyhedral feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty. For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(D_i=\{x_i:x\in C\}\) and let \(f_i:D_i\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave. A separable concave-minimization problem has the form
\[
\min\left\{f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i):x\in C\right\}.
\]
The resulting objective \(f\) is concave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable concave-minimization problem minimizes a sum of univariate concave functions over a nonempty polyhedron; the resulting multivariate objective is concave on that polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty.
For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(f_i:D_i\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave, where \(D_i=\{x_i:x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\) is concave on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-coordinate special case of separable concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\prod_{i=1}^n C_i\neq\varnothing\) and every \(f_i\) attains its minimum on \(C_i\), then \[\min_{x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\min_{t\in C_i}f_i(t),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\sum_i f_i(x_i)=\prod_i\operatorname*{argmin}_{t\in C_i}f_i(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without coupling constraints, the separable problem decomposes exactly into independent univariate minimizations.

Each component minimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Convex Envelope on a Box
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex envelope of a finite separable concave objective on a bounded Cartesian box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), where \(\ell_i<u_i\), and let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\), with each \(f_i\) finite and concave on \([\ell_i,u_i]\). Define \(h_i(t)=\frac{u_i-t}{u_i-\ell_i}f_i(\ell_i)+\frac{t-\ell_i}{u_i-\ell_i}f_i(u_i)\). Then \[\operatorname{vex}_B f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n h_i(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian box, the convex envelope of a separable concave objective is the sum of its coordinate endpoint chords.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_i[\ell_i,u_i]\) with \(\ell_i<u_i\).
Each \(f_i\) is finite and concave on its coordinate interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_B(\sum_i f_i)(x)=\sum_i h_i(x_i)\).

notation.meaning: convex envelope of f on B

Concave Quadratic Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous finite-dimensional quadratic model with a negative-semidefinite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(r\in\mathbb{R}\). A concave quadratic-minimization problem has the form
\[
\min\left\{f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r:x\in C\right\},
\]
with \(Q\preceq0\). The Hessian of \(f\) is \(Q\), so \(f\) is concave on \(\mathbb{R}^n\); if \(Q\prec0\), then \(f\) is strictly concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concave quadratic minimization minimizes a quadratic objective with a negative-semidefinite symmetric Hessian over a prescribed nonempty feasible set; a negative-definite Hessian makes the objective strictly concave.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(r\in\mathbb{R}\).
\(Q\preceq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic objective is concave on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and it is strictly concave when \(Q\prec0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unconstrained boundedness boundary for negative-semidefinite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(Q\preceq0\). If \(Q=0\) and \(q=0\), then \(f\equiv r\) and every point is a global minimizer. In every other case, \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)=-\infty.\] In particular, when \(Q\prec0\), the stationary point \(-Q^{-1}q\) is the unique global maximizer, not a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained concave quadratic has a finite minimum only in the constant case; otherwise it is unbounded below, and a negative-definite stationary point is its maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\) and \(Q\preceq0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representation of negative-definite concave quadratic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\prec0\), \(H=-Q\succ0\), and \(x_c=H^{-1}q\). Then \[\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r=\left(r+\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}q\right)-\tfrac12(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}H(x-x_c).\] Consequently, for every nonempty \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}H(x-x_c).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-definite concave quadratic is a constant minus a positive-definite squared distance, making its minimization an equivalent farthest-point problem.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\) and \(Q\prec0\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}H(x-x_c)\).

Quasiconcave-Minimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point minimization for real-valued quasiconcave objectives on finite-dimensional polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope with vertex set \(\operatorname{ext}(C)=\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\), and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be quasiconcave, meaning that
\[
f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\ge\min\{f(x),f(y)\}
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Then
\[
\min_{x\in C}f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f(v^i).
\]
In particular, this property applies to every concave real-valued function on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued quasiconcave function on a nonempty polytope has a global minimizer at a vertex. The result includes concave objectives as a special case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polytope with \(\operatorname{ext}(C)=\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconcave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f(v^i)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional formulations used by the quasiconcave-minimization interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f\) is quasiconcave if and only if every upper level set \[U_\alpha=\{x\in C:f(x)\geq\alpha\}\] is convex. Equivalently, \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\geq\min\{f(x),f(y)\}\] for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Every concave function is quasiconcave, but the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconcavity is equivalent to convexity of every upper level set and is weaker than concavity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconcave}\iff \{x\in C:f(x)\geq\alpha\}\text{ is convex for every }\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.\)

notation.meaning: upper level set at level alpha

Then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(P).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly quasiconcave objective on a polytope, every global minimizer is a vertex.

\(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) is strictly quasiconcave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(P)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\) be a nonempty polytope and let \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave. Then
\[
\min_{x\in P}f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f(v^i).
\]
In particular, the minimum is attained, and at least one minimizer belongs to \(\operatorname{ext}(P)\). The assertion does not require strict concavity or uniqueness of the minimizing extreme point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every concave real-valued function on a nonempty polytope has a global minimizer at an extreme point of that polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Polytope Extreme-Point Attainment

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Restriction Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constancy at the global minimum on a face whose relative interior contains a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\), and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave. If a global minimizer \(x^\star\) of \(f\) over \(C\) belongs to \(\operatorname{relint}(F)\), then
\[
f(y)=f(x^\star)=\min_{x\in C}f(x)
\]
for every \(y\in F\). Thus the restriction of \(f\) to \(F\) is constant at the global minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a global minimizer of a concave objective lies in the relative interior of a face, the objective is constant at its global minimum value throughout that face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and \(F\) is a nonempty face of \(C\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave.
\(x^\star\in\operatorname{relint}(F)\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(F\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).

notation.meaning: face containing a minimizer in its relative interior

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimizer on the relative boundary of a face need not make a concave objective constant on that face.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=x\) and \(x^\star=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in F\) is globally minimizing while \(f|_F\) is nonconstant.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Hypothesis Is Essential
Recession-Direction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness caused by strict descent along an infinite feasible ray for a concave objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfy \(x+td\in C\) for every \(t\ge0\). If \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave and
\[
f(x+t_0d)<f(x)
\]
for some \(t_0>0\), then
\[
\inf_{y\in C}f(y)=-\infty.
\]
Consequently, finite lower boundedness excludes strict descent along any such feasible recession ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a concave objective, a strict decrease along an infinite feasible ray makes the problem unbounded below. Hence a finite lower bound rules out such ray descent.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex, \(x\in C\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfies \(x+td\in C\) for every \(t\ge0\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave.
There exists \(t_0>0\) such that \(f(x+t_0d)<f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in C}f(y)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: direction of an infinite feasible ray from the base point
positive ray parameter at which strict descent occurs

assumptions_latex: The objective is continuous and concave on its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compact feasibility guarantees attainment, whereas closed unbounded convex feasibility alone does not.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness versus closed unbounded feasibility for attainment of finite concave minima.

source_refs.locator: 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and compact and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, then \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is attained. Closedness and convexity without boundedness are insufficient: let
\[
C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^2:xy\ge1\},\qquad f(x,y)=x.
\]
The set \(C\) is closed and convex as a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and \(f\) is linear, hence concave. Nevertheless,
\[
\inf_{(x,y)\in C}f(x,y)=0,
\]
and no feasible point attains this value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity on a compact feasible set ensures attainment, but a continuous linear objective can have a finite unattained infimum on a closed unbounded convex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment-Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient attainment condition weaker than compactness of the whole feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. If, for some \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the sublevel set \(S_\alpha=\{x\in C:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is nonempty and compact, then \(f\) attains its global minimum on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty compact sublevel set suffices for attainment even when the feasible set is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous.
For some \(\alpha\), \(S_\alpha\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: objective sublevel set at level alpha

\(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave and can be evaluated at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first ranked vertex is a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete vertex enumeration followed by objective-value ranking.

source_refs.locator: 9.1 Extreme Point Ranking p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a nonempty polytope \(P\) and a concave evaluable function \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\). Enumerate \(V=\operatorname{ext}(P)=\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\), evaluate \(f(v^i)\), and order the vertices so that
\[
f(v^{(1)})\le f(v^{(2)})\le\cdots\le f(v^{(m)}).
\]
Initialize \(v^{\mathrm{best}}=v^{(1)}\) and \(U=f(v^{(1)})\). Stop after all vertices have been evaluated and output \((v^{\mathrm{best}},U)\). Extreme-point attainment yields
\[
U=f(v^{\mathrm{best}})=\min_{x\in P}f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate all vertices of the feasible polytope, evaluate and rank them by objective value, and return the lowest-ranked vertex as a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Ranking

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1 Extreme Point Ranking p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation and Ranking Cost after Vertex Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive work of the ranking phase once the complete vertex list is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\operatorname{ext}(P)\) contain \(m\) vertices. Given the complete list, finding a minimizing vertex requires exactly one objective evaluation per vertex and \(O(m)\) value comparisons; producing a complete sorted ranking takes \(O(m\log m)\) comparisons. These bounds exclude the cost of generating \(V\), whose size may itself be exponential in the dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After enumeration, minimum selection uses m evaluations and linear comparisons, while fully sorting all vertices costs order m log m comparisons.
assumptions_latex: The complete vertex list \(V\) with \(|V|=m\) is available.
Objective evaluations are treated as oracle operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{eval}}=m,\qquad N_{\mathrm{compare}}=O(m)\text{ for selection and }O(m\log m)\text{ for full sorting}
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation and Ranking Cost after Vertex Enumeration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplicial chord cuts for pruning regions in concave minimization.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a simplex \(S=\operatorname{conv}\{v^0,\ldots,v^n\}\), write \(x=\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_i(x)v^i\) and define
\[
\ell_S(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_i(x)f(v^i).
\]
Concavity gives \(\ell_S(x)\le f(x)\) on \(S\). Compute \(L_S=\min_{x\in S}\ell_S(x)\). If \(L_S\ge U\), cut off \(S\); otherwise evaluate selected feasible points, update \(U\), and subdivide \(S\). Stop when no active simplex remains or every active bound satisfies \(U-L_S\le\varepsilon\); output the incumbent and its certified gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use affine chords beneath a concave objective to bound each simplex, prune simplices that cannot improve the incumbent, and subdivide the rest.
knowledge_statements.title: Concavity-Cut Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize an active relaxation covering the feasible set and an incumbent value \(U\). For each active region \(R\), compute a valid bound
\[
L_R\le\inf\{f(x):x\in R\cap C\}.
\]
Discard \(R\) when \(L_R\ge U\). Otherwise, evaluate a candidate; if it is feasible, update \(U\), and if it is infeasible, add a valid inequality whose halfspace contains \(C\). Apply an objective-derived concavity cut or subdivide the remaining region, then repeat. Stop when all regions are discarded or \(U-\min_R L_R\le\varepsilon\), and output the incumbent with this gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined cut methods alternate valid feasibility cuts with concavity-based objective bounds, pruning or subdividing regions until the global optimality gap is small enough.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined Cut Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite cone covers with regional lower bounds and refinement.

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Cone Covering Approaches p. 88

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cover \(C\) by active regions \(R_j=C\cap K(a_j;D_j)\), where
\[
K(a;D)=\{a+D\lambda:\lambda\ge0\}.
\]
For each nonempty \(R_j\), compute a valid bound \(L_j\le\inf_{x\in R_j}f(x)\). Discard \(R_j\) if \(L_j\ge U\); otherwise evaluate a feasible candidate, update \(U\), and replace \(K(a_j;D_j)\) by finitely many narrower cones covering its unresolved portion. Stop when no cone remains or \(U-\min_jL_j\le\varepsilon\). Output the incumbent and the terminal bound gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover the feasible set by cones, bound the objective on each cone, discard nonimproving cones, and refine unresolved cones until the target gap is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Covering Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(P_0\supseteq C\), a feasible incumbent \(\bar x\in C\), and \(U_0=f(\bar x)\). At iteration \(k\), choose
\[
v_k\in\arg\min\{f(v):v\in\operatorname{ext}(P_k)\},\qquad L_k=f(v_k).
\]
If \(v_k\in C\), update the incumbent and stop globally. Otherwise obtain \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_k\), valid for every \(x\in C\) but violated by \(v_k\), and set
\[
P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{x:a_k^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_k\}.
\]
Stop when \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\), returning the incumbent and gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize at vertices of a polyhedral outer approximation, separate infeasible trial vertices from the convex feasible set, and stop when lower and upper bounds meet.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Approximation for Concave Minimization

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Outer-Approximation Bound Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value convergence when nested compact outer approximations converge to the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\supseteq P_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq C\) be nonempty compact sets contained in a common compact set, let \(d_H(P_k,C)\to0\), and let \(f\) be continuous on that common compact set. If \(L_k=\min_{x\in P_k}f(x)\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\), then \(L_k\uparrow f^*\). If feasible incumbent values satisfy \(U_k\downarrow f^*\), then \(U_k-L_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested compact outer approximations converging in Hausdorff distance yield lower bounds converging to the true minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq P_{k+1}\subseteq P_k\), with all sets in a common compact set.
\(f\) is continuous on the common compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\uparrow f^*\), and \(U_k-L_k\to0\) whenever \(U_k\downarrow f^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff-Consistent Outer-Approximation Convergence
Polyhedral Annexation for Concave Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic polyhedral-annexation scheme for minimizing a concave function over a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a compact polytope \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), a concave function \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial polytope \(Q_0\subseteq P\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), set \(U_0=+\infty\). At iteration \(k\), minimize \(f\) over the vertices of \(Q_k\), update \(U_k\) with the best feasible value found, and obtain a valid lower bound \(L_k\leq\min_{x\in P}f(x)\) for the unexplored region. If \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\), return the incumbent. Otherwise annex a polyhedral region containing a selected unexplored candidate, producing \(Q_{k+1}\supsetneq Q_k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successively enlarge an explored polytope, evaluate its vertices, maintain a valid unexplored-region bound, and stop when the incumbent–bound gap is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(f\) is concave and finite on \(P\).
Each annexation and lower-bound computation is valid for the remaining region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) certifies an \(\varepsilon\)-global minimizer.

notation.meaning: polyhedral region annexed through iteration k
valid global lower bound at iteration k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexhaustive Annexation Can Preserve a Positive Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convergence when nested annexed polytopes omit a neighborhood of the optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=x\), and \(Q_k=[\tfrac12+\tfrac1{k+3},1]\). Then \(Q_k\subsetneq Q_{k+1}\subset P\), and exact vertex minimization over \(Q_k\) gives \(U_k=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{k+3}\to\tfrac12\). Since the residual set contains \(0\), the value \(b_k=0\) is a valid residual lower bound. Thus the certified global lower bound \(\underline L_k=\min\{U_k,b_k\}=0\) and \(U_k-\underline L_k\to\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict enlargement alone is insufficient when the annexed union omits the optimizer's neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}(U_k-\underline L_k)=\tfrac12>0.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound for the residual set.
Global bound obtained by combining the explored and residual regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexhaustive Annexation Can Preserve a Positive Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient exhaustion and residual-bound consistency conditions for the accepted annexation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a compact polytope, \(f:P\to\mathbb R\) continuous and concave, and \(Q_k\subseteq Q_{k+1}\subseteq P\) nonempty compact polytopes. Let \(U_k=\min_{x\in Q_k}f(x)\), obtained by evaluating the vertices of \(Q_k\). Let \(b_k\le\inf_{x\in P\setminus Q_k}f(x)\) when the residual is nonempty, set \(b_k=+\infty\) otherwise, and define \(\underline L_k=\min\{U_k,b_k\}\). If the Hausdorff distance from \(Q_k\) to \(P\) tends to zero and \(\liminf_k b_k\ge f^*=\min_P f\), then \(U_k\to f^*\), \(\underline L_k\to f^*\), and \(U_k-\underline L_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hausdorff exhaustion and consistent residual bounds make the annexation certificate gap converge to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(f\) is continuous and concave on \(P\).
The nested annexed polytopes converge to \(P\) in Hausdorff distance.
Residual lower bounds are valid and have limit inferior at least \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_k\to f^*,\qquad \underline L_k\to f^*,\qquad U_k-\underline L_k\to0.

notation.meaning: Lower bound for the residual region.
Valid global lower bound combining explored and residual regions.

Successive Underestimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bounding scheme using increasingly accurate underestimators of a concave objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact, let \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave, define \(f^*=\min_{x\in P}f(x)\), and fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Choose functions \(g_k:P\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(g_k(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in P\), and compute \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}g_k(x)\) with \(L_k=g_k(x_k)\). Evaluate \(f(x_k)\) and set \(U_k=\min_{0\leq j\leq k}f(x_j)\). If \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\), return an incumbent attaining \(U_k\); otherwise choose \(g_{k+1}\geq g_k\) that remains a global underestimator and is exact at the selected evaluated points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize nested global lower models, evaluate their minimizers in the true objective, and refine until the incumbent–lower-bound gap meets the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f\) is finite and concave on \(P\).
Each lower-model problem attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every iteration, \(L_k\leq f^*\leq U_k\); hence \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) certifies that the returned incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplicial branch-and-bound using affine vertex interpolants as concave-objective lower models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition a compact polytope \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) into simplices. For a simplex \(S=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_n\}\), define its affine interpolant by \(\ell_S(\sum_i\lambda_i v_i)=\sum_i\lambda_i f(v_i)\), where \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). Concavity gives \(\ell_S(x)\leq f(x)\) on \(S\), so \(L(S)=\min_i f(v_i)\) is a node lower bound. Select a live simplex, subdivide it simplicially, evaluate new vertices, update the incumbent, and fathom any child whose bound is no smaller than the incumbent minus \(\varepsilon\).

\(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and concave.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Successive Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangle-based spatial branching with valid regional lower bounds for concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0=[l,u]\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty compact box, let \(f:R_0\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and concave, define \(f^*=\min_{x\in R_0}f(x)\), and fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Maintain a collection of live boxes. For every live box \(R\), compute a valid bound \(L(R)\leq\min_{x\in R}f(x)\) and a feasible point \(z_R\in R\), and update the incumbent value \(U\) using \(f(z_R)\). Select a live box with smallest bound, choose \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(s\in(l_j,u_j)\), and replace the box by the two children defined by \(x_j\leq s\) and \(x_j\geq s\). Discard every box satisfying \(L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split live boxes, compute valid regional lower bounds and feasible values, and discard boxes that cannot improve the incumbent by more than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(R_0\) is a nonempty compact box.
\(f:R_0\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and concave.
The regional bounding rule is valid on every generated box, and the children cover their parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)<U-\varepsilon\) remains in a live box; therefore an empty live set implies \(U-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Branching Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive, best-bound, and depth-first node-selection regimes within spatial branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a finite live-node set \(\mathcal{L}_k\), where each node \(N\) represents a compact region \(R_N\) and has a valid lower bound \(L_N\). A branching regime selects either all eligible nodes, a best-bound node \(N_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{N\in\mathcal{L}_k}L_N\), or a deepest live node. It replaces each selected node by finitely many children whose regions cover \(R_N\), removes fathomed children, and retains all others. Ties are resolved by a fixed deterministic rule; the incumbent is updated whenever a feasible point with smaller objective value is found.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Fathoming Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe node-deletion predicates for deterministic concave-minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let node \(N\) represent \(R_N\), let \(L_N\leq\min_{x\in R_N}f(x)\), let \(U\) be the value of a feasible incumbent, and fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\). It may also be fathomed when a feasible point \(z_N\in R_N\) satisfies \(f(z_N)=L_N\), provided the incumbent is first updated to \(U\leftarrow\min\{U,f(z_N)\}\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), the bound test is \(L_N\geq U\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage and size invariants for finitely branching spatial search trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the root represent a feasible region \(P\) with objective \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(U\) be a feasible incumbent value, fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and let \(b\geq1\) be an integer. knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave-cost representation of nonnegative activities carrying activation charges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(x_i\in[0,u_i]\), \(u_i>0\), \(F_i\geq0\), and \(c_i\geq0\), and define \(\phi_i(0)=0\) and \(\phi_i(x_i)=F_i+c_i x_i\) for \(x_i>0\). Each \(\phi_i\) is concave on \([0,u_i]\), possibly with an upward jump to its right at zero. The fixed-charge problem is \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i):x\in X\}\), where \(X\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^m[0,u_i]\). An activated formulation introduces \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), imposes \(0\leq x_i\leq u_i y_i\), and minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^m(F_i y_i+c_i x_i)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Economies-of-Scale Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous activity costs whose marginal or average cost decreases with scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and let \(u_i>0\). An economies-of-scale minimization model has the form \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i):x\in X,\ 0\leq x_i\leq u_i\}\), where each \(\phi_i:[0,u_i]\to\mathbb{R}\) is nondecreasing and concave. If \(\phi_i(0)=0\), concavity implies that the average cost \(\phi_i(t)/t\) is nonincreasing for \(t>0\). When differentiable, concavity equivalently makes the marginal cost \(\phi_i'(t)\) nonincreasing. Minimizing these concave costs over a convex feasible region is generally a nonconvex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Economies of scale are modeled by nondecreasing concave activity costs, yielding decreasing average cost and, when differentiable, decreasing marginal cost.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
Each \(\phi_i\) is finite, nondecreasing, and concave on \([0,u_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\phi_i(0)=0\), then \(0<s<t\leq u_i\) implies \(\phi_i(s)/s\geq\phi_i(t)/t\).
