knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Hybrid Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar convexification of a fixed charge plus concave operating cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(x)=F+g(x)\) for \(0<x\leq u\), where \(F\geq0\), \(u>0\), and \(g:[0,u]\to\mathbb R_+\) is finite and concave with \(g(0)=0\). Then \[\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=\frac{F+g(u)}{u}x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a capacitated fixed-charge scale-economy cost is its endpoint chord.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is finite, nonnegative, and concave on \([0,u]\), with \(g(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=x(F+g(u))/u\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Hybrid Cost

children.title: Multiplicative Model Reductions
children.top_down_role: Direct concave reductions for multiplicative model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Model Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive finite products reduced by a monotone logarithmic transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) and \(L(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\log f_i(x)\). Positivity makes both objectives finite, and \(L(x)=\log F(x)\). Hence \(F(x)\leq F(y)\) if and only if \(L(x)\leq L(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\). Moreover, each \(\log f_i\) is concave, so \(L\) is concave. Thus minimizing the multiplicative model over \(C\) is exactly reducible to concave minimization of \(L\), with identical global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive product of concave factors on a convex feasible set has the same minimizers as the concave sum of their logarithms.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(m\geq1\).
\(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each \(f_i:C\to(0,\infty)\) is concave for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m\log f_i(x)\)

source_refs.locator: Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms p. 43

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain boundary for an exact finite real logarithmic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite real-valued identity \(\log\prod_i f_i=\sum_i\log f_i\) requires \(f_i(x)>0\) for every included factor and feasible \(x\). If a factor can vanish, the logarithmic objective takes the extended value \(-\infty\); if a factor can be negative, the real logarithmic formulation is undefined and need not preserve product ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict positivity is essential for the stated finite log-sum reduction; zeros require extended values, and negative factors invalidate it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated finite real logarithmic reduction requires every included factor to be strictly positive throughout the feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Boundary of Log Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive weighted-product variant of logarithmic reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i\geq0\), not all zero, and let \(f_i:C\to(0,\infty)\). Then \[F_a(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)^{a_i},\qquad L_a(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\log f_i(x)=\log F_a(x)\] have identical orderings and global minimizers. If \(C\) is convex and every \(f_i\) with \(a_i>0\) is concave, then \(L_a\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive weighted product reduces exactly to a weighted sum of logarithms, which is concave for nonnegative weights and positive concave factors.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i a_i>0\).
Each factor is strictly positive.
For the curvature conclusion, \(C\) is convex and each positively weighted factor is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_C F_a=\operatorname*{argmin}_C L_a\), and \(L_a\) is concave under the curvature assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Multiplicative Reduction

children.title: Min–Max Model Reductions
children.top_down_role: Direct concave reductions for models organized by maximum operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Min–Max Model Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex min–max models represented by a scalar epigraph variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(E=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:f_i(x)\leq t\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For every fixed \(x\in C\), the smallest feasible value of \(t\) is \(\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\). Consequently, \(x^\star\) minimizes \(\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\) over \(C\) if and only if \((x^\star,t^\star)\) minimizes \(t\) over \(E\), where \(t^\star=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x^\star)\). The set \(E\) is convex, and the lifted objective \(t\) is affine, hence both convex and concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous convex min–max problem is exactly represented by minimizing an epigraph variable subject to all component bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(m\geq1\).
\(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each \(f_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\min\{t:(x,t)\in E\}\)

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Min-Max Problems p. 66

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Min-Max Problems p. 66

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise simplex representation underlying a finite min–max objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i z_i,\qquad \Delta_m=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_i\lambda_i=1\}.\] Consequently, \(\min_{x\in C}\max_i f_i(x)=\min_{x\in C}\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)\), without implying interchange of the two optimization operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum equals maximization of a convex combination over the probability simplex, but this identity alone does not permit swapping min and max.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq1\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i z_i=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\lambda^Tz\).
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum

children.title: Multiplicative Min–Max Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Reduction interfaces for models containing both multiplicative and extremal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Min–Max Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products of positive pointwise maxima expanded into a min–max family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define \(H(x)=\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}f_{ji}(x)\) and \(\mathcal A=\prod_{j=1}^p I_j\). Because all factors are positive and each index set is finite and nonempty, selections can be made independently in each factor. Therefore \(H(x)=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A}\prod_{j=1}^p f_{j,\alpha_j}(x)\). The original multiplicative problem is consequently equivalent to a finite min–max problem indexed by \(\mathcal A\). Their optimal values coincide, and they have the same global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product of positive finite maxima equals the maximum over all products obtained by selecting one term from each factor.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(p\geq1\).
\(C\) is nonempty and compact.
Every \(f_{ji}:C\to(0,\infty)\), with \(j=1,\ldots,p\) and \(i\in I_j\), is continuous.
Each index set \(I_j\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}f_{ji}(x)=\min_{x\in C}\max_{\alpha\in\prod_{j=1}^p I_j}\prod_{j=1}^p f_{j,\alpha_j}(x)\)

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Min-Max Problems p. 66

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Min-Max Problems p. 66

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial size of the selection family produced by hybrid expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite nonempty index sets \(I_1,\ldots,I_p\), the selection set \(\mathcal A=\prod_{j=1}^p I_j\) has cardinality \[|\mathcal A|=\prod_{j=1}^p|I_j|.\] Thus explicit enumeration can be exponential in \(p\), even when the product-of-maxima expression is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding a product of finite maxima creates the product of the component family sizes and can be exponentially larger than the compact expression.
assumptions_latex: Each \(I_j\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal A|=\prod_j|I_j|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Expansion Size

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed-Factor Failure of Independent Maximum Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for distributing products over independent maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonnegativity of all candidate factors is sufficient for \[\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}a_{ji}=\max_{\alpha\in\prod_jI_j}\prod_{j=1}^pa_{j,\alpha_j}.\] Without this sign condition the identity can fail: if each of two factors has candidates \(\{-2,-1\}\), the product of the two maxima is \(1\), whereas the maximum selectable product is \(4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent maximum selection distributes through products of nonnegative factors but can fail for signed factors.
assumptions_latex: The index sets are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Signed factors do not in general satisfy the product-of-maxima expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Factor Failure of Independent Maximum Selection

notation.meaning: Vector of variables required to be binary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous representation of binary restrictions by one concave inequality.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\phi(y)=\sum_{j=1}^q y_j(1-y_j)\) on \([0,1]^q\). Every summand is nonnegative on this box and vanishes exactly when \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). Hence \(y\) is binary if and only if \(\phi(y)=0\), equivalently \(\phi(y)\leq0\). Since \(\phi\) is concave, binary restrictions in a mixed-integer model can be replaced exactly by box constraints and one reverse-convex inequality. The resulting continuous formulation preserves precisely the feasible points and objective values of the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary restrictions equal box constraints plus one concave inequality forcing the sum of fractionalness terms to vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Programming Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-Box Requirement for the Fractionalness Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the concave integrality inequality when its box restrictions are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar value \(y=2\), one has \(y(1-y)=-2\le0\), yet \(y\notin\{0,1\}\). Hence \(y(1-y)\le0\) enforces binarity only when combined with \(0\le y\le1\); the same failure applies componentwise to the aggregate inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the unit-box constraints, the fractionalness inequality admits nonbinary values such as two.
assumptions_latex: The restriction \(0\le y\le1\) is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y(1-y)\le0\not\Rightarrow y\in\{0,1\}
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Box Requirement for the Fractionalness Inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extension of the binary reduction route to finitely bounded integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\mathbb Z\) satisfy \(\ell\le z\le u\), where \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z\), and set \(m=\lceil\log_2(u-\ell+1)\rceil\). The restriction is represented exactly by \(z=\ell+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^ky_k\), \(z\le u\), and \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\). Replacing the binary restrictions by \(0\le y\le1\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y_k(1-y_k)\le0\) gives an exact continuous reverse-convex formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely bounded integer variable can be binary encoded and represented exactly by box constraints and one concave integrality inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z\) with \(\ell\le u\).
\(z\) is required to be integer with \(\ell\le z\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\mathbb Z\cap[\ell,u]\iff\exists y\in[0,1]^m:\ z=\ell+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^ky_k,\ z\le u,\ \sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y_k(1-y_k)\le0
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Binary Expansion Reduction

children.title: Bilinear Reduction Routes
children.top_down_role: Indirect concave-minimization routes based on bilinear reformulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: McCormick Residual Bound on a Rectangle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local consistency bound for bounded bilinear spatial refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and let \((x,y,w)\) satisfy the four McCormick inequalities for \(w=xy\) on this rectangle. Then \[|w-xy|\leq\frac{(u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)}4.\] Consequently, the maximum residual tends to zero along rectangles whose width product tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point in a McCormick relaxation has bilinear residual at most one quarter of the product of the interval widths.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x\leq x\leq u_x\) and \(\ell_y\leq y\leq u_y\).
\((x,y,w)\) satisfies all four McCormick inequalities on that rectangle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|w-xy|\leq (u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\).
knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Residual Bound on a Rectangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spatial Branch-and-Bound for Bounded Bilinear Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick spatial-search route for a bounded model whose exposed nonconvexities are lifted bilinear equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a compact model with lifted relations \(w_q=x_{i_q}x_{j_q}\), with the remaining node formulation convex. A node \(B\) is a product box for the participating variables. Its relaxation replaces every product graph by its four McCormick inequalities on \(B\). Maintain live boxes, a verified feasible incumbent \(U\), and valid lower bounds \(L(B)\). Select a live box; fathom it if its relaxation is infeasible or \(L(B)\ge U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise update \(U\) using any verified feasible point and bisect a factor interval of a product having nonzero relaxation residual, installing two covering children with recomputed envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on bounded product factors, solve McCormick node relaxations, update only with genuinely feasible points, and prune only by infeasibility or certified bounds.
assumptions_latex: All factors in lifted bilinear terms have finite node bounds.
The non-product part of every node relaxation is convex and valid.
Every child pair covers its parent box.
Every node lower bound is valid for the original restricted model.
Every incumbent is feasible for the original bilinear model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No fathoming step removes a feasible point with objective value less than \(U-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Current box for variables participating in bilinear products.
Valid lower bound for node B.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Branch-and-Bound for Bounded Bilinear Lifts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined global-bound and local product-consistency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a verified feasible incumbent and \(\underline L=\min_{B\in\mathcal L}L(B)\), with \(\underline L=U\) if no live node remains. If the live boxes cover all unfathomed feasible points and \(U-\underline L\le\varepsilon\), then the incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-global. On a live rectangle for product \(w_q=x_{i_q}x_{j_q}\), widths \(\Delta_{i_q},\Delta_{j_q}\) additionally certify \(|w_q-x_{i_q}x_{j_q}|\le\Delta_{i_q}\Delta_{j_q}/4\) throughout its McCormick relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and minimum live-node bound certify global tolerance; rectangle widths separately certify bilinear residual tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is attained by a point feasible for the original model.
All live-node bounds are valid.
Live nodes cover all feasible points not already safely fathomed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U-f^*\le\varepsilon,\qquad |w_q-x_{i_q}x_{j_q}|\le\Delta_{i_q}\Delta_{j_q}/4\text{ on each live node}.

notation.meaning: Minimum valid lower bound over live nodes.
Current factor-interval widths for product q.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Spatial Termination Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Term Residual Depth Under Factor Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local branch-depth bound for one bilinear product, not a global search-tree bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial rectangle for \(w=xy\) have widths \(\Delta_x,\Delta_y\). If every descendant step bisects one factor interval, then after \(t\) such steps on a branch the width product is \(\Delta_x\Delta_y2^{-t}\), and every McCormick-feasible point satisfies \(|w-xy|\le\Delta_x\Delta_y/(4\,2^t)\). Hence tolerance \(\eta>0\) is guaranteed once \(t\ge\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(\Delta_x\Delta_y/(4\eta))\rceil\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each factor bisection halves the scalar McCormick residual bound, giving logarithmic branch depth for a prescribed product tolerance.
assumptions_latex: One lifted product is refined at every counted descendant step.
Each counted step bisects exactly one factor interval.
McCormick inequalities are recomputed on every child.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\ge\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\log_2\frac{\Delta_x\Delta_y}{4\eta}\right\rceil\right\}\Longrightarrow |w-xy|\le\eta.

notation.meaning: Number of counted factor bisections along the branch.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Term Residual Depth Under Factor Bisection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convergence of Fair Bilinear Spatial Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract convergence theorem for the specified bounded spatial route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Apply the spatial scheme to a feasible compact model with continuous data and finite optimum. Assume live boxes always cover the unfathomed feasible set; every live box capable of attaining the smallest persistent lower bound is selected fairly; every infinite selected branch shrinks all participating factor intervals to zero; and node lower bounds are consistent, meaning that along a nested branch converging to \(x\), \(\liminf_kL(B_k)\ge f(x)\) whenever \(x\) is feasible. Assume also that refinement along boxes containing a global minimizer produces verified feasible incumbents whose values approach that minimizer's value. Then \(U_k-\underline L_k\to0\), where \(\underline L_k\) is the minimum live-node bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair shrinking refinement, locally consistent bounds, and asymptotically complete feasible recovery make the certified global gap vanish.
assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is nonempty and compact and has finite optimum.
Live boxes cover every unfathomed feasible point.
Promising boxes are selected fairly and every infinite selected branch localizes.
Node lower bounds are consistent under localization.
Feasible recovery is asymptotically complete along boxes containing a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_k-\underline L_k\to0.

notation.meaning: Minimum valid lower bound over live nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Convergence of Fair Bilinear Spatial Refinement

assumptions_latex: Finite bounds \(\ell_x\leq x\leq u_x\) and \(\ell_y\leq y\leq u_y\) are known.
A bilinear relation \(w=xy\) occurs in the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{k\geq0}R_k=\{(x,y,w):w=xy\}\) when the nested partition diameters tend to zero

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce \(w\) for \(xy\). Initialize with the four McCormick inequalities on \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\). Solve the resulting convex relaxation, choose a box containing a nonzero residual \(|w-xy|\), and bisect one of its variable intervals. Recompute the McCormick inequalities on each child box and repeat. A node may stop when it is infeasible, dominated by an incumbent, or satisfies a prescribed residual and optimality tolerance. The output is the best feasible incumbent; under exhaustive nested refinement with box diameters tending to zero, the relaxations converge to the bilinear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded bilinear terms admit McCormick relaxations that converge to the exact graph under exhaustive spatial partitioning.

children.title: DC Reduction Routes
children.top_down_role: Indirect concave-minimization routes based on DC reformulations.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Reduction Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph lifting of a DC objective into concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:g(x)\leq t\leq U\}\). This set is compact and convex. The lifted objective \(t-h(x)\) is concave because it is affine in \(t\) and \(-h\) is concave. For any fixed \(x\), minimization over feasible \(t\) selects \(t=g(x)\). Therefore the DC problem \(\min_{x\in C}\{g(x)-h(x)\}\) and the concave-minimization problem \(\min_{(x,t)\in E}\{t-h(x)\}\) have equal optimal values, and their optimal solutions correspond under projection onto \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph lifting converts a continuous DC objective into an equivalent concave objective over a compact convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(g,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuous and convex.
\(U\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(U\geq\max_{x\in C}g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}(g(x)-h(x))=\min_{(x,t)\in E}(t-h(x))\)

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Lift Boundary for the DC Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes value equivalence from the compact convex formulation required by the stated concave-minimization route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E_U=\{(x,t):x\in C,\ g(x)\le t\le U\}\), every \(x\in C\) has a lifted representative if and only if \(U\ge\sup_{x\in C}g(x)\). If no finite such \(U\) exists, this construction cannot produce a compact lifted feasible set. Omitting \(t\le U\) preserves \(\inf_{x\in C}(g(x)-h(x))\) through minimization over \(t\), but the resulting epigraph is generally noncompact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite uniform upper bound on the first convex component is necessary for this route to produce a compact lift, although the untruncated epigraph still preserves the infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex.
\(g,h:C\to\mathbb R\) are finite-valued and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall x\in C)(\exists t:(x,t)\in E_U)\iff U\ge\sup_{x\in C}g(x)
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Lift Boundary for the DC Epigraph Route

children.top_down_role: Structural interfaces linking bilinear reformulations to DC model forms.

assumptions_latex: \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar bilinear decomposition into two convex quadratics.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190
2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g(x,y)=\frac14(x+y)^2\) and \(h(x,y)=\frac14(x-y)^2\). Both \(g\) and \(h\) are convex quadratic functions on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and direct expansion yields \(xy=g(x,y)-h(x,y)\). Thus every scalar bilinear term has an exact difference-of-convex representation. For vectors, a finite sum of bilinear terms is represented by summing these component decompositions, with coefficient signs absorbed by interchanging the two convex components when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bilinear term is exactly the difference of two convex quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear-to-DC Interfaces

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq a\perp b\geq0\iff\sum_{j=1}^q a_jb_j=0\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative complementarity represented by one bilinear equality.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative vectors, each product \(a_jb_j\) is nonnegative. Consequently, the componentwise conditions \(a_jb_j=0\) for all \(j\) are equivalent to the single equality \(\psi(a,b)=\sum_{j=1}^q a_jb_j=0\). Equivalently, since \(\psi(a,b)\geq0\), they may be imposed by \(\psi(a,b)\leq0\). This reduction replaces a complementarity system by a bilinear nonconvex constraint without changing its feasible set; bounded instances may subsequently be treated through bilinear relaxations or DC decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under nonnegativity, componentwise complementarity is equivalent to one equality setting the sum of all pairwise products to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegativity Is Essential for Aggregate Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp cancellation failure for the aggregate-product equality when signed components are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,-1)\). Then \(\sum_{j=1}^2a_jb_j=0\), although \(a_1b_1=1\ne0\) and \(a_2b_2=-1\ne0\). Thus the aggregate equality does not imply componentwise zero products without termwise nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed product terms can cancel, so a zero aggregate sum need not enforce componentwise complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in\mathbb R^2\) are not restricted to the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j=1}^2a_jb_j=0\not\Rightarrow (\forall j)\ a_jb_j=0
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegativity Is Essential for Aggregate Complementarity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ball \(B_d\) is compact and convex, and every point of its boundary sphere \(S^{d-1}=\{x:\|x\|_2=1\}\) is extreme; no interior point is extreme. Hence \(\operatorname{ext}(B_d)=S^{d-1}\), an uncountable set. Although \(f\) has a global minimizer at an extreme point, the polyhedral strategy of listing all vertices has no finite analogue on \(B_d\). The extreme-point optimality principle therefore remains valid, while exhaustive finite enumeration fails when polyhedrality is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean ball has uncountably many extreme points, so the extreme-point principle does not yield a finite enumeration method.

knowledge_statements.title: General Concave-Minimization Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-hardness through concave quadratic minimization over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(L\succeq0\), the quadratic function \(q(x)=-x^\mathsf{T}Lx\) is concave. Its minimum over \([-1,1]^{|V|}\) is attained at a vertex \(s\in\{-1,1\}^{|V|}\). For such a sign vector, \(\frac14s^\mathsf{T}Ls\) equals the weight of the cut encoded by \(s\). Therefore \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}q(x)=-4\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)\). Computing the global minimum of a concave quadratic over a box is consequently NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted MAX-CUT reduces exactly to minimizing a concave quadratic over a box, establishing NP-hardness of this restricted concave-minimization family.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is an undirected graph with nonnegative rational edge weights.
\(L\) is the weighted Laplacian of \(G\), using the convention \(x^\mathsf{T}Lx=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}-x^\mathsf{T}Lx=-4\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single reverse-convex constraint model is an optimization problem of the form \(\min\{f(x):x\in C,\ g(x)\geq0\}\), where \(C\) is convex and \(g\) is convex. Its feasible set is \(F=C\cap\{x:g(x)\geq0\}=C\setminus\{x:g(x)<0\}\). The excluded strict sublevel set \(\{x\in C:g(x)<0\}\) is convex, whereas its complement in \(C\) need not be convex. The adjective “single” refers to the presence of exactly one such convex exclusion function, irrespective of the number of inequalities used to describe \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single reverse-convex model optimizes over a convex base set after excluding one convex strict sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Single Reverse-Convex Constraint Models

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\), where \(C_i=\{x\in P:g_i(x)<0\}\).

notation.meaning: convex exclusion induced by the ith constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional models with at least two convex exclusion functions on a convex base region.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multiple reverse-convex constraint model has feasible set
\[
F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
For each \(i\), define the convex exclusion
\[
C_i=\{x\in P:g_i(x)<0\}.
\]
The model equivalently retains the points of \(P\) outside every exclusion:
\[
F=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C_i)=P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple reverse-convex model retains the points of a convex base region that satisfy every convex inequality in the reverse direction, equivalently excluding a finite union of convex strict sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Reverse-Convex Constraint Models

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(q\geq1\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^q\).
For \(j=1,\ldots,q\), \(a_j^\top\) denotes the \(j\)-th row of \(A\), and inequalities involving \(Ax\) and \(b\) are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus C=P\cap\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}\), where \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax<b\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open polyhedral exclusions represented by finitely many strict affine inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x<b_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,q\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P\setminus C=P\cap\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\},
\]
so membership outside the exclusion is certified by the failure of at least one strict defining inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of an open polyhedron is a finite union of closed halfspaces, so a point lies outside the exclusion exactly when at least one strict defining inequality fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Convex Exclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary convention for polyhedral exclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_{\rm cl}=\{x:a_j^\top x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\), then \[\mathbb R^n\setminus C_{\rm cl}=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x:a_j^\top x>b_j\}.\] Thus replacing strict defining inequalities by non-strict inequalities changes the complementary branches from closed to open halfspaces and changes boundary feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed polyhedral exclusion has open complementary branches; the closed-halfspace complement formula for an open exclusion cannot be reused unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{\rm cl}\) is defined by finitely many non-strict affine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\setminus C_{\rm cl}=\bigcup_j\{x:a_j^\top x>b_j\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Determines the Complement Branches

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent scalar representation of an open polyhedral exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x:a_j^\top x<b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\) and define \(g(x)=\max_{1\le j\le q}(a_j^\top x-b_j)\). Then \(g\) is polyhedral convex and \[C=\{x:g(x)<0\},\qquad \mathbb R^n\setminus C=\{x:g(x)\ge0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open polyhedron is the strict sublevel set of the maximum of its affine defining residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(q\ge1\) and \(a_j\in\mathbb R^n,b_j\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{g<0\}\) for \(g(x)=\max_j(a_j^\top x-b_j)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-of-Affine Defining Function

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex.
\(g:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and continuously differentiable.
\(C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is open and convex, \(\partial C\cap U\subseteq\{x\in U:g(x)=0\}\), and the gradient supplies first-order boundary geometry at zero-level points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty differentiable convex strict-sublevel exclusions in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A smooth convex exclusion is the nonempty strict sublevel set
\[
C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\},
\]
where \(g\) is convex and continuously differentiable on the open convex set \(U\). The set \(C\) is open and convex, and continuity gives
\[
\partial C\cap U\subseteq\{x\in U:g(x)=0\}.
\]
At any \(\bar x\in U\) satisfying \(g(\bar x)=0\), convexity gives
\[
g(y)\geq\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(y-\bar x)\quad\text{for every }y\in U.
\]
In particular, every \(y\in C\) satisfies \(\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(y-\bar x)<0\), which supplies affine supporting geometry for the exclusion boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex exclusion is a nonempty strict sublevel set of a continuously differentiable convex function on an open convex domain. Its boundary lies on the zero level, where the gradient supplies affine supporting geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Exclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessity of a Nonempty Strict Sublevel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nonzero supporting-gradient geometry when the exclusion is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(g\) is continuously differentiable and convex, \(g(0)=0\), and \(\nabla g(0)=0\), but \(\{x:g(x)<0\}=\varnothing\). Hence a zero-level point need not have a nonzero supporting gradient when nonemptiness of the strict sublevel is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function x squared has an empty negative sublevel and zero gradient at its zero-level point, showing why nonemptiness is essential.
assumptions_latex: The nonemptiness assumption on \(\{g<0\}\) is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(0)=0\) and \(\nabla g(0)=0\) although \(g\) is smooth and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity of a Nonempty Strict Sublevel

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex.
\(g:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex but need not be differentiable.
\(C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is open and convex, and each \(s\in\partial g(\bar x)\) satisfies \(g(y)\geq g(\bar x)+s^\top(y-\bar x)\) for every \(y\in U\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of g at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite convex exclusions whose boundary geometry is described by subgradients.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonsmooth convex exclusion is the nonempty strict sublevel set
\[
C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\}
\]
of a finite convex function \(g\) on an open convex set \(U\), without requiring differentiability. For \(\bar x\in U\), its convex subdifferential is
\[
\partial g(\bar x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:g(y)\geq g(\bar x)+s^\top(y-\bar x)\text{ for every }y\in U\}.
\]
If \(g(\bar x)=0\), then every \(s\in\partial g(\bar x)\) satisfies
\[
s^\top(y-\bar x)<0\quad\text{for every }y\in C,
\]
so the subgradients describe affine supporting directions for the exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex exclusion is a nonempty convex strict sublevel set on an open convex domain. Its first-order supporting geometry is represented by the convex subdifferential rather than a unique gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Exclusions

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(m\geq1\), and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:P\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
The reverse-convex program minimizes \(f(x)\) over \(x\in P\) subject to \(g_i(x)\geq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each reverse-convex constraint has the exact DC form \(0-g_i(x)\leq0\), while the objective has the DC form \(f(x)-0\); the feasible set and objective values are unchanged.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact difference-of-convex encoding of reverse-convex inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reverse-convex program
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in P,\ g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}
\]
has the exact difference-of-convex formulation
\[
\min\{f(x)-0:x\in P,\ 0-g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
In each displayed difference, both components are convex. The reformulation preserves objective values, feasible points, and global minimizers; it changes only the algebraic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every reverse-convex inequality with a convex left-hand side is exactly a difference-of-convex inequality, obtained by writing zero minus the convex function as at most zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical DC Reformulations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical DC Encoding Does Not Convexify
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representational rather than convexifying character of the canonical DC route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=x^2-1\), the reverse-convex constraint \(g(x)\ge0\) is exactly the canonical DC inequality \(0-g(x)\le0\), but its feasible set is \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\), which is nonconvex. Thus exact DC encoding alone neither convexifies the feasible set nor supplies a convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Writing a reverse-convex inequality in DC form preserves its nonconvex feasible set; it is an algebraic reformulation, not a convexification.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x)=x^2-1\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:0-g(x)\le0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical DC Encoding Does Not Convexify

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(m\geq2\), and \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex exclusions.
The aggregate set \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i=P\setminus C\), so the aggregate \(C\) gives an exact single convex-exclusion representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregation when the union of the specified exclusions remains convex.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a multiple-exclusion model have feasible set
\[
F=P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
If the aggregate set
\[
C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i
\]
is convex, then
\[
F=P\setminus C,
\]
which is an exact single convex-exclusion representation. Without convexity of this aggregate set, the set identity remains true, but this particular aggregate does not in general define a single convex exclusion of the same model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the union of the specified convex exclusions is itself convex, their aggregate gives an exact single-exclusion representation. Without that hypothesis, the same union still represents the removed set but generally is not one convex exclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-to-Single Exclusion Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Union of Convex Exclusions Need Not Be Convex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of direct multiple-to-single aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(C_1=(-2,0)\) and \(C_2=(0,2)\). Both exclusions are open and convex, but \(C_1\cup C_2=(-2,0)\cup(0,2)\) is not convex because it contains \(-1\) and \(1\) but not their midpoint \(0\). Hence direct aggregation does not generally remain in the single-convex-exclusion model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex exclusions can have a nonconvex union, so direct aggregation into one convex exclusion requires the convex-union hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\cup C_2\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.title: A Union of Convex Exclusions Need Not Be Convex

assumptions_latex: \(n,p,r\geq1\), \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(F\subseteq P\).
For \(j=1,\ldots,r\), \(h_j:\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x\widehat F\), where \(\widehat F=\{(x,y)\in P\times Y:h_j(x,y)\geq0\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended formulations whose projection recovers the specified original feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 8. Dual Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A projection-based reverse-convex representation of \(F\subseteq P\) is an extended set
\[
\widehat F=\{(x,y)\in P\times Y:h_j(x,y)\geq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,r\}
\]
satisfying
\[
F=\operatorname{proj}_x\widehat F=\{x\in P:\exists y\in Y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in\widehat F\}.
\]
Exactness comprises both inclusions: every lifted feasible pair projects into \(F\), and every \(x\in F\) admits at least one feasible lift \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection-based representation introduces auxiliary variables and convex functions used in reverse-convex inequalities so that projecting the lifted feasible set onto the original variables gives exactly the specified feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 8. Dual Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 181

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is polyhedral and \(C\subseteq P\) is convex.
\(Q\subseteq P\) is a polyhedron satisfying \(C\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus Q\subseteq P\setminus C\), so annexing \(Q\) yields a valid inner representation of the reverse-convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid inner representations obtained by covering an exclusion with an annexed polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 10.2 Polyhedral Annexation p. 99
8.1 Polyhedral Annexation Method p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the reverse-convex feasible region \(F=P\setminus C\), choose a polyhedral annex \(Q\) with
\[
C\subseteq Q\subseteq P.
\]
Then the residual polyhedral set
\[
F_Q=P\setminus Q
\]
is a valid inner representation because \(F_Q\subseteq F\). If \(Q=C\), the representation is exact; otherwise it deliberately removes the additional region \(Q\setminus C\). A sequence of annexes \(Q_k\supseteq C\) approaching \(C\) produces increasingly accurate residual representations when the associated set convergence is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering a convex exclusion by a polyhedron and removing that polyhedron gives a valid inner feasible region; exactness holds only when the annex equals the exclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Annexation Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2 Polyhedral Annexation p. 99
8.1 Polyhedral Annexation Method p. 181

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited local material is only a table of contents and does not establish that polyhedral annexation means covering an exclusion C by a polyhedron Q and replacing the feasible region by P\Q. Moreover, the statement incorrectly calls P\Q a polyhedral set: the relative complement of one polyhedron in another is generally a finite union of polyhedra, not a polyhedron. Because the exact annexation convention and resulting representation cannot be recovered reliably from the available source, authoritative full-text support is required.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(q\geq1\), \(a_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(b_j\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\).
\(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x<b_j\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,q\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\bigl(P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite disjunctive representation of the complement of an open polyhedral exclusion.

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the open polyhedral exclusion
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x<b_j\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,q\},
\]
define
\[
D_j=P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}.
\]
De Morgan's law gives the exact finite disjunction
\[
P\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q D_j.
\]
Thus a point is feasible precisely when it belongs to at least one branch, equivalently when at least one strict inequality defining the exclusion fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of an open polyhedral exclusion is exactly the union of branches obtained by reversing one defining strict inequality at a time.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Exclusion Representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the finite reversed-affine-branch construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), the complement of the open Euclidean unit ball \(B=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2<1\}\) is not a finite union of closed halfspaces. Otherwise, taking complements would express \(B\) as a finite intersection of open halfspaces, contrary to its nonpolyhedral curved boundary. Thus the seed's finite halfspace-disjunction formula depends essentially on polyhedral exclusion geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exterior of a Euclidean ball is not a finite union of closed halfspaces, so the finite reversed-inequality construction does not extend to curved exclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\setminus B\) is not representable as a finite union of closed halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Halfspace Disjunction Requires Polyhedrality

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and compact, and \(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, open relative to \(P\), and convex.
\(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and strictly convex.
The unique minimizer \(x^0\) of \(f\) over \(P\) belongs to \(C\), and \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer \(x^*\) of \(f\) over \(P\setminus C\) lies in \(\partial_P C\).

notation.meaning: relative boundary of C in P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary localization when the strictly convex objective's base-region minimizer is excluded.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in P\setminus C\}.
\]
Compactness and continuity ensure existence of a minimizer. If the unique minimizer \(x^0\) of \(f\) on \(P\) lies in the excluded set \(C\), then every global minimizer \(x^*\) of the reverse-convex problem satisfies
\[
x^*\in\partial_P C.
\]
Thus no reverse-convex minimizer can lie in the relative interior of \(P\setminus C\); optimality is localized to the boundary separating the excluded convex region from its feasible complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a strictly convex objective's unique minimizer lies inside one convex exclusion, every minimizer remaining after that exclusion lies on its relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Exclusion Boundary Localization

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of boundary localization when the base-region minimizer remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=(1,2]\), and \(f(x)=x^2\). The unique minimizer of \(f\) on \(P\) is \(0\notin C\), and it remains the unique minimizer on \(P\setminus C=[-2,1]\), whereas \(\partial_P C=\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the base minimizer is not excluded, it can remain optimal away from the exclusion boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=\{0\}\not\subseteq\partial_P C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexcluded Base Minimizer Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity is needed to localize every optimizer rather than guarantee a boundary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=(-1,1)\), and \(f\equiv0\), every point of \(P\setminus C\) is optimal, including points outside \(\partial_P C=\{-1,1\}\). Thus ordinary convexity does not localize every minimizer, although boundary minimizers still exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict convexity, boundary minimizers may coexist with optimal points away from the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=P\setminus C\not\subseteq\partial_P C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative openness of the exclusion ensures the retained complement is closed; dropping it can destroy attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=[-1,1]\), and \(f(x)=x^2\). The base minimizer \(0\) lies in \(C\), but \(P\setminus C=[-2,-1)\cup(1,2]\) has infimum \(1\) and no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed exclusion can leave a nonclosed feasible complement on which the localized boundary infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P\setminus C}f(x)=1\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Exclusion Attainment Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weaker convex-objective variant guaranteeing existence, but not exclusivity, of a boundary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) is compact and convex, \(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, relatively open, and convex, and a continuous convex function \(f\) has a minimizer \(x^0\in C\), then whenever \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\), the minimum of \(f\) over \(P\setminus C\) is attained at some point of \(\partial_P C\). Other minimizers may lie away from that boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a merely convex objective whose base minimizer is excluded, at least one reverse-convex minimizer lies on the exclusion boundary, although not every minimizer need do so.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact and convex.
\(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, relatively open, and convex, with \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\).
\(f:P\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and convex and has a minimizer \(x^0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f\cap\partial_P C\neq\varnothing\).

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, \(P\subseteq U\), and \(m\geq1\).
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(g_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex, and \(C_i=\{x\in U:g_i(x)<0\}\) is nonempty.
\(F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and \(\bar x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active exclusion set is \(I(\bar x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\); these are exactly the indices whose boundaries contain \(\bar x\), and their subgradients supply supporting directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local supporting geometry of nonempty exclusion boundaries active at a feasible point.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible point \(\bar x\in F\), define
\[
I(\bar x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(\bar x)=0\}.
\]
Because each \(C_i\) is nonempty and each finite convex function \(g_i\) is continuous on \(U\), these are exactly the indices satisfying
\[
\bar x\in\partial C_i.
\]
For every \(i\in I(\bar x)\) and every \(s_i\in\partial g_i(\bar x)\), convexity yields
\[
g_i(y)\geq s_i^\top(y-\bar x)\quad\text{for every }y\in U.
\]
Hence every \(y\in C_i\) satisfies \(s_i^\top(y-\bar x)<0\). The active subgradients therefore record supporting geometry for all exclusion boundaries incident at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible point, an exclusion is active when its convex defining function vanishes. For nonempty exclusions on an open convex domain, these are exactly the incident exclusion boundaries, and their subgradients provide supporting directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Active Exclusion Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood characterization showing that only active reverse-convex exclusions contribute incident boundary geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be finite convex functions on an open set \(U\), let \(F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\ \forall i\}\), and fix \(\bar x\in F\). If \(j\notin I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\), then \(g_j(\bar x)>0\). Continuity gives a neighborhood \(V_j\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(g_j(x)>0\) throughout \(V_j\). Because there are finitely many indices, there is one neighborhood \(V\) on which every inactive exclusion remains strictly satisfied. Consequently, only indices in \(I(\bar x)\) contribute exclusion boundaries incident at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every inactive reverse-convex constraint remains strictly satisfied near the point, so only active exclusions contribute incident boundary geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open.
Each \(g_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex, and there are finitely many indices.
\(\bar x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists V\ni\bar x\text{ such that }g_j(x)>0\quad\forall x\in V,\ \forall j\notin I(\bar x).

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty open convex set.
\(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\), then \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine separation certificates proving that a point lies outside an open convex exclusion.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Convex Sets p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation-based exclusion certificate for \(x\notin C\) is a pair \((a,\beta)\) satisfying
\[
a\neq0,\qquad a^\top y<\beta\text{ for every }y\in C,\qquad a^\top x\geq\beta.
\]
These inequalities place the entire open convex exclusion strictly in the halfspace
\[
\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:a^\top z<\beta\}
\]
and place \(x\) on the separating hyperplane or in the opposite closed halfspace. Consequently, the displayed data certify \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane certifies that a point is outside an open convex exclusion when every point of the exclusion lies strictly on one side while the tested point lies on the hyperplane or in the opposite closed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Based Exclusion Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Convex Sets p. 33

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex exclusions need not admit a single affine certificate for every exterior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=B((-2,0),1)\cup B((2,0),1)\) and \(x=(0,0)\). Then \(C\) is open and \(x\notin C\), but \(x\in\operatorname{conv}C\); hence no \((a,\beta)\) satisfies \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior point in the convex hull of a nonconvex exclusion may have no single affine certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin C\), but no seed-form affine certificate exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Openness Requirement for Strict Pointwise Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex but nonopen exclusion may have a missing boundary point that admits no strict-on-every-point separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(u,0):u<0\}\) and \(x=(0,0)\). The set \(C\) is convex and \(x\notin C\). Any affine functional bounded above on the upper half-plane must have zero coefficient on \(u\); it then has equality at every point \((u,0)\in C\), so no certificate with \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without openness, a missing boundary point of a convex set need not admit the certificate's strict pointwise separation.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(u,0):u<0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin C\), but no seed-form strict affine certificate exists.

Thus seed-form certificates are sound and complete for point nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a nonempty open convex exclusion has a seed-form affine separation certificate.

\(x\notin C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(v^j)<0\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), then \(P\subseteq\{x\in X:g(x)<0\}\), and hence \(P\cap\{x\in X:g(x)\geq0\}=\varnothing\). The vertex list and inequalities \(g(v^j)<0\) constitute a polyhedral exclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope is safely excluded when a convex reverse-constraint function is strictly negative at every vertex.

\(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex, and the reverse-convex constraint is \(g(x)\geq0\).

Evaluations of \(g\) can be certified.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasibility \(g(x)\geq0\), inequalities \(g(v)\leq0\) at all vertices imply only \(g(x)\leq0\) on \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\). They do not certify disjointness from \(\{g\geq0\}\). For \(P=[-1,1]\) and \(g(x)=x^2-1\), both vertices have value zero and are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonstrict vertex inequalities cannot exclude a cell from a closed reverse-convex feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\) is a polytope and \(g\) is convex.
Feasibility is defined by \(g(x)\geq0\).

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and \(F=X\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\), with every \(g_i\) convex.
A finite polyhedral partition of \(X\) and a valid lower-bounding rule for the objective are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every iteration, \(F\subseteq O_{k+1}\subseteq O_k\subseteq X\); hence minimizing a valid relaxation over \(O_k\) gives a global lower bound.

notation.meaning: current outer approximation of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested polyhedral outer approximation obtained by certified removal of infeasible cells.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Outer Approximation Method p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(O_0=X\). At iteration \(k\), partition the unresolved portion of \(O_k\) into finitely many polytopes. Whenever a cell \(P\) has a certificate that \(P\subseteq\{x:g_i(x)<0\}\) for some \(i\), set \(O_{k+1}=O_k\setminus\operatorname{int}P\); otherwise retain or refine the cell. Compute a valid objective lower bound over the retained cells and an incumbent from reverse-convex feasible points. Stop when the smallest retained lower bound is no less than the incumbent within the prescribed tolerance; return that incumbent and the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method maintains a nested polyhedral superset of the feasible set by removing only cells certified infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Outer Approximation

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Outer Approximation Method p. 174

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pointwise violation cannot replace a whole-cell infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[-2,2]\), \(F=\{x\in X:x^2-1\geq0\}\), and \(f(x)=(x-3/2)^2\). The cell \(P=[0,2]\) contains the violating sample \(x=0\), but it also contains the unique global minimizer \(x^*=3/2\in F\). Deleting \(P\) merely because the sampled point violates the reverse-convex constraint removes the global optimizer. Safe deletion therefore requires a certificate that the entire deleted cell is disjoint from \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a cell from one violating sample can remove its global optimizer; infeasibility must be certified over the whole cell.
assumptions_latex: The cell \(P=[0,2]\) is rejected solely from the violating sample \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\notin F\quad\text{but}\quad x^*=3/2\in P\cap F,\qquad f(x^*)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Pointwise Cell Deletion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Exhaustive Reverse-Convex Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convergence under exhaustive refinement, exclusion consistency, and consistent monotone regional bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact, \(F\subseteq X\) be nonempty and closed, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Suppose finite retained-cell partitions define \(F\subseteq O_{k+1}\subseteq O_k\subseteq X\); only cells certified disjoint from \(F\) are deleted; every competitive infinite nested cell chain has diameter tending to zero and a limit in \(F\); and valid cell bounds are monotone under refinement and consistent, so \(P_j\downarrow\{x\}\) implies \(L(P_j)\to f(x)\). If competitive cells are processed fairly, then \(L_k:=\min_{P\in\mathcal P_k}L(P)\) increases to \(f^*:=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). For every feasible incumbent value \(U_k\), termination with \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) certifies that its incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe deletion, exhaustive vanishing-mesh refinement, exclusion consistency, and consistent monotone bounds make the global lower bound converge to the optimum; the incumbent gap is a global certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact, \(F\) is nonempty and closed, and \(f\) is continuous.
Only cells certified disjoint from \(F\) are deleted.
Every competitive retained nested chain is fairly refined to zero diameter and has its limit in \(F\).
Cell lower bounds are valid, monotone under refinement, and consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\uparrow f^*,\qquad U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U_k\leq f^*+\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: finite retained-cell partition at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell-exclusion cuts based on convexity and vertex evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select an index \(i\) and a polyhedral cell \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\) such that \(g_i(v)<0\) for every \(v\in V\). The resulting certificate gives \(P\subseteq\{x:g_i(x)<0\}\). Update the retained region by \(R\leftarrow R\setminus\operatorname{int}P\); this update preserves every point feasible for the full reverse-convex system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex cutting mechanism removes a polyhedral cell only after its vertices certify that the entire cell violates one constraint.

\(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and defines the constraint \(g_i(x)\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(R\leftarrow R\setminus\operatorname{int}P\) preserves every point satisfying all reverse-convex constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why all vertices must violate the same convex reverse constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-1,1]\), \(g_1(x)=x\), and \(g_2(x)=-x\), with feasibility requiring both functions to be nonnegative. Vertex \(-1\) violates \(g_1\), and vertex \(1\) violates \(g_2\), but \(x=0\) is feasible. Thus vertex-dependent constraint indices cannot certify deletion of the cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different violated constraints at different vertices do not certify cell infeasibility; one common constraint must be negative at every vertex.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility requires \(g_1(x)\geq0\) and \(g_2(x)\geq0\).

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an unresolved compact polytope.
A hyperplane \(H=\{x:a^\top x=\beta\}\) intersects \(P\), with \(a\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=P^-\cup P^+\), the child interiors are disjoint, and no point of \(P\) is lost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lossless hyperplane subdivision of unresolved reverse-convex search cells.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) so that both sides of \(H\) meet \(P\). Replace \(P\) by \(P^-=P\cap\{x:a^\top x\leq\beta\}\) and \(P^+=P\cap\{x:a^\top x\geq\beta\}\). Apply all exclusion and objective-bound tests independently to the children. Empty children are discarded; every nonempty child failing all fathoming tests enters the active set. The rule is lossless because \(P=P^-\cup P^+\), while refinement can make later convex-exclusion certificates decisive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unresolved polytope is split by a hyperplane into lossless child cells, which are then tested independently.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned lossless splitting with vanishing mesh under repeated midpoint longest-side selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[\ell_j,u_j]\), choose \(k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_j(u_j-\ell_j)\) and split the kth interval at its midpoint. The two closed child boxes cover \(B\), have disjoint interiors, and repeated longest-side midpoint bisection along an infinite nested branch yields diameters tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Midpoint bisection of a longest box side is lossless and produces zero-diameter refinement along every infinite branch.

Every continuing branch uses midpoint longest-side bisection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=B^-\cup B^+\), \(\operatorname{int}B^-\cap\operatorname{int}B^+=\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A splitting regime is exhaustive when every parent is replaced by finitely many closed children covering it and every infinite nested branch \(P_0\supseteq P_1\supseteq\cdots\) satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}(P_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage-preserving finite splits are exhaustive when every infinite nested branch shrinks to zero diameter.

Every split has finitely many closed children covering the parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall(P_k)\text{ generated along an infinite branch},\ \operatorname{diam}(P_k)\to0.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Split Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination invariant for alternating certified exclusion, bounding, and subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select \(P\in\mathcal A\). Discard \(P\) if a reverse-convex exclusion certificate applies or if \(L(P)\geq U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise search \(P\) for a feasible point and decrease \(U\) when one improves the incumbent. If \(P\) remains unresolved, split it into finitely many children whose union is \(P\), compute their valid lower bounds, and insert the unfathomed children into \(\mathcal A\). Stop when \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\) or \(U-\min_{Q\in\mathcal A}L(Q)\leq\varepsilon\); output the incumbent and its certified global gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut, bound, incumbent, and split operations are coordinated so that no feasible point capable of improving the incumbent beyond tolerance is lost.
assumptions_latex: The active list \(\mathcal A\) contains finitely described polyhedral cells covering every unresolved feasible point.
Every exclusion test and node lower bound used by the procedure is valid.
A feasible incumbent with finite value \(U\in\mathbb{R}\) is available, and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active cells continue to cover every feasible point capable of improving the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\), and termination certifies the prescribed absolute global optimality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible set is \([-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\), while the initial cell has vertices \(-2\) and \(2\) with \(g(-2)=g(2)=3>0\). Hence the vertex exclusion test does not remove any part of \(X\), although every point of \((-1,1)\) is infeasible. Any cut-only procedure restricted to this test stalls on the initial cell. knowledge_statements.title: Combined Primal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid primal scheme combining outer approximation, local feasible search, cutting, and branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal A\) with the compact initial region and set \(U=+\infty\). Repeatedly select a node, apply valid outer-approximation or polyhedral-exclusion cuts, search for a point feasible for the original constraints, update \(U\) from any improving feasible point, and compute valid node lower bounds. Fathom a node when it is certified infeasible or its lower bound is at least \(U-\varepsilon\); otherwise split it and insert its unfathomed children. When \(\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\), define \(L=\min_{P\in\mathcal A}L(P)\) and stop with an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal incumbent if \(U<+\infty\) and \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\). If \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\), return the incumbent as globally optimal when \(U<+\infty\), and otherwise report certified infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined primal method alternates exclusion, feasible search, bounding, and branching, returning a certified incumbent when the global gap closes or reporting infeasibility when exhaustive search finds none.
assumptions_latex: The reverse-convex problem has a compact initial region and valid exclusion, bounding, and branching procedures.
Every candidate incumbent is checked against the original constraints.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\) is the accepted absolute optimality tolerance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional convergence of hybrid exclusion, feasible-search, bounding, and branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D be compact, F\subseteq D nonempty and closed, and f continuous. Then, for an infinite execution with nonempty active sets, the least active-node bound L_k and best verified feasible value U_k satisfy L_k\to f^*, U_k\to f^*, and U_k-L_k\to0.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-function projection of a two-block reverse-convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\), let \(f:K\to\mathbb R\), and let \(h_i:K\to\mathbb R\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,r\). For each \(x\in X:=\operatorname{proj}_x K\), define \(Y(x):=\{y:(x,y)\in K,\ h_i(x,y)\geq0\text{ for every }i\}\) and \(v(x):=\inf_{y\in Y(x)}f(x,y)\), with \(v(x)=+\infty\) when \(Y(x)=\varnothing\). Then the reverse-convex problem has the exact projected representation \[\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in K,\ h_i(x,y)\geq0\ \forall i\}=\inf_{x\in X}v(x).\] If an outer minimizer and its inner minimizer exist, their pair is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating one variable block through its exact conditional value function preserves the global optimal value and reconstructs global solutions when both minima are attained.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) is nonempty.
\(h_i\) is convex on \(K\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{(x,y)\in K,\ h(x,y)\geq0}f(x,y)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{proj}_xK}v(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition by fixing a parameter block and solving conditional reverse-convex subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), let \(K(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f_\theta:K(\theta)\to\mathbb R\) and convex functions \(h_{i,\theta}:K(\theta)\to\mathbb R\) be given. Define \(F(\theta):=\{x\in K(\theta):h_{i,\theta}(x)\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r\}\) and \(v(\theta):=\inf_{x\in F(\theta)}f_\theta(x)\), using \(+\infty\) for an empty fiber. The joint problem decomposes exactly as \[\inf\{f_\theta(x):\theta\in P,\ x\in F(\theta)\}=\inf_{\theta\in P}v(\theta).\] Any attained minimizer of the right-hand side, paired with an attained fiber minimizer, solves the joint problem globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the parameter produces conditional subproblems whose value function can be minimized to recover the exact joint optimum.

\(h_{i,\theta}\) is convex in \(x\) on \(K(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cutting-plane outer approximation of a compactly restricted Lagrangian dual hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{z\in C}\{f(z):h_i(z)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}\), define \(L(z,\lambda):=f(z)-\lambda^{\mathsf T}h(z)\) and \(q(\lambda):=\inf_{z\in C}L(z,\lambda)\). Choose a compact multiplier set \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R_+^r\), an initial finite set \(Z_0\subset C\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), solve \[\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda,t}\{t:t\leq L(z,\lambda)\text{ for every }z\in Z_k\}\] to obtain \((\lambda^k,t^k)\), compute \(z^k\in\arg\min_{z\in C}L(z,\lambda^k)\), and stop when \(t^k-L(z^k,\lambda^k)\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise set \(Z_{k+1}:=Z_k\cup\{z^k\}\). The returned multiplier is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for the restricted dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master problem bounds the dual value using sampled Lagrangian cuts; an exact inner oracle adds a violated cut until the dual gap is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(\Lambda\) are nonempty and compact.
\(L\) is continuous on \(C\times\Lambda\).
The inner minimization oracle is exact.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single convex exclusion can disconnect an otherwise convex host.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the convex host be \(C=[-2,2]\), and impose the reverse-convex constraint \(g(x):=x^2-1\geq0\). Although \(g\) is convex on \(C\), the feasible set is \[F=\{x\in C:g(x)\geq0\}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2].\] Thus one reverse-convex inequality can produce two disjoint feasible components. Consequently, connectedness of the convex host does not imply connectedness of the reverse-convex feasible region, and a local search confined to one component need not inspect the other component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excluding the open interval where a convex quadratic is negative splits a convex interval into two disconnected feasible components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in C:g(x)\geq0\}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) is disconnected.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed example and its disconnected feasible set are correct, and counterexample is the appropriate knowledge kind. No citation or explicit standard-field rationale supports the record.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Exclusion Combinatorial Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit separable family realizes exponential growth in feasible components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(m\geq1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\). On the convex host \(C=[0,1]^m\), impose \(m\) reverse-convex inequalities \[g_i(x):=(x_i-1/2)^2-\delta^2\geq0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each \(g_i\) is convex, and the feasible set equals the Cartesian product \[F=\prod_{i=1}^m\bigl([0,1/2-\delta]\cup[1/2+\delta,1]\bigr).\] Hence \(F\) has exactly \(2^m\) pairwise disjoint, full-dimensional box components. Any exact component-enumeration method therefore requires at least \(2^m\) component outputs on this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent convex exclusions in each coordinate create exactly two choices per coordinate and therefore exponentially many feasible boxes.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\) and \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has exactly \(2^m\) connected components.

notation.meaning: half-width of each excluded coordinate interval

children.title: Reverse-Convex Boundary Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate geometric structure on reverse-convex solution boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp criterion for an algebraically active but geometrically vacuous reverse-convex zero level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(g:U\to\mathbb R\) be convex. If \(g(\bar x)=0\) and \(0\in\partial g(\bar x)\), then \(g(y)\geq0\) for every \(y\in U\). Hence \(\{y\in U:g(y)<0\}=\varnothing\), the reverse-convex inequality is redundant on \(U\), and \(\bar x\) is not incident to a nonempty exclusion boundary. Equivalently, if \(\{g<0\}\ne\varnothing\), then \(0\notin\partial g(x)\) at every zero-level point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero subgradient at a zero-level point forces the convex exclusion to be empty, so algebraic activity there is not genuine boundary geometry.
