children.title: Zero-Inclusive Variable Domains
children.top_down_role: Variable domains containing zero, where standard positive-domain transformations fail.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp continuity and one-sided differentiability behavior of a positive real power at a zero boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a>0\), defining \(f(0)=0\) extends \(f(x)=x^a\) continuously from \((0,u]\) to \([0,u]\). Its finite right derivative at zero exists if and only if \(a\geq1\): it equals \(1\) for \(a=1\), equals \(0\) for \(a>1\), and is unbounded for \(0<a<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive power extends continuously by zero, but has a finite right derivative at zero exactly when its exponent is at least one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in C([0,u])\), and \(f'_+(0)\) is finite iff \(a\geq1\), with values \(+\infty\) for \(0<a<1\), \(1\) for \(a=1\), and \(0\) for \(a>1\).

notation.meaning: right derivative at the zero boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Power Regularity at Zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero as an Infinite Logarithmic Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary behavior of zero under the conventional positive logarithmic chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The map \(y\mapsto x=e^y\) sends \(\mathbb R\) onto \((0,\infty)\), and \(e^y\to0\) only as \(y\to-\infty\). Consequently, for \(u>0\), \((0,u]\) maps to \(( -\infty,\log u]\), while \(x=0\) has no finite logarithmic coordinate. Representing zero therefore requires an extended coordinate, a limiting closure, or a separate model regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero corresponds only to y→−∞, so a zero-inclusive bounded interval becomes unbounded in log coordinates and its endpoint has no finite image.
assumptions_latex: The conventional transformation is \(x=e^y\) with finite \(y\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,u]\leftrightarrow(-\infty,\log u],\qquad x=0\text{ corresponds only to }y=-\infty\text{ in an extended sense}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Zero as an Infinite Logarithmic Boundary
Zero-Inclusive Variable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure or qualification of real-power signomial expressions when an original variable may equal zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a generalized monomial \(m(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_j}\), the conventional real signomial domain is \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\). If an admissible point has \(x_i=0\), then \(y_i=\log x_i\) is undefined. Moreover, \(x_i^{a_i}\) diverges as \(x_i\downarrow0\) when \(a_i<0\), the case \(a_i=0\) requires a convention at the expression \(0^0\), and for \(a_i>0\) the continuous value is \(0\), although differentiability at the boundary depends on \(a_i\). Thus a zero-inclusive domain is not automatically covered by the standard positive-domain signomial formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Including zero invalidates logarithmic coordinates; negative exponents diverge there, zero exponents require a convention, and positive exponents may still have limited boundary regularity.
assumptions_latex: A generalized monomial contains a factor \(x_i^{a_i}\).
The admissible domain contains a point with \(x_i=0\).
The exponent satisfies \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The logarithmic representation fails at \(x_i=0\), and the monomial's boundary behavior must be determined from the sign and value of \(a_i\).

notation.meaning: a variable whose domain includes zero

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: logarithmic and real-power boundary behavior

children.title: Negative Variable Domains
children.top_down_role: Variable domains restricted partly or wholly to negative values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued interpretation of a rational power on a strictly negative variable domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x<0\) and let \(a=p/q\in\mathbb Q\) be in lowest terms with \(q>0\). Under the real-root interpretation, \(x^{p/q}\) is real if and only if \(q\) is odd. When \(q\) is odd, \(x^{p/q}=(-1)^p|x|^{p/q}\). Integer exponents are therefore admissible, whereas rational exponents with even reduced denominator are not real-valued on negative bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced rational power is real on a negative base exactly when its denominator is odd.
assumptions_latex: \(a=p/q\) is in lowest terms with \(q>0\).
Powers are interpreted through real roots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{p/q}\in\mathbb R\iff q\text{ is odd};\quad x^{p/q}=(-1)^p|x|^{p/q}\text{ when }q\text{ is odd}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Exponent Admissibility on Negative Bases

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-aware logarithmic parametrization of a coordinate restricted to strictly negative values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The substitution \(x=-e^y\) is a bijection from \(\mathbb R\) to \(( -\infty,0)\). For an admissible rational exponent \(a=p/q\) with odd reduced denominator, \(x^a=(-1)^p e^{ay}\). Thus a strictly negative coordinate can use one sign-aware log-magnitude chart, but only powers satisfying the negative-base real-valuedness condition remain real in that chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly negative variable has the chart x=−exp(y); admissible rational powers become a fixed sign times exp(ay).
assumptions_latex: \(a=p/q\) is reduced and \(q\) is odd.
Powers use the real-root interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=-e^y\) bijects \(\mathbb R\) with \(( -\infty,0)\), and \(x^{p/q}=(-1)^p e^{(p/q)y}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Orthant Log-Magnitude Chart

children.title: Sign-Indefinite Variable Domains
children.top_down_role: Domains permitting variables to cross between positive and negative values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise exponential representation of nonzero sign regimes when all powers are real-valued on each selected orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(k\) coordinates may take either nonzero sign. For each sign vector \(s\in\{-1,1\}^k\), the substitutions \(x_i=s_i e^{y_i}\) bijectively parametrize the corresponding open orthant. Hence the nonzero portion of the sign-indefinite domain is covered by at most \(2^k\) orthant charts. A power expression is real on a chart only when its exponents are admissible for every negative base, and points with zero coordinates require separate boundary treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonzero part of a sign-indefinite domain can require up to 2^k sign-aware exponential charts, subject to negative-base exponent restrictions.

Sign-Indefinite Variable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domains in which one decision coordinate can take both negative and positive values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) contain feasible points \(x^-\) and \(x^+\) satisfying \(x_i^-<0<x_i^+\). No real variable \(y_i\) can make \(x_i=\exp(y_i)\) cover both values, because \(\exp(y_i)>0\) for every \(y_i\in\mathbb{R}\). At \(x_i=0\), \(\log x_i\) is undefined, and at negative values arbitrary real powers need not be real-valued. Hence a single standard signomial chart cannot cover a sign-indefinite coordinate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable that takes both negative and positive values cannot be covered by one real logarithmic chart, so the standard positive-domain signomial representation fails.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No single real logarithmic coordinate represents the full sign-indefinite domain, and the standard generalized-signomial formulation does not cover it.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Log-Domain Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finite variable bounds after logarithmic transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(y_i=\log x_i\), a sequence \(x_i^{(k)}\downarrow0\) satisfies \(y_i^{(k)}\to-\infty\), while \(x_i^{(k)}\to+\infty\) implies \(y_i^{(k)}\to+\infty\). Thus a positive domain lacking a strict lower bound \(x_i\geq\ell_i>0\) or a finite upper bound \(x_i\leq u_i<\infty\) transforms into an unbounded log-domain region. Bounding-based deterministic relaxations therefore require additional domain bounds or a separate argument establishing bounded relevant level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approaching zero or infinity in positive variables produces unbounded logarithmic coordinates, obstructing finite-box relaxations without additional bounds or bounded-level-set guarantees.

children.title: Exponential Magnitude Growth
children.top_down_role: Magnitude growth induced by exponential transformed-space representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude range of one exponential term when finite exponent bounds need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\neq\varnothing\), \(t(y)=c\exp(a^{\mathsf T}y)\), and \(c\neq0\). If \(L=\inf_{y\in Y}a^{\mathsf T}y\) and \(U=\sup_{y\in Y}a^{\mathsf T}y\) are finite, then \(\inf_{y\in Y}|t(y)|=|c|e^L\) and \(\sup_{y\in Y}|t(y)|=|c|e^U\). Hence \(\sup|t|/\inf|t|=e^{U-L}\), whether or not either bound is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite exponent infimum and supremum give the same exponential magnitude-ratio identity even when extrema are not attained.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\neq\varnothing\).
\(t(y)=c\exp(a^{\mathsf T}y)\) with \(c\neq0\).
\(L=\inf_Y a^{\mathsf T}y\) and \(U=\sup_Y a^{\mathsf T}y\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_Y|t|=|c|e^L,\quad \sup_Y|t|=|c|e^U,\quad \frac{\sup_Y|t|}{\inf_Y|t|}=e^{U-L}.\)

notation.meaning: finite infimum and supremum of the exponent

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Exponent-Range Variant
Exponential Magnitude Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude variation of one exponential term over a set on which its exponent attains finite extrema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\neq\varnothing\), let \(t(y)=c\exp(a^{\mathsf T}y)\) for \(y\in Y\), and suppose \(c\neq0\). If \(L=\min_{y\in Y}a^{\mathsf T}y\) and \(U=\max_{y\in Y}a^{\mathsf T}y\), then \(\min_{y\in Y}|t(y)|=|c|\exp(L)\) and \(\max_{y\in Y}|t(y)|=|c|\exp(U)\). Consequently, the ratio of maximum to minimum magnitude is \(\exp(U-L)\), so it grows exponentially with the exponent range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an exponential term's exponent attains minimum L and maximum U, its maximum-to-minimum magnitude ratio is exp(U-L).
assumptions_latex: The set satisfies \(Y\neq\varnothing\).
The term is \(t(y)=c\exp(a^{\mathsf T}y)\) with \(c\neq0\).
The function \(a^{\mathsf T}y\) attains the finite extrema \(L\) and \(U\) on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The term-magnitude ratio is \(\exp(U-L)\) and grows exponentially with the attained exponent range.

notation.meaning: attained minimum and maximum scalar exponents

children.title: Overflow Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter and variable regimes that exceed finite numerical range.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled evaluation and logarithmic range testing for a finite nonnegative exponential sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{k=1}^m e^{q_k}\) with finite \(q_k\), and set \(m_q=\max_k q_k\). Then \(\log S=m_q+\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^m e^{q_k-m_q}\right)\), and every inner exponential has a nonpositive argument. In exact arithmetic, if \(\Omega\) is the largest finite representable magnitude, then \(S>\Omega\) if and only if \(\log S>\log\Omega\), allowing the range test before forming \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifted log-sum-exp avoids positive inner exponential arguments and permits a logarithmic overflow test.
assumptions_latex: Every \(q_k\) is finite.
\(\Omega\) is the largest finite positive representable magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log S=m_q+\log(\sum_k e^{q_k-m_q}),\quad q_k-m_q\leq0,\quad S>\Omega\iff\log S>\log\Omega.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Overflow-Safe Log-Sum-Exp Evaluation
Overflow Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range overflow of an exponential term in finite-range arithmetic, distinguished from intermediate overflow in a particular evaluation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be the largest finite positive magnitude representable by the arithmetic, and let \(t=c\exp(z)\) with \(c\neq0\). The exact magnitude of the term exceeds the finite representable range exactly when \(|c|\exp(z)>\Omega\), equivalently when \(z>\log(\Omega/|c|)\). In this regime no finite floating-point result can represent the exact term. A naive computation that forms \(\exp(z)\) before multiplying by \(c\) may overflow even earlier, so scaled or logarithmic evaluation may also be required below this product-range threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact scaled exponential lies beyond the finite range when its magnitude exceeds the largest representable number; a naive intermediate exponential can overflow even earlier.
assumptions_latex: The arithmetic has largest finite positive magnitude \(\Omega\).
The exact term is \(t=c\exp(z)\) with \(c\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact term is outside the finite representable range if and only if \(z>\log(\Omega/|c|)\), while algorithmic intermediate overflow can occur at a lower threshold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-range threshold for the exact product

children.title: Underflow Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where transformed terms collapse below usable numerical resolution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Underflow caused by separately evaluating an exponential before applying its scale coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t=c e^z\) with \(c\neq0\), and let \(\omega\) be the smallest positive subnormal value. It is possible that \(e^z<\omega/2\) while \(|c|e^z\geq\omega/2\). Under round-to-nearest evaluation that first rounds \(e^z\), the intermediate becomes zero and multiplication by \(c\) cannot recover the nonzero exact product. Computing the log-magnitude \(\ell=\log|c|+z\) or otherwise combining the scale before rounding distinguishes this avoidable intermediate failure from underflow of the final exact product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential intermediate can round to zero even when the scaled exact product would not; log-magnitude evaluation exposes the distinction.
assumptions_latex: The arithmetic supports subnormal numbers with smallest positive subnormal value \(\omega\).
Intermediate and final values use round-to-nearest.
\(t=c e^z\) with \(c\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e^z<\omega/2\leq |c|e^z\) implies that naive separate evaluation can return zero although the exact scaled magnitude is above the stated zero-rounding threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Intermediate Underflow
Underflow Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-rounding of a positive exponential magnitude under round-to-nearest arithmetic with subnormal numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\omega>0\) be the smallest positive subnormal number representable by the arithmetic, and suppose an exact positive magnitude is rounded once using round to nearest. For \(t=c\exp(z)\) with \(c\neq0\), the computed magnitude rounds to zero whenever \(|c|\exp(z)<\omega/2\), equivalently whenever \(z<\log(\omega/(2|c|))\). Magnitudes above this zero-rounding threshold can still lie in the subnormal underflow region and incur reduced relative accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With subnormals and round-to-nearest, a scaled exponential below half the smallest positive subnormal rounds to zero; larger tiny values may remain subnormal with reduced accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The arithmetic supports subnormal numbers and has smallest positive subnormal value \(\omega\).
The exact term magnitude is rounded once using round to nearest.
The term is \(t=c\exp(z)\) with \(c\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact magnitude rounds to zero when \(z<\log(\omega/(2|c|))\), while a broader underflow region may contain nonzero subnormal results.

children.title: Numerical-Range Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous scale disparities across transformed signomial terms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaled representation for a finite signed exponential sum with reduced intermediate dynamic range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(s=\sum_{k=1}^m c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\) with \(c_k\neq0\), set \(q_k=\log|c_k|+a_k^{\mathsf T}y\), \(m_q=\max_k q_k\), and \(\sigma_k=\operatorname{sign}(c_k)\). Then \(s=e^{m_q}\sum_{k=1}^m\sigma_k e^{q_k-m_q}\), where every inner exponential lies in \((0,1]\). This avoids large positive exponential arguments inside the sum but cannot remove cancellation or make an unrepresentable final result representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring out the largest log-magnitude makes every inner exponential at most one but does not cure cancellation or final-range failure.
assumptions_latex: The sum has finitely many nonzero coefficients \(c_k\).
Every \(q_k=\log|c_k|+a_k^{\mathsf T}y\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s=e^{m_q}\sum_k\sigma_k e^{q_k-m_q},\qquad q_k-m_q\leq0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Exponent Scaling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of a nonzero signed exponential sum to componentwise relative perturbations of its terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s=\sum_{k=1}^m t_k\neq0\), where \(t_k=c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\), and define \(\kappa_{\rm sum}=\sum_k|t_k|/|s|\). If \(|\Delta t_k|\leq\varepsilon|t_k|\) for every \(k\), then \(|\Delta s|/|s|\leq\kappa_{\rm sum}\varepsilon\). Thus opposite-sign cancellation is ill-conditioned when \(|s|\ll\sum_k|t_k|\), independently of literal overflow or underflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cancellation sensitivity is measured by the sum of term magnitudes divided by the magnitude of their signed sum.
assumptions_latex: \(s=\sum_{k=1}^m t_k\neq0\).
\(t_k=c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\).
\(|\Delta t_k|\leq\varepsilon|t_k|\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{|\Delta s|}{|s|}\leq\kappa_{\rm sum}\varepsilon,\qquad \kappa_{\rm sum}=\frac{\sum_k|t_k|}{|s|}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation Condition Number

assumptions_latex: Nonzero term magnitudes at a point are \(M_k=|c_k|\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\).
At least two terms are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dynamic-range ratio is \(\exp(\max_k q_k-\min_k q_k)\), which can cause loss of smaller contributions and severe mixed-sign cancellation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative scaling among exponential terms evaluated at one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonzero terms \(t_k=c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\), define \(q_k=\log|c_k|+a_k^{\mathsf T}y\). Their magnitude ratio is \(\rho=\max_k|t_k|/\min_k|t_k|=\exp(\max_k q_k-\min_k q_k)\). A large spread in \(q_k\) can make smaller same-sign terms numerically invisible. If large terms have opposite signs, their subtraction can additionally lose significant digits even when the final signomial value is moderate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential terms have dynamic range equal to the exponential of their log-magnitude spread, amplifying omission and cancellation errors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preprocessing of a signed exponential sum before termwise relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(y)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y). For each distinct exponent vector a, set d_a=\sum_{k:a_k=a}c_k. Then F(y)=\sum_a d_a\exp(a^{\mathsf T}y) identically, and terms with d_a=0 may be removed. Aggregation therefore eliminates cancellation between identical exponential atoms before termwise relaxation, although it does not guarantee tightness for the remaining mixed-sign terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining identical exponential atoms is exact and removes their algebraic cancellation before termwise relaxation, but other mixed-sign gaps can remain.
assumptions_latex: F is a finite signed exponential sum.
Terms are aggregated only when their exponent vectors are identical.

knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation-Aware Exponent Aggregation
Weak Mixed-Sign Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termwise interval relaxations that discard exact cancellation between opposite-sign terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L>0\), consider \(f(y)=\exp(y)-\exp(y)=0\) on \(y\in[0,L]\). A termwise interval lower bound that replaces the positive term by its minimum and the subtracted term by its maximum gives \(f(y)\geq1-\exp(L)\). The exact minimum is \(0\), so the lower-bound gap equals \(\exp(L)-1\), which tends to infinity as \(L\to\infty\). Thus independent treatment of mixed-sign terms can be arbitrarily weak when it discards their shared argument and exact cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent interval bounds for opposite-sign exponential terms can have an arbitrarily large gap even when the original terms cancel exactly.
assumptions_latex: The interval-width parameter satisfies \(L>0\).
The relaxation bounds positive and negative exponential terms independently using interval extrema.
The relaxation does not retain cancellation between identical terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation gap is \(\exp(L)-1\) and is unbounded as \(L\to\infty\), although the original mixed-sign signomial is identically zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconvex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional two-block biconvex minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty convex sets, let \(S\subseteq X\times Y\), and let \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\). For each \(y\in Y\), define \(S_y=\{x\in X:(x,y)\in S\}\), and for each \(x\in X\), define \(S_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in S\}\). The model \(\min\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in S\}\) is biconvex when every section \(S_y\) and \(S_x\) is convex and, for every nonempty section, \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(S_y\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is convex on \(S_x\). Joint convexity of \(S\) or \(f\) is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconvex model has convex feasible sections in each of two variable blocks, and its objective is convex in either block when the other block is fixed; joint convexity is not required.
assumptions_latex: \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are nonempty and convex.
\(S\subseteq X\times Y\) and \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_y\text{ and }S_x\text{ are convex, while }f(\cdot,y)\text{ and }f(x,\cdot)\text{ are convex on the corresponding nonempty sections}.\)

Then every iterate is feasible and \(f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\le f(x^{k+1},y^k)\le f(x^k,y^k)\). If these values are bounded below, they converge to a finite limit; this does not imply convergence of the iterates or global optimality.

Convex-Concave Block Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle-type convex-concave structure on two convex blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be convex. A function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) has convex-concave block structure if \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). A corresponding block model optimizes or bounds the saddle value \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\); this definition alone does not assert equality with \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave block model uses a function convex in the minimizing block and concave in the maximizing block, with no automatic minimax equality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\cdot,y)\text{ is convex and }L(x,\cdot)\text{ is concave}.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided certificate for an attained convex-concave saddle value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point exactly when \(L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\). It then attains both the min-max and max-min values, whose common value is \(L(x^*,y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-sided saddle inequality certifies attainment of both the min-max and max-min values.
assumptions_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_X\max_YL=\max_Y\min_XL=L(x^*,y^*).
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Concave Structure Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-domain family showing why compactness or comparable coercive regularity is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,1)\) and \(L(x,y)=x-y\). The function is affine, hence convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). Both max-min and min-max values equal \(0\), but neither outer optimum is attained because the required boundary value \(0\) is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On open convex blocks, an affine convex-concave model can have minimax equality without attaining either saddle value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_X\sup_YL=\sup_Y\inf_XL=0\text{, but no saddle point exists}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Concave Structure Does Not Ensure Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating block curvature from minimax equality and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every extended-real function on nonempty sets, \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\le\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\). Convex-concave block curvature alone does not guarantee equality or attainment; additional topological regularity is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Max-min never exceeds min-max, but convex-concave curvature alone does not ensure equality or attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_Y\inf_XL\le\inf_X\sup_YL.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Inequality Without Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact continuous finite-dimensional specialization of the minimax theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty compact convex sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Then \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), and both extrema are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex-concave function on compact convex blocks has equal, attained min-max and max-min values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
\(L\) is continuous.
\(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_X\max_YL=\max_Y\min_XL\text{, with attainment}.

Partly Convex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity restricted to a designated decision block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m,p\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_p:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). The constrained model \(\min\{f(x,y):g_i(x,y)\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,p,\ (x,y)\in X\times Y\}\) is partly convex in \(x\) if, for every fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(f(\cdot,y)\) and \(g_i(\cdot,y)\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), are convex on \(X\). No convexity in \(y\), nor joint convexity in \((x,y)\), is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partly convex model becomes a convex optimization problem in one designated block after all remaining variables are fixed; no convexity in the other block or joint convexity is required.
assumptions_latex: \(n,m,p\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty.
\(f,g_1,\ldots,g_p:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\cdot,y),g_1(\cdot,y),\ldots,g_p(\cdot,y)\text{ are convex on }X\text{ for every }y\in Y.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate for the convex block after the other block is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y\in Y\). Suppose \(f(\cdot,y)\) and \(g_i(\cdot,y)\) are convex and differentiable on a convex set \(X\). If a feasible \(x^*\), multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(s\in N_X(x^*)\) satisfy complementary slackness and \(0=\nabla_xf(x^*,y)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla_xg_i(x^*,y)+s\), then \(x^*\) globally minimizes the fixed-\(y\) subproblem. This does not certify global optimality over \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions certify the fixed convex-block problem, not the entire partly convex model.
assumptions_latex: The fixed-block objective and inequality functions are convex and differentiable.
\(X\) is convex.
Primal feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, complementary slackness, and stationarity hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\arg\min\{f(x,y):x\in X,\ g_i(x,y)\le0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Block KKT Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partly Convex Need Not Be Biconvex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation from the symmetric two-block sibling class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=Y=[-1,1]\), let \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^4\). For every fixed \(y\), \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex. For fixed \(x\), however, \(f(x,\cdot)=-y^4+x^2\) is not convex. Thus the model is partly convex in \(x\) but neither biconvex nor jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity in one designated block need not extend to the other block or to the joint variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is partly convex in }x\text{ but is neither biconvex nor jointly convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Partly Convex Need Not Be Biconvex

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block Affinity Does Not Imply Joint Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal bilinear objective with indefinite joint curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,y)=xy\), \(\nabla^2f=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(-1\). Thus \(f\) is affine in either variable when the other is fixed but is neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on any open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective xy is affine in each block but has both positive and negative joint-curvature directions.
assumptions_latex: The domain is open, convex, and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x,y)=xy\) is separately affine but neither jointly convex nor jointly concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Affinity Does Not Imply Joint Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-pair attainment over a Cartesian product of compact polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty compact polytopes and \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Qy+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+c\). Then a global minimizer over \(X\times Y\) exists, and one can be chosen in \(\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear-plus-affine objective over a product of compact polytopes has a global minimizer at a pair of extreme points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact polytopes.
The feasible set is exactly \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y):f(x^*,y^*)=\min_{X\times Y}f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Attainment for Bilinear Objectives
Bilinear Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous two-block models whose objective contains bilinear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision vectors \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), a bilinear-objective model has objective \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Qy+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+c\), possibly together with constraints defining a feasible set \(S\subseteq X\times Y\). The coupling term is affine in \(x\) for fixed \(y\) and affine in \(y\) for fixed \(x\), but it is generally nonconvex jointly when \(Q\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear-objective model couples two variable blocks through a term x-transpose-Q-y; it is block-affine but generally not jointly convex.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}Qy+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+c.\)

Bilinear Constraint Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint systems containing cross-products of two variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), a bilinear constraint has the form \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_i y+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i^{\mathsf T}y+c_i\leq0\), with equality constraints permitted by replacing the inequality with equality. A bilinear-constraint model contains at least one such constraint. Each constraint function is affine in either block when the other is fixed, although its joint feasible set need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear-constraint model contains a constraint coupling two variable blocks through cross-products; each fixed-block constraint is affine, but joint feasibility may be nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) and the remaining coefficients have compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_i y+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i^{\mathsf T}y+c_i\leq0\text{ or }=0.\)

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Primal Problem Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-complicating-variable primal subproblems in GOP decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v^*=\min\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\leq0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\}\), where fixing \(y\) leaves a convex problem in \(x\). For each parameter \(\bar y\in Y\), the GOP primal problem is \(P(\bar y):\ p(\bar y)=\inf\{f(x,\bar y):g(x,\bar y)\leq0,\ x\in X\}\). Whenever \(P(\bar y)\) is feasible and solved globally, any optimizer \(\bar x\) gives the original problem the feasible value \(f(\bar x,\bar y)\), hence an upper bound on \(v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the complicating block produces a convex primal subproblem; any feasible global solution supplies a valid incumbent and upper bound for minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex, and fixing any \(y\in Y\) makes the objective and inequality functions convex in \(x\).
The original problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*\leq f(\bar x,\bar y)=p(\bar y)\text{ whenever }P(\bar y)\text{ is feasible and attained}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Relaxed-Dual Problem Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support lower-bounding master family in GOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*\) be the minimum of the original GOP model, and let \(\ell_j:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be valid support functions satisfying \(\ell_j(y)\leq p(y)\) for every \(y\in Y\). After collecting indices \(J_k\), a relaxed-dual problem is \(RD_k:\ L_k=\inf_{y\in Y,\,t\in\mathbb{R}}\{t:t\geq\ell_j(y)\ \text{for all }j\in J_k\}\). Thus \(L_k=\inf_{y\in Y}\max_{j\in J_k}\ell_j(y)\leq v^*\). Adding another valid support cannot decrease \(L_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed dual minimizes the maximum of finitely many valid supports, producing a lower bound that cannot decrease when new supports are added.
assumptions_latex: \(p(y)\) is the fixed-block primal value function.
\(\ell_j(y)\leq p(y)\) for every \(y\in Y\) and \(j\in J_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq v^*\quad\text{and}\quad J_k\subseteq J_{k+1}\Longrightarrow L_k\leq L_{k+1}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Support Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting functions obtained from fixed-block primal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(g:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}^q\). Define \(p(y)=\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\leq0,\ x\in X\}\) and the partial Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda)=f(x,y)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x,y)\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^q_+\). Fix \(\bar y\in Y\). If the subproblem defining \(p(\bar y)\) has a finite attained optimum, strong duality holds, and \(\bar\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^q_+\) is an optimal multiplier, then \(\ell_{\bar y}(y)=\inf_{x\in X}\mathcal{L}(x,y,\bar\lambda)\) satisfies \(\ell_{\bar y}(y)\leq p(y)\) for every \(y\in Y\) and \(\ell_{\bar y}(\bar y)=p(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal nonnegative multiplier from a strongly dual convex fixed-block subproblem defines a global lower support for the fixed-block value function and makes that support exact at the generating point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are nonempty.
\(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}^q\).
The subproblem at \(\bar y\) has a finite attained optimum, strong duality holds, and \(\bar\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^q_+\) is dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\bar y}(y)\leq p(y)\text{ for every }y\in Y,\qquad \ell_{\bar y}(\bar y)=p(\bar y).\)

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the fixed-block primal problem at y.
Partial Lagrangian of the fixed-block primal problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates weak-duality validity of a Lagrangian support from strong-duality exactness at its generating parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(y)=\inf\{f(x,y):x\in X,\ g(x,y)\leq0\}\), every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^q_+\) defines \(\ell_\lambda(y)=\inf_{x\in X}[f(x,y)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x,y)]\) and satisfies \(\ell_\lambda(y)\leq p(y)\) for every \(y\). At an anchor \(\bar y\) with finite \(p(\bar y)\), equality \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)=p(\bar y)\) is not guaranteed by primal feasibility or convexity alone; it holds precisely when \(\lambda\) attains a zero-gap Lagrangian dual value at \(\bar y\). Thus failure of strong duality or dual attainment can destroy anchor exactness without destroying global lower-support validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative multiplier gives a valid lower support by weak duality, but the support touches the primal value at an anchor only when a zero-gap dual optimum is attained there.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty.
\(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^q_+\).
\(p(\bar y)\) is finite when anchor exactness is discussed.

Primal-Problem Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation of a GOP primal subproblem from a relaxed-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a relaxed-dual solution \(y^k\in Y\). Form \(P(y^k)\) by fixing \(y=y^k\), and solve this convex problem globally. If it is feasible, return an optimizer \(x^k\), value \(U^k=f(x^k,y^k)\), and optimal constraint multipliers \(\lambda^k\); use \(U^k\) to update the incumbent and \((y^k,\lambda^k)\) to generate a new Lagrangian support. If \(P(y^k)\) is infeasible, return a valid feasibility cut or infeasibility certificate. Stop this generation step after either output is obtained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix the relaxed-dual block, solve the resulting convex primal problem, and return either a feasible incumbent with multipliers or a valid infeasibility cut.
assumptions_latex: \(P(y^k)\) is a convex problem for every relaxed-dual point \(y^k\).
The convex solver returns a global solution or a valid infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(y^k)\text{ returns }(x^k,U^k,\lambda^k)\text{ or a valid infeasibility certificate}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed-Dual Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone refinement by adding valid GOP supports or feasibility cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an absolute gap tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\) and initialize a globally solvable relaxed dual \(RD_0\) with a finite collection of valid supports and feasibility cuts. At iteration \(k\), solve \(RD_k\) globally to obtain a trial point \(y^k\) and certified lower bound \(L_k\), then solve the fixed-block primal problem \(P(y^k)\). If \(P(y^k)\) has an attained feasible optimum, update the incumbent upper bound \(U_k\) and append a valid Lagrangian support. If \(P(y^k)\) is infeasible, append a valid feasibility cut supplied by the assumed separation mechanism. Retain all earlier valid constraints when forming \(RD_{k+1}\). If a finite incumbent exists and \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\), stop and return its feasible point; otherwise continue. The returned point has objective value at most \(\varepsilon\) above the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the relaxed dual, evaluate its trial point through the fixed-block primal problem, and retain a valid support or feasibility cut. Stop when a finite incumbent and certified lower bound differ by at most the prescribed absolute tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon\geq0\) is an absolute optimality-gap tolerance.
Every relaxed-dual problem is solved globally and yields a valid lower bound.
Each feasible primal subproblem supplies a valid support, and the infeasibility mechanism supplies a valid feasibility cut whenever the primal subproblem is infeasible.
All previously generated valid constraints are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq L_{k+1}\leq v^*,\qquad U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U_k\leq v^*+\varepsilon.\)

notation.meaning: Certified relaxed-dual lower bound at iteration k.
Finite incumbent upper bound when one has been generated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Uniformly Consistent Relaxed-Dual Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional convergence of globally solved nested value-function lower models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Y be compact and \phi:Y\to\mathbb R continuous. Begin with a valid support q_0\le\phi. For k\ge1, globally minimize m_k=\max_{0\le i<k}q_i at y^k, put L_k=m_k(y^k), evaluate \phi(y^k), and add q_k satisfying q_k\le\phi and 0\le\phi(y)-q_k(y)\le\omega(\|y-y^k\|) for all y\in Y, where \omega(t)\to0 as t\downarrow0. If U_k is the least sampled value, then L_k\uparrow v^*, U_k\downarrow v^*, and U_k-L_k\to0, where v^*=\min_Y\phi.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness, exact master solves, retained valid supports, and a common local-consistency modulus force the primal and relaxed-dual bounds to converge.
assumptions_latex: Y is compact and \phi is continuous and finite.
Every accumulated lower model is minimized globally.
All supports are retained and satisfy the common consistency modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\uparrow v^*,\qquad U_k\downarrow v^*,\qquad U_k-L_k\to0.

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Incumbent Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-feasible-value update for minimization-form GOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U_0=+\infty\) and leave the incumbent undefined. At iteration \(k\), if the primal problem produces a feasible point \(z^k=(x^k,y^k)\) with value \(u_k=f(z^k)\), set \(U_k=\min\{U_{k-1},u_k\}\) and retain a feasible point attaining \(U_k\); otherwise set \(U_k=U_{k-1}\). The sequence is nonincreasing, and every finite \(U_k\) is a valid upper bound on the global minimum \(v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep the best feasible objective value found so far; it decreases monotonically and remains a valid upper bound for a minimization problem.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted point \(z^k\) satisfies all original constraints.
The GOP model is expressed as minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*\leq U_k\leq U_{k-1}\text{ whenever }U_k<+\infty.\)

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Lower-Bound Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and monotonicity of nested GOP relaxed-dual bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_k\) be the globally solved value of a GOP relaxed dual whose support and feasibility-cut collection is contained in that of iteration \(k+1\). If every retained relaxation constraint is valid for the original minimization problem, then \(L_k\leq v^*\) for every \(k\). Because refinement only adds constraints to the relaxed dual, its feasible set contracts and \(L_{k+1}\geq L_k\). A safe implementation may therefore store \(\widehat L_k=\max_{0\leq j\leq k}L_j\) as the certified lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid nested relaxed duals yield nondecreasing lower bounds; retaining the largest certified value protects bound management from obsolete weaker bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each relaxed-dual constraint is a valid relaxation constraint for the original problem.
Successive relaxed duals retain all previously active valid constraints and are solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq L_{k+1}\leq v^*,\qquad \widehat L_k=\max_{0\leq j\leq k}L_j\leq v^*.\)

notation.meaning: Relaxed-dual value computed at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solver Objectives Are Not Automatically Certified Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation requirement for incorporating numerical relaxed-dual output into GOP bound state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization-form relaxed dual, a numerical solver's reported objective may update the certified GOP lower bound only if that value is itself certified below the relaxed-dual optimum and every relaxation relation is valid for the original problem. An approximate feasible objective is generally an upper bound on the relaxation's minimum, not a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A raw approximate relaxed-dual objective is not necessarily a valid GOP lower bound; its direction and relaxation validity must be certified.
assumptions_latex: The relaxed dual is expressed as minimization.
The numerical solve may terminate without a global lower-bound certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Storage for Nonnested Certified Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe aggregation when successive lower-bounding models are not nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_k\) are independently certified lower bounds for the same minimization problem and validity domain, then \(\widehat L_k=\max_{0\le j\le k}\ell_j\) is a certified lower bound and \(\widehat L_{k+1}\ge\widehat L_k\), even when the generating models are not nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the maximum of independently valid lower bounds preserves validity and yields monotone storage without nested relaxations.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\ell_j\) is certified for the same original problem and validity domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat L_k=\max_{j\le k}\ell_j\le v^*,\qquad\widehat L_{k+1}\ge\widehat L_k.

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Optimality-Gap Tracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-based stopping rule for a deterministic minimization GOP procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). At iteration \(k\), let \(x_k^{\mathrm{inc}}\in F\) be the best feasible point found through that iteration and set \(U_k=f(x_k^{\mathrm{inc}})\). When a new feasible point \(x^k\) is found, retain whichever of \(x_{k-1}^{\mathrm{inc}}\) and \(x^k\) has smaller objective value. Let \(L_k\leq f^*\) be the current valid global lower bound obtained from the active relaxed-dual partition. Define \(g_k=U_k-L_k\) and \(r_k=g_k/\max\{1,|U_k|\}\). Stop at absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\) when \(g_k\leq\varepsilon\), or at relative tolerance \(\tau\geq0\) when \(r_k\leq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain the best feasible incumbent and a valid global lower bound. Their difference certifies the absolute error, while its stated normalization supplies the relative stopping test.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\), and \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\) is finite.
\(x_k^{\mathrm{inc}}\in F\) and \(L_k\leq f^*\leq U_k\).
\(\varepsilon\geq0\) and \(\tau\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_k\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(x_k^{\mathrm{inc}})-f^*\leq\varepsilon\), and \(r_k\leq\tau\Rightarrow f(x_k^{\mathrm{inc}})-f^*\leq\tau\max\{1,|U_k|\}\).

notation.meaning: best feasible incumbent through iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Bound Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by retaining a lower bound after its validity domain changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(L(S)\) is a lower bound valid only for the subregion \(S\), meaning \(L(S)\leq\inf_{x\in F\cap S}f(x)\). If GOP subsequently replaces the active region by \(T\not\subseteq S\) but continues to use \(L(S)\) as a lower bound on \(F\cap T\), then the inequality \(L(S)\leq f^*\) need not hold. For example, let \(F=T=\{0,1\}\), \(S=\{1\}\), \(f(0)=0\), and \(f(1)=1\). Then \(L(S)=1\) is valid on \(S\) but exceeds the global optimum \(f^*=0\); a zero reported gap against incumbent value \(1\) is therefore false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound becomes unsafe when reused outside the region or relaxation for which it was proved valid, potentially producing a false zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(L(S)\leq\inf_{x\in F\cap S}f(x)\).
\(T\not\subseteq S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(S)\leq f^*\) is not guaranteed on \(T\).

notation.meaning: lower bound certified only on S

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Dual Lower-Bound Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality basis for GOP relaxed-dual lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal minimization problem \(f^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\). For multipliers \(\lambda\geq0\) and \(\mu\) unrestricted, define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}h(x)\) and \(q(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\mu)\). Every primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\mu)\leq f(x)\), so \(q(\lambda,\mu)\leq f^*\). Consequently, any GOP relaxed-dual problem whose feasible solutions furnish such valid underestimators supplies a global lower bound; maximizing over admissible multipliers or partitions preserves lower-bound validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every admissible Lagrangian or relaxed-dual value underestimates the primal optimum, so GOP may maximize these values to strengthen its global lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) and the primal feasible set is nonempty.
\(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(\lambda,\mu)\leq f^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Dual Bounds Need Not Be Exact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of the GOP dual lower-bound principle when strong duality is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\mu}q(\lambda,\mu)\). Weak duality guarantees only \(d^*\le f^*\), and equality can fail for a nonconvex problem. For example, take \(X=\{a,b\}\), impose \(g(x)\le0\), and set \((f(a),g(a))=(1,-1)\) and \((f(b),g(b))=(0,1)\). Then only \(a\) is feasible, so \(f^*=1\), whereas \(q(\lambda)=\min\{1-\lambda,\lambda\}\) for \(\lambda\ge0\), giving \(d^*=1/2<f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing valid dual lower bounds need not recover the primal optimum; a positive duality gap can remain without strong-duality hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: The primal is a minimization problem and inequality multipliers are nonnegative.
No convexity, constraint qualification, or other strong-duality hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^*\le f^*,\qquad d^*=\tfrac12<f^*=1\text{ in the displayed example}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Dual Bounds Need Not Be Exact

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Corner-linearization lower bound for the GOP Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: GOP relaxed-dual bounding for a fixed iteration and primal parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\mathbf y^k\). For every \(i\in I_c^k\), let \(x_i^L\) and \(x_i^U\) be the bounds on \(x_i\), and let \(CB\) be the set of their lower/upper-bound combinations. Then, for every \(\mathbf y\),
\[
L^*(\bar{\mathbf x},\mathbf y,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\geq \min_{B_j\in CB}\left\{\left.L(\mathbf x^{B_j},\mathbf y,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\right|_{\mathbf x^k}^{\mathrm{lin}}:\ g_i^k(\mathbf y)\geq0\ \text{if }x_i^{B_j}=x_i^L,\quad g_i^k(\mathbf y)\leq0\ \text{if }x_i^{B_j}=x_i^U\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed GOP iteration, the indicated Lagrangian quantity is bounded below by the minimum linearized Lagrangian value over all lower/upper-bound assignments of the connected x variables satisfying the corresponding qualifying sign conditions. The inequality holds for every y.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf y^k\text{ is fixed}
i\in I_c^k\implies x_i^L\leq x_i\leq x_i^U
CB=\{B_j:B_j\text{ assigns each connected }x_i\text{ to }x_i^L\text{ or }x_i^U\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L^*(\bar{\mathbf x},\mathbf y,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\geq \min_{B_j\in CB}\left\{\left.L(\mathbf x^{B_j},\mathbf y,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\right|_{\mathbf x^k}^{\mathrm{lin}}:\ g_i^k(\mathbf y)\geq0\text{ at lower bounds},\ g_i^k(\mathbf y)\leq0\text{ at upper bounds}\right\}\quad\forall\mathbf y

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Lagrangian Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concavity, weak duality, and supergradient properties used in GOP dual construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\), and define \(f^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\), set \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}h(x)\) and \(q(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\mu)\). The function \(q\) is concave and satisfies \(q(\lambda,\mu)\leq f^*\). If \(q(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\) and an inner minimizer \(x_{\lambda,\mu}\) exists, then \((g(x_{\lambda,\mu}),h(x_{\lambda,\mu}))\) is a supergradient of \(q\) at \((\lambda,\mu)\), relative to the multiplier domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-valued Lagrangian dual function is concave and lower-bounds the primal value; at an attained inner minimum, the constraint residuals form a supergradient on the multiplier domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\), and \(f,g,h\) have the displayed real-valued domains.
The primal feasible set is nonempty.
\(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\).
For the supergradient assertion, \(q(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\) and the inner infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\text{ is concave}\), \(q(\lambda,\mu)\leq f^*\), and \((g(x_{\lambda,\mu}),h(x_{\lambda,\mu}))\in\partial^+q(\lambda,\mu)\) under the attainment and finiteness assumptions.

notation.meaning: superdifferential relative to the multiplier domain

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Lagrangian Minimizers Give Approximate Supergradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate-inner-minimization variant of the Lagrangian residual-supergradient property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y=(\lambda,\mu)\) in the multiplier domain and suppose \(q(y)\in\mathbb R\). If \(x_\varepsilon\in X\) satisfies \(\mathcal L(x_\varepsilon,y)\le q(y)+\varepsilon\), and \(r(x_\varepsilon)=(g(x_\varepsilon),h(x_\varepsilon))\), then every admissible \(y'\) satisfies \[q(y')\le q(y)+r(x_\varepsilon)^{\mathsf T}(y'-y)+\varepsilon.\] Thus \(r(x_\varepsilon)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-supergradient of \(q\) at \(y\). When the inner infimum is not attained, the exact minimizer-residual formula may be unavailable, while approximate inner minimizers still yield approximate supergradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residuals of an epsilon-optimal Lagrangian inner solution form an epsilon-supergradient; without inner attainment, the exact minimizer-residual formula may be unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(q(y)\) is finite at the multiplier point \(y\).
An \(\varepsilon\)-optimal inner point \(x_\varepsilon\) exists for some \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(x_\varepsilon)\in\partial^+_\varepsilon q(y).

notation.meaning: epsilon-superdifferential of the concave dual function

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Lagrangian Minimizers Give Approximate Supergradients
Finite Approximate-Global Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of GOP at a prescribed absolute global-optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be compact and \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Consider a GOP partition procedure maintaining a feasible incumbent value \(U_k\) and valid regional lower bounds whose minimum is \(L_k\). Assume its refinements are exhaustive and uniformly consistent: for every \(\delta>0\), after finitely many refinements every active region \(R\) satisfies \(U(R)-L(R)\leq\delta\), where \(U(R)\) is a feasible regional upper bound whenever \(F\cap R\neq\varnothing\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the procedure reaches a finite iteration \(K\) with \(U_K-L_K\leq\varepsilon\). Its incumbent \(x^K\) is therefore \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal: \(f(x^K)\leq f^*+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness, continuity, valid bounds, and finitely achieved uniform bound consistency, GOP terminates finitely with an incumbent within ε of the global optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and compact, and \(f\) is continuous on \(F\).
All regional bounds are valid.
Partition refinement is exhaustive and uniformly consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists K<\infty:\ U_K-L_K\leq\varepsilon\) and \(f(x^K)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite ε-Convergence of the GOP Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of GOP at any prescribed positive tolerance under the stated compactness, continuity, and multiplier hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be nonempty compact convex sets with $Y\subset V$. knowledge_statements.title: GOP Optimality-Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori certificate formed from a feasible incumbent and valid GOP lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with global value \(f^*\), a GOP gap certificate is a triple \((\bar x,L,\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(\bar x\in F\), \(L\leq f^*\), and \(f(\bar x)-L\leq\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Its verification requires checking primal feasibility of \(\bar x\), the provenance and validity of the relaxed-dual bound \(L\), and the displayed numerical inequality. Since \(L\leq f^*\leq f(\bar x)\), the certificate implies \(0\leq f(\bar x)-f^*\leq f(\bar x)-L\leq\varepsilon\). When \(\varepsilon=0\), \(\bar x\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and a valid lower bound certify ε-global optimality when their objective gap is at most ε; a zero gap certifies exact optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in F\).
\(f(\bar x)-L\leq\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Primal Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound infeasibility certificate for a GOP primal region or the complete primal domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_R=\{x\in X\cap R:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\) be the primal feasible set restricted to a GOP region \(R\). If a relaxation has feasible set \(Q_R\) satisfying \(F_R\subseteq Q_R\) and a verifiable certificate establishes \(Q_R=\varnothing\), then \(F_R=\varnothing\), so region \(R\) may be discarded. If the certified regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_N\) cover \(X\), each corresponding relaxation is empty, and no feasible point lies outside their union, then the original primal problem is infeasible. Failure of a local primal subproblem alone is not a global infeasibility certificate unless this covering and relaxation-validity condition is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty outer relaxation certifies regional infeasibility; global infeasibility follows only when such certified regions cover the entire primal domain.
assumptions_latex: \(F_R\subseteq Q_R\) for every certified region.
\(Q_R=\varnothing\) is independently verifiable.
For global infeasibility, \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N R_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_R=\varnothing\Longrightarrow F_R=\varnothing\); if the certified regions cover \(X\), then \(F=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Mathematical Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core invariant connecting GOP primal incumbents, valid global lower bounds, and certified gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a GOP minimization sequence with finite optimum \(f^*\), let \(U_k\) be the best feasible objective value found through iteration \(k\). Let \(B_k\) be a valid global lower bound obtained by aggregating the active regional bounds while accounting for every discarded region through a sound fathoming rule, so \(B_k\leq f^*\). Define the running lower bound by \(L_0=B_0\) and \(L_{k+1}=\max\{L_k,B_{k+1}\}\). Retaining the best incumbent gives \(U_{k+1}\leq U_k\), while validity gives \(L_k\leq f^*\leq U_k\) and \(L_{k+1}\geq L_k\). Consequently, the certified gap \(G_k=U_k-L_k\) is nonnegative and nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound regional aggregation and fathoming produce valid global lower bounds; running lower bounds increase, incumbents decrease, and the certified gap cannot increase.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem has a finite global optimum \(f^*\).
Every \(U_k\) is the objective value of a feasible incumbent.
Every aggregate bound satisfies \(B_k\leq f^*\).
Partition coverage is preserved, and every discarded region is handled by a sound fathoming rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq f^*\leq U_k\) and \(0\leq G_{k+1}\leq G_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Property–Certificate Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface mapping GOP feasibility, coverage, and bound invariants to checkable certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), represent the GOP certificate interface by \(\mathcal C_k=(\bar x_k,U_k,\mathcal P_k,\{\ell_R\}_{R\in\mathcal P_k})\), where \(\bar x_k\in F\), \(U_k=f(\bar x_k)\), the finite family \(\mathcal P_k\) covers \(F\), and \(\ell_R\leq\inf_{x\in F\cap R}f(x)\) for every \(R\in\mathcal P_k\). With \(L_k=\min_{R\in\mathcal P_k}\ell_R\), one has \(L_k\leq f^*\leq U_k\); hence \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-global-optimality certificate. For infeasibility, if each region has an outer relaxation \(Q_R\supseteq F\cap R\) and every \(Q_R\) is verifiably empty, then the covering property certifies \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface packages a feasible incumbent, complete regional coverage, and valid regional bounds. A small aggregate gap certifies approximate global optimality, while empty covering outer relaxations certify infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Models with Linear Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-objective specialization of GOP over a linearly constrained bounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic model with linear constraints has the form \[\min_{x\in P}q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d,\qquad P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b,\ Ex=e,\ \ell\leq x\leq u\},\] where \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), the coefficient arrays have compatible finite dimensions, and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(\ell\leq u\). The matrix \(Q\) need not be positive semidefinite. If \(P\neq\varnothing\) and \(D=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\), then the objective is convex on \(P\) exactly when \(z^{\mathsf T}Qz\geq0\) for every \(z\in D\); failure of this condition gives the nonconvex quadratic specialization addressed by global methods such as GOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a quadratic objective over linear equalities, inequalities, and finite variable bounds. Nonconvexity occurs when the quadratic curvature is negative along a direction in the affine hull of the feasible polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(A,E,b,e,c,\ell,u\) have compatible finite dimensions.
\(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\ell\leq u\).
The curvature characterization is applied when \(P\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists z\in\operatorname{span}(P-P):z^{\mathsf T}Qz<0)\Rightarrow q\text{ is nonconvex on }P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded one-variable polynomial optimization specialization of the GOP framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded univariate polynomial model minimizes \[p(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{d}a_rx^r\] over a nonempty compact semialgebraic set \(F=\{x\in[\ell,u]:p_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where each \(p_i\) is a real polynomial and \(\ell<u\). Candidate minimizers occur among feasible interval endpoints, feasible real roots of \(p'(x)\), and boundary points generated by real roots of the constraint polynomials. A GOP specialization may partition \([\ell,u]\) and use polynomial underestimators to produce certified regional lower bounds.

The data satisfy \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(d,q\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^k\), \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m}\), \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb{R}^r\).
For every relevant \(x\in X\), the set \(Y(x)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:Gu\le h-Hx\}\) is nonempty and the lower-level quadratic program attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible pairs are exactly \(\{(x,y):x\in X,\ Ax+By\le b,\ y\in S_Q(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Follower solution mapping for the quadratic program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The descriptor linear–quadratic refers respectively to leader and follower objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilevel linear–quadratic model is \[\min_{x\in X,\,y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{c^\top x+d^\top y:Ax+By\le b,\ y\in S_Q(x)\},\] with follower response \[S_Q(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{\tfrac12u^\top Qu+(q+Rx)^\top u:Gu\le h-Hx\right\}.\] Thus the leader objective and explicit constraints are affine, whereas the follower objective is quadratic in its decision variable and may depend affinely on the leader variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilevel linear–quadratic model has a linear leader objective, while feasible follower responses are optimizers of a parameterized quadratic program with affine constraints.

children.title: Bilevel Quadratic–Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Bilevel GOP models with quadratic structure at both levels.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.

The leader data satisfy \(P\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(D\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^k\).
The follower data satisfy \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m}\), \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb{R}^r\).
For every relevant \(x\in X\), the follower feasible set is nonempty and the follower objective attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both optimization levels have quadratic objectives, and bilevel feasibility is imposed by \(y\in S_Q(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous quadratic–quadratic bilevel models with affine constraints at both levels.

source_refs.locator: 5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilevel quadratic–quadratic model has the form \[\min_{x\in X,\,y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{\tfrac12x^\top Px+x^\top Cy+\tfrac12y^\top Dy+c^\top x+d^\top y:Ax+By\le b,\ y\in S_Q(x)\right\},\] where \[S_Q(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{\tfrac12u^\top Qu+(q+Rx)^\top u:Gu\le h-Hx\right\}.\] The Hessian matrices need not be positive semidefinite unless convexity is imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilevel quadratic–quadratic model uses quadratic objectives at both levels and restricts the follower decision to the optimizer set of a parameterized quadratic program with affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilevel Quadratic–Quadratic Models
