children.title: Cross-Level Quadratic Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling patterns created by quadratic terms spanning bilevel components.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
The data satisfy \(P\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(r\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-level quadratic coupling is present exactly when \(C\ne0\), equivalently when the mixed derivative block \(\nabla^2_{xy}\phi=C\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic representation of bilinear interaction between leader and follower variables.

source_refs.locator: 5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the joint quadratic function \[\phi(x,y)=\tfrac12x^\top Px+x^\top Cy+\tfrac12y^\top Qy+p^\top x+q^\top y+r,\] the equivalent block representation is \[\phi(x,y)=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\begin{pmatrix}P&C\\C^\top&Q\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}+p^\top x+q^\top y+r.\] The term \(x^\top Cy\) is the cross-level coupling term and disappears precisely when \(C=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-level quadratic coupling is the bilinear term between leader and follower variables; its coefficient matrix is the off-diagonal block of the joint Hessian.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Level Quadratic Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur-Complement Convexity Test for Coupled Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-curvature test showing when cross-level coupling preserves or destroys convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M=\begin{pmatrix}P&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&Q\end{pmatrix}. The joint quadratic is convex on \mathbb R^{n+m} exactly when M\succeq0. If P\succ0, this is equivalent to Q-C^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}C\succeq0; if Q\succ0, it is equivalent to P-CQ^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\succeq0. Thus convex diagonal blocks alone are insufficient: in the scalar case P=Q=1 and C=2 give eigenvalues 3 and -1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint convexity depends on the full block Hessian, equivalently on a Schur complement when a diagonal block is positive definite.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb S^n\), \(Q\in\mathbb S^m\), and \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\succeq0;\quad P\succ0\Rightarrow[M\succeq0\iff Q-C^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}C\succeq0].
knowledge_statements.title: Schur-Complement Convexity Test for Coupled Quadratics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for absence of quadratic interaction between leader and follower variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \phi(x,y)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+x^{\mathsf T}Cy+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}Qy+p^{\mathsf T}x+q^{\mathsf T}y+r, the following are equivalent: C=0; \nabla^2_{xy}\phi=0; and \phi(x,y)=\phi_x(x)+\phi_y(y)+r for quadratic functions \phi_x and \phi_y. This objective separability does not imply decomposition when constraints still couple x and y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic objective is additively block-separable exactly when the cross-Hessian vanishes, although constraints may still couple the blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=0\iff\nabla^2_{xy}\phi=0\iff\phi(x,y)=\phi_x(x)+\phi_y(y)+r.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Separability Criterion

children.title: Bilevel Quadratic Tractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits on exploitable GOP decomposition for bilevel quadratic forms.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the follower minimizes \(f_x(y)=\tfrac12y^\top Qy+q(x)^\top y\) over \(Y(x)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:Gy\le h-Hx\}\), where \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m}\), \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), \(h\in\mathbb{R}^r\), and \(q(x)\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
The affine follower constraints satisfy a constraint qualification at every point for which KKT necessity is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Q\succeq0\), follower KKT conditions characterize global optimality; if convexity on the follower feasible set is absent, KKT feasibility alone need not characterize global optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for exact follower KKT replacement, not a general polynomial-time classification.

source_refs.locator: 5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\succeq0\), then \(f_x\) is convex and the affine follower feasible set is convex; under the stated qualification, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity are necessary and sufficient for follower global optimality. When the follower problem is nonconvex on its feasible set, those KKT conditions are only necessary at regular local minimizers and may also hold at points that are not global follower solutions. Consequently, a KKT-based single-level replacement is not generally exact in the nonconvex case unless additional global-optimality certification is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex follower quadratic admits an exact KKT characterization under the stated qualification, whereas a genuinely nonconvex follower problem can satisfy KKT conditions at points that are not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilevel Quadratic Tractability Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Exactness Does Not Imply Polynomial-Time Bilevel Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary separating exact follower representation from tractability of the complete bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when Q=0, so that the follower is linear and its primal–dual or KKT characterization is exact, the general rational bilevel model contains bilevel linear programming and remains NP-hard. Consequently convex-follower KKT exactness is a representation result, not a polynomial-time classification of the complete bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact convex-follower KKT reformulation does not make the overall bilevel problem polynomial-time solvable.
assumptions_latex: Input coefficients are rational and binary encoded.
The claim concerns the general model family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\succeq0\ \text{and exact follower KKT replacement}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{polynomial-time solvability of the bilevel model}.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Exactness Does Not Imply Polynomial-Time Bilevel Solvability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that KKT feasibility does not imply a global follower response outside the convex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \min\{-y^2:-1\le y\le1\}, the point y=0 is feasible and satisfies stationarity and complementarity with zero bound multipliers. Its value is 0, whereas y=\pm1 have value -1. Hence y=0 is a KKT point but not a global follower minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior stationary point of a concave quadratic on an interval satisfies KKT but is worse than both endpoints.
assumptions_latex: The follower Hessian is \(Q=-2<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\mathrm{KKT}\setminus\operatorname*{argmin}_{-1\le y\le1}(-y^2).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Follower KKT Counterexample

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Uniqueness Boundaries on the Follower Feasible Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact KKT characterization from uniqueness for a fixed follower problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed x, let D_x=\operatorname{span}(Y(x)-Y(x)). If z^{\mathsf T}Qz\ge0 for every z\in D_x, the follower objective is convex on Y(x), so under the stated qualification its KKT conditions characterize global minimizers. If z^{\mathsf T}Qz>0 for every nonzero z\in D_x, the objective is strictly convex on Y(x) and the follower optimizer is unique. Global conditions Q\succeq0 and Q\succ0 are sufficient but need not be necessary when Y(x) lies in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT exactness requires convexity on feasible directions, while strict convexity on those directions additionally gives a unique follower response.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedron and the follower minimum is attained.
The stated constraint qualification holds for KKT necessity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q|_{D_x}\succeq0\Rightarrow(\mathrm{KKT}\iff\mathrm{global\ optimum}),\qquad Q|_{D_x}\succ0\Rightarrow|S_Q(x)|=1.

notation.meaning: direction space of the affine hull of the follower feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Uniqueness Boundaries on the Follower Feasible Hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness Boundaries for a Single-MILP Disjunctive Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundaries for binary-selector and big-M encodings of a finite GOP relaxed-dual disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\) be the reference domain and let the intended set be \(\bigcup_{k=1}^K F_k\), where \(F_k=\{w\in W:r_{kj}(w)\le 0\ \forall j\}\). A selector formulation with \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\) can be projection-equivalent to this union only if its selector constraints enforce the intended alternative logic and every inactive-disjunct constant satisfies \(M_{kj}\ge \sup_{w\in W}r_{kj}(w)\). An undersized \(M_{kj}\) can exclude a point belonging to another disjunct, while selector logic permitting all disjuncts to be inactive can admit points outside the union. Hence invalid big-M bounds or incorrect selector logic destroy projection equivalence in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact single-MILP disjunctive encoding requires valid big-M bounds and selector constraints enforcing the intended alternatives; otherwise valid union points may be lost or spurious points admitted.
assumptions_latex: The intended relaxed-dual representation is a finite union of affine systems over a reference domain \(W\).
The formulation uses binary selectors and conditional big-M inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Invalid }M_{kj}\text{ or incorrect selector logic can imply }\operatorname{proj}_w(F_{\mathrm{MILP}})\ne\bigcup_{k=1}^K F_k.

notation.meaning: reference domain used to validate inactive-disjunct bounds
upper bound used to deactivate residual r_kj

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Boundaries for a Single-MILP Disjunctive Encoding

assumptions_latex: The relaxed-dual disjunction has finitely many alternatives, each described by affine inequalities.
Finite valid bounds are available for every product between a binary indicator and a bounded continuous expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting MILP has the same feasible projections and objective values as the finite relaxed-dual disjunctive formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite disjunctive encoding of a GOP relaxed dual under valid variable bounds.

source_refs.locator: 3.13 Reformulation of the Relaxed Dual as a Single MILP Problem p. 126

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let disjunct \(k\) require affine residuals \(r_{kj}(w)\le0\). Introduce \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\), impose the selector constraints required by the relaxed-dual disjunction, and replace each conditional inequality by \[r_{kj}(w)\le M_{kj}(1-z_k),\] where \(M_{kj}\) is a valid upper bound on \(r_{kj}\). Any binary–continuous product \(v=z_kt\), with \(L_k\le t\le U_k\), is represented by \[L_kz_k\le v\le U_kz_k,\quad t-U_k(1-z_k)\le v\le t-L_k(1-z_k).\] The assembled formulation is a single MILP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite GOP relaxed-dual disjunction can be encoded as one MILP using binary selectors and valid bound-based linearizations.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-MILP Relaxed-Dual Reformulation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), initialize \(U=+\infty\), \(L=-\infty\), and an empty collection of GOP cuts. Repeatedly solve a primal subproblem to obtain a feasible point and update \(U\); generate the associated valid relaxed-dual constraints; solve their MILP reformulation to update \(L\) and select the next partition or candidate. Discard any region whose lower bound is at least \(U\). Stop when \(U-L\le\varepsilon\), or report infeasibility when every region is validly eliminated; output the incumbent otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The implementation alternates primal feasible solves and MILP relaxed-dual bounds, pruning regions until the global bound gap meets the requested tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: GOP/MILP node generation with binary-pattern exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm specialization; initialization, Steps 1–3, lower-bound selection, and convergence are inherited from the referenced base GOP procedure and are not expanded in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain a set \(A_j\) of binary cuts for each node \(j\), with \(A_1=\varnothing\). At the current node \(C\), solve the MILP (3.66)--(3.72). If \(\mu_B^\star<f^U-\epsilon\), create \(j=N+1\), set \(P(j)=C\), increment \(N\), and store \((\mu_B^j,y^j)\); if \(\mu_B^\star\geq f^U-\epsilon\), fathom that solution. Let \(\alpha^C\) be the resulting binary vector, \(J_C=\{i:\alpha_i^C=1\}\), and \(NJ_C=|J_C|\). When regenerating solutions from a previously partitioned node \(C\), add
\[\sum_{i\in J_C}\alpha_i-\sum_{i\notin J_C}\alpha_i\leq NJ_C-1\]
to \(A_C\) and resolve (3.66)--(3.72) with the accumulated cuts. If the new optimum satisfies \(\mu_B^\star<f^U-\epsilon\), create and store another child of \(C\) and update \(\alpha^C\); otherwise fathom node \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The GOP/MILP specialization solves a mixed-integer relaxed-dual problem at the current node. A solution below the incumbent cutoff is stored as a child, whereas one meeting the cutoff is fathomed. When a partitioned node is revisited, a no-good cut excludes its previous binary pattern; the master is resolved and either another child is stored or the node is fathomed.
assumptions_latex: A_j\text{ is the set of binary cuts maintained for node }j,\quad A_1=\varnothing.
f^U\text{ is the current upper bound and }\epsilon\text{ is the prescribed tolerance}.
C\text{ is the selected node, and formulation (3.66)--(3.72) is its GOP master MILP}.
\text{The omitted initialization, Steps 1--3, lower-bound selection, and convergence operations are inherited from the referenced base GOP algorithm.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_B^\star<f^U-\epsilon\Rightarrow\text{store a child solution};\qquad \mu_B^\star\geq f^U-\epsilon\Rightarrow\text{fathom as specified};\qquad A_C\leftarrow A_C\cup\left\{\sum_{i\in J_C}\alpha_i-\sum_{i\notin J_C}\alpha_i\leq NJ_C-1\right\}\text{ when regenerating from }C.

children.title: Node-Level GOP Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Use of GOP decomposition within individual tree-search regions.

assumptions_latex: Each search node \(v\) carries a region \(D_v\) containing all descendants' feasible points.
The local GOP relaxation is valid on \(D_v\), and any primal point used for an upper bound is feasible for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each node produces a valid lower bound \(L_v\) and possibly improves the global incumbent \(U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic integration of GOP bounding operations into one branch-and-bound node.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. The GOP Primal-Relaxed Dual Decomposition Approach: Theory p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an open node \(v\), restrict the GOP primal and relaxed-dual constructions to \(D_v\). Solve the node relaxation to obtain \(L_v\). If \(L_v\ge U\), fathom \(v\). Otherwise solve or recover a feasible primal point in \(D_v\), update \(U\) with its objective value, and generate valid GOP cuts or partition information. If the node remains unresolved and \(U-L_v\) exceeds tolerance, return the strengthened node description and branching information; otherwise fathom it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each search node, GOP supplies a regional lower bound, feasible incumbents, and cuts or partition information before pruning or branching.

children.title: GOP-Guided Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching choices informed by GOP primal or relaxed-dual information.

assumptions_latex: An open node \(v\) has region \(D_v\) and valid lower bound \(L_v<U\).
A finite set of admissible splits partitions \(D_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected split maximizes a declared GOP-based score while preserving exhaustive coverage of \(D_v\).

notation.meaning: GOP branching score for candidate split s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch selection driven by GOP relaxation information rather than an unspecified fixed variable order.

source_refs.locator: 3.14 A Linear Branching Scheme for the GOP Algorithm p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible split \(s\), form child regions \(D_{v,1}(s),\ldots,D_{v,r_s}(s)\) whose union is \(D_v\), and compute a declared score \(\sigma_v(s)\) from GOP information, such as predicted child lower bounds, relaxed-dual violations, or partition sensitivity. Choose \[s^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{s}\sigma_v(s),\] create the corresponding children, and inherit all globally valid GOP cuts. Empty children are discarded; no child may be discarded solely because its score is poor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GOP-guided branching scores exhaustive candidate splits using relaxation bounds, violations, or sensitivities, then branches on a highest-scoring split.

children.title: Tree-Level GOP Bounds
children.top_down_role: GOP-derived bounds maintained across a global search tree.

assumptions_latex: The active-node regions cover every feasible point not already validly fathomed.
Each active node \(v\in\mathcal{A}\) has a valid regional lower bound \(L_v\), and \(U\in\mathbb{R}\) is the objective value of a feasible incumbent.
The problem is a minimization problem with finite optimal value \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(\min\varnothing=+\infty\), the quantity \(L=\min\{U,\min_{v\in\mathcal{A}}L_v\}\) is a valid global lower bound and satisfies \(L\le f^*\le U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global bound aggregation for a minimization tree whose active regions exhaust the unresolved domain.

source_refs.locator: 3.5 The Global Optimization (GOP) Algorithm p. 84

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the active-node set and let \(L_v\) bound from below the objective over the region of each \(v\in\mathcal{A}\). With the convention \(\min\varnothing=+\infty\), define \[L=\min\left\{U,\min_{v\in\mathcal{A}}L_v\right\}.\] If \(U\) is the objective value of the best feasible incumbent, then \(L\le f^*\le U\). A node satisfying \(L_v\ge U\) cannot contain a solution improving the incumbent and may be fathomed without changing the best attainable objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tree lower bound is the smaller of the incumbent value and the least valid lower bound among active nodes; the incumbent is a global upper bound, and nodes bounded no better than it may be fathomed.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Level GOP Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5 The Global Optimization (GOP) Algorithm p. 84

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination certificates derived from valid regional GOP bounds and exhaustive unresolved-region coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\min\{U,\min_{v\in\mathcal A}L_v\}\) be the valid tree lower bound from the seed. If a feasible incumbent has value \(U<+\infty\) and \(U-L\le\varepsilon\), then its absolute global suboptimality is at most \(\varepsilon\). More generally, if \(U-L\le\varepsilon_{\rm abs}+\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\max\{1,|U|\}\), its suboptimality is bounded by that mixed tolerance. If \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\), every removed region was validly certified infeasible or unable to contain a better feasible point, and no feasible incumbent exists, then the original problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent meeting the gap tolerance against the valid tree lower bound is globally certified; exhaustive removal without any feasible incumbent certifies infeasibility when every removal was valid.
assumptions_latex: L\le f^*\le U\text{ whenever a feasible incumbent exists}
\varepsilon,\varepsilon_{\rm abs},\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\ge0
\text{Active regions cover every unresolved feasible point.}
\text{Every removed region has a valid infeasibility or safe-fathoming certificate.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U-L\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U-f^*\le\varepsilon;\qquad \mathcal A=\varnothing\ \land\ U=+\infty\Longrightarrow\text{infeasibility}.

notation.meaning: certified global lower bound and feasible-incumbent upper bound

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decomposition–tree coordination policy may attach a GOP cut \(c\) to node \(v\) only when \(D_v\subseteq V(c)\). Globally valid cuts may be shared by all nodes; locally valid cuts may pass only to descendants whose regions lie in \(V(c)\). Feasible incumbents update the common upper bound, while node relaxed-dual values update regional lower bounds. Branching must replace a parent by children covering its unresolved region. Under these rules, pruning by \(L_v\ge U\) is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cuts are shared only where valid, incumbents and bounds are synchronized, and child regions must cover the unresolved parent region.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select a bounded variable \(t\in[\ell,u]\) whose interval contributes to the relaxed-dual gap, and choose \(\tau\in(\ell,u)\). Replace the current node by two children imposing respectively \[\ell\le t\le\tau\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau\le t\le u.\] Recompute interval-dependent linear GOP relaxations and lower bounds in each child, discard infeasible or bound-dominated children, and return the remaining nodes. Repetition stops when nodes are fathomed or the global bound gap meets the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear GOP branching splits a bounded variable's interval, rebuilds the child relaxations, and retains only feasible children capable of improving the incumbent.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial feasible incumbent with value \(U_0\), initialize one active relaxed-dual region with a valid lower bound. At iteration \(k\), select one active region, solve its relaxed-dual problem, discard it if its bound is at least \(U_k\), and otherwise solve the associated primal problem at the generated complicating-block point. Update \(U_{k+1}\) with any improved feasible value, generate the valid GOP cuts and child regions, and set \(L_{k+1}\) to the minimum bound over active regions. Process exactly one region at a time and stop when the active set is empty or \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A serial GOP solver processes one relaxed-dual region at a time, updates the incumbent and valid cuts, and terminates when the certified global gap meets tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the incumbent \(U\), the active regional queue, and workers \(\mathcal W\). The coordinator dispatches distinct active regions to available workers. Each worker solves its assigned relaxed-dual problem and, when promising, its associated primal problem, then returns a valid lower bound, feasible candidates, and generated regions or cuts. The coordinator atomically updates \(U\), incorporates returned cuts and regions, and prunes every region whose valid bound is at least \(U\). Define \(L\) as the minimum valid bound over queued and in-flight regions. Terminate only after all messages are incorporated and either no region remains or \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Computational Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible evaluation protocol for GOP implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance, a GOP computational study records the best feasible value \(U\), a valid lower bound \(L\), the normalized gap \(g=(U-L)/\max\{1,|U|\}\), elapsed time, iteration count, and numbers of primal and relaxed-dual subproblems. For a stated tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), success means that a feasible incumbent is returned and \(g\leq\varepsilon\). Comparisons aggregate only instances run under stated common feasibility, stopping, hardware, and time-limit conventions; an unverified best-known objective must not be substituted for \(L\) in a certified gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid GOP study reports reproducible data, resource counts, feasibility conventions, and certified gaps based on genuine global lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: Every reported test instance specifies its model, parameter data, and solver tolerances.
All compared methods use identical feasibility and objective conventions.
A reference optimum or independently valid lower bound is available whenever a global gap is reported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported gap \(g=(U-L)/\max\{1,|U|\}\) is a reproducible certificate metric only when \(L\) is a valid global lower bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: GOP algorithm for the NRTL equilibrium model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The procedure uses referenced primal, local, and relaxed-dual subproblems whose complete definitions and convergence hypotheses are not restated in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\bar{\mathbf n}^{0}\), the tolerance, the root region, \(P^U=+\infty\), \(M^L=-\infty\), and the root bounds. At iteration \(K\): (1) evaluate the primal problem (G-P), optionally solve (G-N) locally when the primal value improves the incumbent, and update \(P^U\); (2) collect the Lagrangians associated with predecessor nodes; (3) for each qualifying bound combination \(B_l\), solve the relaxed-dual problem
\[
\min_{\mu_B,\mathbf n}\ \mu_B
\]
subject to the current and predecessor Lagrangian cuts, \(\mathcal L_{n_i^k}^{B}\le n_i^k\le\mathcal U_{n_i^k}^{B}\), and \(A\mathbf n=b\). Fathom the region if \(\mu_B^*\ge P^U\); otherwise retain it with lower bound \(\mu_B^*\). (4) Select a retained node having minimum lower bound, set \(M^L\) to that bound, and use its mole vector and region at the next iteration. (5) Stop if
\[
\left|\frac{P^U-M^L}{P^U}\right|\le\varepsilon_r;
\]
otherwise increment \(K\) and repeat. Under the referenced GOP convergence hypotheses, the NRTL specialization is \(\varepsilon\)-globally convergent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm alternates primal evaluation and optional local improvement with relaxed-dual lower-bounding over qualifying regions. Regions whose lower bounds cannot improve the incumbent are fathomed; otherwise the retained region with the smallest lower bound supplies the next iterate. The relative upper–lower gap is used as the stopping test. The source asserts epsilon-global convergence under the referenced GOP hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: P^U\ne 0\quad\text{when the displayed relative-gap test is evaluated}
\text{the referenced GOP convergence hypotheses apply to the NRTL formulation}
\text{the primal, local, and relaxed-dual subproblems and their cuts are defined as referenced}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If }\left|\frac{P^U-M^L}{P^U}\right|\le\varepsilon_r\text{, the algorithm stops; under the referenced GOP hypotheses it is }\varepsilon\text{-globally convergent}

knowledge_statements.title: Phase-Equilibrium Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isothermal-isobaric Gibbs-energy formulation without chemical reactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a finite component set, let \(\mathcal P\) be a finite admissible phase set, and let the overall composition satisfy \(z_i\geq0\) for every \(i\in\mathcal I\) and \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}z_i=1\). The phase-equilibrium interface is the global optimization problem \[\min_{\beta,x}\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\beta_p g^p(T,P,x^p)\] subject to \(\beta_p\geq0\), \(x_i^p\geq0\), \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}x_i^p=1\), \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\beta_p=1\), and \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\beta_p x_i^p=z_i\) for every \(i\in\mathcal I\). Phases with \(\beta_p=0\) are absent. Global, rather than merely local, minimization is required when the Gibbs-energy models or phase-splitting products make the formulation nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase equilibrium is represented by globally minimizing total Gibbs energy over phase fractions and phase compositions subject to simplex and component-balance constraints.
assumptions_latex: Temperature \(T\), pressure \(P\), a finite component set \(\mathcal I\), and a finite admissible phase set \(\mathcal P\) are fixed.
The overall composition satisfies \(z_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}z_i=1\).
Each phase composition lies in the component simplex and has a defined molar Gibbs-energy model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any global minimizer represents a stable phase split at the specified \(T\), \(P\), and \(z\).

notation.meaning: molar Gibbs energy of phase p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order coexistence conditions and their global-stability boundary for nonreactive phase equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a constraint-qualified local minimizer of the nonreactive phase-split Gibbs problem, every component transferable among present phases has a common chemical potential. Thus, for present phases \(p,q\), \[\mu_i^p(T,P,x^p)=\mu_i^q(T,P,x^q)\] whenever component \(i\) is interior to the relevant phase-composition faces, with corresponding one-sided inequalities at zero amounts. These coexistence conditions are necessary. They are sufficient for stable equilibrium when the total Gibbs-energy problem is convex on its feasible phase-split set; under nonconvex phase models they may also hold at metastable or unstable stationary splits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Present phases equalize transferable-component chemical potentials, but in nonconvex models this stationarity condition does not distinguish stable equilibrium from metastable stationary splits.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ and }P\text{ are fixed.}
\text{The phase Gibbs functions are differentiable on the relevant composition faces.}
\text{A constraint qualification holds at the candidate phase split.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Chemical potentials agree across present phases at stationarity; absent convexity, global Gibbs minimality is additionally required for stability.}

notation.meaning: Chemical potential of component i in phase p.

children.title: Chemical-Equilibrium Interface
children.top_down_role: GOP formulations for equilibrium composition and reaction systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Chemical-Equilibrium Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-phase Gibbs minimization with elemental conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The chemical-equilibrium interface is \[\min_{n\geq0}\ G(T,P,n)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad An=b.\] Here \(n_j\) is the amount of species \(j\), and each row of \(An=b\) enforces conservation of one element. When \(G\) is differentiable and the usual constraint qualification holds, an equilibrium candidate satisfies \(\mu_j+(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda)_j\geq0\), with equality for every \(j\) such that \(n_j>0\), where \(\mu_j=\partial G/\partial n_j\) and \(\lambda\) is a multiplier vector for \(An=b\). The interface selects the globally minimizing candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chemical equilibrium globally minimizes Gibbs energy over nonnegative species amounts while conserving each chemical element.
assumptions_latex: Temperature \(T\), pressure \(P\), elemental totals \(b\), and a finite species set are fixed.
The formula matrix \(A\) records the amount of each conserved element in each species.
Species chemical potentials and the total Gibbs-energy function are defined on the nonnegative composition domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer gives a chemically stable species composition consistent with the conserved elemental totals.

notation.meaning: multiplier vector for the elemental-balance equality

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. The GOP Approach in Phase and Chemical Equilibrium Problems p. 193

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. The GOP Approach in Phase and Chemical Equilibrium Problems p. 193

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary chemical-potential complementarity and its global-sufficiency boundary in single-phase chemical equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{G(n):An=b,\ n\geq0\}\), a constraint-qualified local minimizer satisfies, for some \(\lambda\), \[\mu(n)+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda\geq0,\qquad n_j\bigl(\mu_j(n)+(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda)_j\bigr)=0\quad\forall j.\] If \(G\) is convex on the feasible composition set, these conditions are sufficient for global optimality. If \(G\) is nonconvex, they are generally only necessary, and equilibrium still requires global Gibbs-energy minimization or an independent global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chemical-potential complementarity certifies global chemical equilibrium under convexity but is only a stationarity test for a nonconvex Gibbs model.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is differentiable on the relevant feasible face.}
\{n\geq0:An=b\}\text{ is nonempty, and a constraint qualification holds for the necessity claim.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ convex implies KKT sufficiency; without convexity, KKT generally does not certify global equilibrium.}

notation.meaning: Vector of species chemical potentials on the relevant feasible face.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiphase Gibbs minimization with simultaneous chemical reactions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. The GOP Approach in Phase and Chemical Equilibrium Problems p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reactive phase-equilibrium interface is \[\min_{n_{ip}\geq0}\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}G^p(T,P,n^p)\] subject to \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\sum_i A_{ei}n_{ip}=b_e\) for every conserved element \(e\). The variables permit both redistribution of species among phases and changes in species amounts through reaction, while elemental totals remain fixed. A phase is absent when \(\sum_i n_{ip}=0\). Because phase appearance, reaction, and nonideal Gibbs models may create multiple stationary points, equilibrium is identified with a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reactive phase equilibrium globally minimizes multiphase Gibbs energy while reactions and phase transfer vary species amounts under elemental conservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Reactive Phase-Equilibrium Interface

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. The GOP Approach in Phase and Chemical Equilibrium Problems p. 193

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order equilibrium conditions coupling elemental conservation, chemical reaction, and phase transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the reactive multiphase Gibbs problem, let \(\lambda_e\) be multipliers for the elemental balances and let \(\mu_{ip}=\partial G^p/\partial n_{ip}\). At a constraint-qualified local minimizer, \[\mu_{ip}+\sum_e A_{ei}\lambda_e\geq0,\qquad n_{ip}\left(\mu_{ip}+\sum_e A_{ei}\lambda_eight)=0\] for every species-phase pair \((i,p)\). Consequently, a species present in two phases has equal chemical potential across those phases. Moreover, for an element-balanced perturbation \(
u\) over species-phase amounts, \(A
u=0\), stationarity gives \(
u^{\mathsf T}\mu=0\) whenever both perturbation directions are locally feasible. These conditions are sufficient for global equilibrium under convexity of the total Gibbs problem but generally only necessary in a nonconvex model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reactive phase equilibrium combines elemental-potential complementarity, equality of chemical potentials across present phases, and zero affinity along reversible element-balanced reaction directions; without convexity these are only stationarity conditions.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each }G^p\text{ is differentiable on the relevant nonnegative face.}
\text{The elemental-balance system is feasible, and a constraint qualification holds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Present species satisfy elemental-potential equality, phase transfer equalizes chemical potentials, and reversible element-balanced directions have zero affinity; global sufficiency requires convexity or an independent global certificate.}

notation.meaning: Chemical potential of species i in phase p.

knowledge_statements.title: Pooling-Network Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard pool-quality formulation for a perfectly mixed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pooling-network interface has source-to-pool, pool-to-terminal, and permitted bypass flows \(f_{ij}\geq0\). For every pool \(p\), total flow satisfies \(\sum_i f_{ip}=\sum_j f_{pj}\). For each quality \(k\), perfect mixing requires \[q_{pk}\sum_i f_{ip}=\sum_i c_{ik}f_{ip},\qquad w_{pjk}=q_{pk}f_{pj},\] where \(c_{ik}\) is source quality. Terminal material and attribute balances combine pool contributions \(w_{pjk}\) with bypass contributions \(c_{ik}f_{ij}\). The products involving \(q_{pk}\) and flow variables form the nonconvex pooling interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pooling network conserves flow and quality through perfectly mixed intermediate pools, producing bilinear products between pool qualities and outgoing flows.
assumptions_latex: The directed network contains finite sets of sources, intermediate pools, and terminals, with nonnegative arc flows.
Source qualities are fixed, while each pool is perfectly mixed.
Flow conservation and finite arc or node capacities hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equalities \(q_{pk}\sum_i f_{ip}=\sum_i c_{ik}f_{ip}\) and \(w_{pjk}=q_{pk}f_{pj}\) encode the pooling nonconvexity.

notation.meaning: flow on directed arc from node i to node j
quality k of material mixed in pool p
attribute-k flow from pool p to terminal j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent source-proportion and path-flow representation of perfect mixing at a positive-throughput intermediate pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a pool \(p\) with throughput \(T_p=\sum_j y_{pj}>0\), let \(\lambda_{ip}\ge0\) be the fraction supplied by source \(i\), with \(\sum_i\lambda_{ip}=1\), and define \(v_{ipj}=\lambda_{ip}y_{pj}\). Then \(x_{ip}=\sum_jv_{ipj}=\lambda_{ip}T_p\), the pool quality is \(q_{pk}=\sum_i c_{ik}\lambda_{ip}\), and the attribute flow to terminal \(j\) is \(\sum_i c_{ik}v_{ipj}=q_{pk}y_{pj}\). Thus the source-proportion and pool-quality formulations are equivalent for positive throughput. At \(T_p=0\), normalized proportions and qualities are not determined by flow and require omission, a convention, or a disjunctive treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-throughput perfectly mixed pool can be represented by either common pool qualities or common source proportions multiplying every outgoing flow; zero throughput leaves normalized variables indeterminate.

knowledge_statements.title: Blending-System Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct blending model with fixed source qualities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A blending-system interface uses flows \(f_{ij}\geq0\) from sources \(i\) to products \(j\). Product throughput is \(F_j=\sum_i f_{ij}\), and its attribute-\(k\) amount is \(M_{jk}=\sum_i c_{ik}f_{ij}\). When \(F_j>0\), the blended quality is \(M_{jk}/F_j\). Source availability, product demand, and bounds \(L_{jk}F_j\leq M_{jk}\leq U_{jk}F_j\) complete the direct blending interface. Since \(c_{ik}\), \(L_{jk}\), and \(U_{jk}\) are fixed, these constraints are linear in the flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct blending combines fixed-quality source streams; throughput, attribute balances, and lower or upper product-quality limits are linear in flow variables.
assumptions_latex: Products receive nonnegative flows directly from sources, without variable-quality intermediate pools.
Each source has fixed quality coefficients.
Product throughput and quality specifications are stated as linear bounds on total flow and attribute flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With fixed source qualities, all material and quality-balance expressions are affine in the blending flows.

fixed quality k of source i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainable Quality Convex Hull in Direct Blending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact attainable-quality characterization for one directly blended product before additional capacity or coupling restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a product receive flows \(f_i\ge 0\) from eligible fixed-quality sources with quality vectors \(c_i\in\mathbb R^K\), and let \(F=\sum_i f_i>0\). Its quality vector is \(q=F^{-1}\sum_i c_if_i\), so \(q\in\operatorname{conv}\{c_i\}\). Conversely, every point of this convex hull is attainable at a prescribed positive throughput when the corresponding flows satisfy all source, arc, and coupling bounds. For one attribute without such restrictions, the attainable interval is \([\min_i c_i,\max_i c_i]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-throughput direct blend has quality in the convex hull of its eligible fixed source qualities; capacity and coupling constraints may restrict the attainable subset.
assumptions_latex: f_i\ge0
F=\sum_i f_i>0
c_i\in\mathbb R^K
\text{The flows realizing a proposed convex combination satisfy every source, arc, and coupling bound.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\in\operatorname{conv}\{c_i\},\qquad K=1\Longrightarrow q\in[\min_i c_i,\max_i c_i].

notation.meaning: fixed quality vector of eligible source i
flow from source i to the product

children.title: Pooling–Blending Coupling
children.top_down_role: Application settings coupling pool allocation with downstream blend requirements.

assumptions_latex: Every pool is perfectly mixed and has a common outgoing quality for each attribute.
A terminal may receive both pool outflows and direct source bypasses.
All arc flows are nonnegative and satisfy network flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling is localized in \(w_{pjk}=q_{pk}f_{pj}\); terminal blending remains affine once \(w_{pjk}\) is introduced.

notation.meaning: flow from pool p to terminal j
attribute-k amount conveyed from pool p to terminal j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear link between pool mixing and terminal blending balances.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Large Scale Pooling and Blending Problems p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each pool-to-terminal arc and quality, define \(w_{pjk}=q_{pk}f_{pj}\). Pool mixing imposes \[q_{pk}\sum_i f_{ip}=\sum_i c_{ik}f_{ip},\] while terminal \(j\) receives total flow \(F_j=\sum_p f_{pj}+\sum_i f_{ij}\) and attribute amount \[M_{jk}=\sum_p w_{pjk}+\sum_i c_{ik}f_{ij}.\] Thus pooling determines the variable qualities \(q_{pk}\), blending aggregates their outgoing attribute flows, and the bilinear equalities \(w_{pjk}=q_{pk}f_{pj}\) are the explicit coupling between the two subsystems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pool qualities multiply outgoing flows, and those attribute flows then enter otherwise linear terminal blending balances together with direct bypass streams.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine and Bilinear Pool–Blend Coupling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp local condition under which an individual pool-to-terminal product relation becomes affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a pool-to-terminal arc, the transmission relation is \(w=qf\). It is affine when either \(q\) or \(f\) is fixed. If both factors range independently over nondegenerate intervals \([\underline q,\overline q]\) and \([\underline f,\overline f]\), its graph is nonconvex; in particular, the midpoint of the two graph points at \((\underline q,\underline f)\) and \((\overline q,\overline f)\) does not satisfy the product equality. Terminal aggregation remains affine after introducing \(w\), but exact variable-quality transmission remains nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pool-to-terminal transmission is affine when either pool quality or outgoing flow is fixed; when both vary independently over nondegenerate intervals, the exact product graph is nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: w=qf
\underline q<\overline q
\underline f<\overline f
q\in[\underline q,\overline q]
f\in[\underline f,\overline f]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{graph}(w=qf)\text{ is nonconvex when both factor intervals have positive width.}

children.title: Quality-Specification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Product-quality structures that shape GOP pooling or blending formulations.

assumptions_latex: For each product \(j\), total flow \(F_j\) and attribute amount \(M_{jk}\) are consistently defined.
Quality bounds satisfy \(L_{jk}\leq U_{jk}\).
Zero-throughput products are permitted only under the homogeneous amount-form specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(F_j>0\), \(L_{jk}F_j\leq M_{jk}\leq U_{jk}F_j\) is equivalent to \(L_{jk}\leq M_{jk}/F_j\leq U_{jk}\).

notation.meaning: amount of attribute k in product j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower, upper, ranged, and exact product-quality specifications.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Large Scale Pooling and Blending Problems p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a produced stream with \(F_j>0\), a lower specification is \(M_{jk}\geq L_{jk}F_j\), an upper specification is \(M_{jk}\leq U_{jk}F_j\), and a ranged specification imposes both. An exact specification \(S_{jk}\) is the special case \(M_{jk}=S_{jk}F_j\). In a pooling model, \(M_{jk}\) includes bilinear pool contributions; in a direct blending model it is affine. The homogeneous amount form remains well-defined at \(F_j=0\), whereas the ratio \(M_{jk}/F_j\) does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product quality may have lower, upper, ranged, or exact limits, expressed homogeneously using attribute amount and total product flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Scale Indefinite Quadratic Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linearly constrained indefinite quadratic programs whose dimensions motivate structure-exploiting decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A large-scale indefinite quadratic interface supplies the finite-dimensional problem \[\min_{x\in P}\ \frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b,\ Ex=d,\ \ell\leq x\leq u\},\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue and \(P\) is nonempty and compact. For structure-exploiting GOP treatment, the interface also exposes a variable partition and the quadratic or bilinear terms used to construct convex primal subproblems and valid relaxed-dual bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This interface represents a finite-dimensional bounded linearly constrained quadratic program with an indefinite symmetric Hessian and exposes structure used for large-scale decomposition.
assumptions_latex: The decision vector lies in \(\mathbb R^n\) and is subject to linear equalities, inequalities, and finite bounds.
The symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
The feasible polyhedron \(P\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Because \(Q\) is indefinite, the quadratic objective is nonconvex and local optimality alone does not certify a global solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Exploitable Block Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of GOP when conditional primal convexity cannot be maintained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exploitable block-convexity condition fails if there exist a fixed \(y\), a feasible point \(x\), a nonzero direction \(d\), and \(\delta>0\) such that \(x+td\) is feasible for every \(t\in[-\delta,\delta]\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2_{xx}F(x,y)d<0\). Then the tangent model in \(x\) is not guaranteed to underestimate \(F(\cdot,y)\), so relaxed-dual cuts whose validity depends on conditional convexity are not automatically valid global lower bounds. For \(F(x,y)=-x^2-y^2+\alpha xy\) on \([-1,1]^2\), either one-variable coordinate block has second derivative \(-2\), so neither coordinate choice supplies a convex primal block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every admissible primal coordinate block has negative curvature along a feasible segment, GOP tangent cuts can lose their global-underestimator property and the standard bound certificate can fail.
assumptions_latex: The function \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable with respect to the designated primal block \(x\).
GOP requires convexity in \(x\) after fixing the complicating block \(y\).
Primal supporting cuts are used as global underestimators in the relaxed-dual construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negative curvature along a feasible primal-block segment invalidates the supporting-hyperplane lower-bound guarantee and removes the standard GOP global-bound guarantee for cuts based on that convexity.

notation.meaning: nonzero primal-block direction defining a feasible local segment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural and Encoded Size of a Relaxed-Dual Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes representation-level structural counts from exact input length under a specified encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicitly represented relaxed-dual formulation, let \(n\) be its scalar-variable count, \(m\) its row count, \(N\) its number of stored coefficient incidences, and \(q\) its number of integrality markers. The tuple \((n,m,N,q)\) is a structural-size descriptor. Under a fixed finite binary encoding, the exact input length \(L\) is the total encoded length of all coefficients, right-hand sides, bounds, indices, and variable-type data. Neither row count nor the structural tuple alone determines \(L\). For a sparse block of \(K\) affine cuts \(a_k^{\mathsf T}z\le b_k\), its row and coefficient contribution is \(K\) and \(N_{\mathrm{cut}}=\sum_{k=1}^K\operatorname{nnz}(a_k)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed-dual size can be described by variables, rows, nonzero incidences, and integrality data, while exact input length also depends on how every datum is encoded.
assumptions_latex: The formulation is stored explicitly.
Exact input length is evaluated under a fixed finite binary encoding.

Every coefficient, bound, and integrality marker has a finite binary encoding.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(t\), write the relaxed-dual master using \(n_t\) scalar decision variables, \(m_t\) structural constraints, and \(K_t\) retained generated cuts. children.title: Relaxed-Dual Cut-Pool Growth
children.top_down_role: Accumulation, retention, and redundancy patterns within the relaxed-dual cut pool.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\ge 1\), \(K_t=K_0+\sum_{s=1}^{t}c_s\); hence \((K_t)\) is nondecreasing, and \(c_s\ge r>0\) implies \(K_t\ge K_0+rt\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_0\) be the initial cut count, and let iteration \(s\) generate \(c_s\ge 0\) cuts. If no generated cut is deleted, aggregated, or replaced, then \[K_t=K_0+\sum_{s=1}^{t}c_s.\] Consequently, \((K_t)_{t\ge0}\) is nondecreasing. If every iteration generates at least \(r>0\) cuts, then \(K_t\ge K_0+rt\); if \(c_s\ge \alpha s\) for \(\alpha>0\), then \(K_t\ge K_0+\alpha t(t+1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without deletion or aggregation, the cut pool grows by the cumulative number of generated cuts and can grow linearly or quadratically with iterations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Explicit Cut-Storage and Full-Evaluation Burden
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed computational model for dense explicit storage and evaluation of every retained cut; sparse, indexed, aggregated, or lazy implementations are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a relaxed-dual master explicitly stores \(K\) dense affine cuts \(a_k^{\mathsf T}z\le b_k\) in \(d\) variables. Coordinate storage uses \(K(d+1)\) scalar slots. In a unit-cost scalar-arithmetic model, a management pass that evaluates every dot product \(a_k^{\mathsf T}z\) performs \(\Theta(Kd)\) arithmetic operations and reads \(\Theta(Kd)\) coefficients. These counts exclude master reoptimization, presolve, factorization, and any redundancy-certification subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dense explicit cuts, storage and a complete evaluation pass scale as the number of cuts times the master dimension.
assumptions_latex: All \(K\) cuts are stored explicitly and densely.
The pass evaluates every retained cut at a supplied point.
Scalar storage access and arithmetic have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(K,d)=K(d+1)=\Theta(Kd),\qquad T_{\mathrm{eval}}(K,d)=\Theta(Kd).

children.title: Lagrangian Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Multiplier nonuniqueness, weak discrimination, and related relaxed-dual instability.

assumptions_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\), where \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are continuously differentiable.
The feasible point \(x^*\) satisfies the KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT point is Lagrangian-degenerate precisely when its multiplier set \(\Lambda(x^*)\) is not a singleton.

notation.meaning: Set of KKT multipliers associated with the point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses multiplier nonuniqueness as the local meaning of Lagrangian degeneracy.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. The GOP Primal-Relaxed Dual Decomposition Approach: Theory p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\), define \(L(x,\lambda):=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\). At a feasible KKT point \(x^*\), define \[\Lambda(x^*):=\{\lambda\ge0:\nabla_xL(x^*,\lambda)=0,\ \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0\ \text{for every }i\}.\] In the multiplier-nonuniqueness sense, \(x^*\) is Lagrangian-degenerate if and only if \(|\Lambda(x^*)|>1\). This condition concerns dual representation at a fixed primal point, not multiplicity of primal minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KKT point is Lagrangian-degenerate when more than one nonnegative complementary multiplier vector satisfies stationarity at that same primal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The claim is correct but canonically belongs under Active-Set Degeneracy; its placement here also depends on the unresolved meaning of “Lagrangian degeneracy.”
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min 0\) subject to \(x\le0\) and \(2x\le0\). At \(x^*=0\), the active gradients are linearly dependent, whereas stationarity and nonnegativity give \(\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0\) and hence \(\Lambda(0)=\{(0,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent active gradients need not produce multiple KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}[1\;2]<2\quad\text{and}\quad |\Lambda(0)|=1.

children.title: Active-Set Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Ambiguous or unstable identification of constraints governing local subproblem behavior.

assumptions_latex: The inequality functions \(g_i\) are continuously differentiable at a feasible point \(x^*\).
The active index set is \(I(x^*):=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Active-set degeneracy holds exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}J_I(x^*)<|I(x^*)|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible point \(x^*\), let \(I(x^*):=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}\), and form the active-gradient matrix \[J_I(x^*):=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla g_i(x^*)^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix}_{i\in I(x^*)}.\] The active set is degenerate in the linear-independence sense if and only if \[\operatorname{rank}J_I(x^*)<|I(x^*)|.\] Equivalently, there exists a nonzero vector \(v\in\mathbb R^{|I(x^*)|}\) such that \(J_I(x^*)^{\mathsf T}v=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active set is degenerate when its active constraint gradients are linearly dependent, equivalently when the active-gradient matrix lacks full row rank.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\le0,\quad 2x\le0.\] At \(x^*=0\), both active gradients are dependent, but KKT stationarity \(\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0\) with \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0\) has the unique solution \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent active gradients can coexist with unique KKT multipliers.
assumptions_latex: Multipliers for inequalities written as \(g_i(x)\le0\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}J_I(0)<|I(0)|\) and \(|\Lambda(0)|=1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional sufficient condition for dependence among active inequality gradients.

assumptions_latex: \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) is feasible.
Every active inequality is differentiable at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|I(x^*)|>n\Longrightarrow\operatorname{rank}J_I(x^*)<|I(x^*)|\).

children.title: Coupled Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiplier ambiguity reinforces unstable active-set identification.

assumptions_latex: The differentiable inequality-constrained problem and KKT multiplier set are defined as in the preceding degeneracy conditions.
The point \(x^*\) is feasible and satisfies the KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coupled degeneracy occurs when both \(|\Lambda(x^*)|>1\) and \(\operatorname{rank}J_I(x^*)<|I(x^*)|\).

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the primal point.
Active-constraint Jacobian at the primal point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the simultaneous multiplier-nonuniqueness and active-gradient-dependence regime.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. The GOP Primal-Relaxed Dual Decomposition Approach: Theory p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be a feasible KKT point, let \(\Lambda(x^*)\) be its multiplier set, and let \(J_I(x^*)\) be its active-gradient matrix. The point lies in a coupled degeneracy regime when \[|\Lambda(x^*)|>1\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{rank}J_I(x^*)<|I(x^*)|.\] Thus both the dual representation of stationarity and the active constraint representation are nonunique. Either inequality failing excludes this coupled regime, although one of the two individual degeneracies may remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled degeneracy means that KKT multipliers are nonunique while the active constraint gradients are simultaneously linearly dependent.

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Search Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Search inefficiency and stalled refinement attributable to persistent degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic decomposition run produces nondecreasing lower bounds \(B_t\), nonincreasing incumbent bounds \(U_t\), and retained cut spaces \(\mathcal C_t\).
Tolerances \(\varepsilon_B,\varepsilon_U\ge0\) and a window length \(q\ge1\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run is degeneracy-stagnant over \([t,t+q]\) when all subproblems are coupled-degenerate and neither bound nor the cut span changes beyond the stated tolerances.

notation.meaning: Relaxed-dual lower bound and incumbent upper bound.
Linear span of retained cut coefficient vectors.
Number of consecutive iterations in the stagnation window.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure boundary; it does not assert that every degenerate run must stagnate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(q\ge1\) and tolerances \(\varepsilon_B,\varepsilon_U\ge0\). A run is degeneracy-stagnant on iterations \([t,t+q]\) if every generating subproblem in that window is coupled-degenerate and \[B_{t+q}-B_t\le\varepsilon_B,\qquad U_t-U_{t+q}\le\varepsilon_U,\qquad \mathcal C_{t+q}=\mathcal C_t.\] Here \(\mathcal C_s\) is the span of retained cut normals after iteration \(s\). The condition records failure to improve either bound or add an independent cut; degeneracy alone, without these consequences, is not stagnation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search is degeneracy-stagnant when consecutive coupled-degenerate subproblems yield no material bound improvement and no enlargement of the cut-normal span.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Search Stagnation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed stagnation window, tolerances, and cut-span equality form a bespoke operational failure boundary. No evidence supports this particular definition or its attribution to degeneracy.

children.title: Problem Scaling Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Disparities in variable, constraint, objective, or coefficient magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced Row Magnitudes Do Not Guarantee Good Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates row-magnitude balance from numerical sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A_\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&\varepsilon\end{bmatrix}\), where \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the Euclidean row-norm ratio tends to \(1\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), whereas \(\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly equal row magnitudes can coexist with arbitrarily poor conditioning when the rows are nearly dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
Row magnitudes and conditioning are measured in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\max_i\|a_i\|_2}{\min_i\|a_i\|_2}\to1\quad\text{while}\quad\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Row Magnitudes Do Not Guarantee Good Conditioning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representation-dependent diagnostic for nonzero constraint rows in a fixed norm; it covers row scaling but not all variable, objective, or nonlinear-function scales named by the leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonzero represented rows \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), define \(s_i:=\|(a_i,b_i)\|\) in a fixed norm and \[R_{\mathrm{row}}:=\frac{\max_i s_i}{\min_i s_i}.\] Then \(R_{\mathrm{row}}\ge1\), with equality exactly when all represented row magnitudes agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-row imbalance is the largest-to-smallest nonzero augmented-row magnitude ratio in a fixed representation and norm.
assumptions_latex: Every included augmented row \((a_i,b_i)\) is nonzero.
One norm and one formulation representation are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\mathrm{row}}:=\frac{\max_i\|(a_i,b_i)\|}{\min_i\|(a_i,b_i)\|}\ge1.

notation.meaning: Magnitude of represented constraint row i.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Row Scaling Imbalance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the represented row-scale diagnostic from an invariant property of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) by \(\alpha_i a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le\alpha_i b_i\), where \(\alpha_i>0\), preserves the feasible half-space but changes its augmented-row magnitude from \(s_i\) to \(\alpha_i s_i\). Consequently, \(R_{\mathrm{row}}\) can be changed arbitrarily by equivalent positive row scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row rescaling preserves the mathematical constraints but can arbitrarily change the row-imbalance diagnostic.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\alpha_i\) is strictly positive.
The row norm is absolutely homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}=\{x:\alpha_i a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le\alpha_i b_i\},\qquad s_i'=\alpha_i s_i.

notation.meaning: Positive scaling applied to constraint row i.

knowledge_statements.title: Row-Imbalance Diagnostics Depend on Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-dependent disparity among positive bounded-coordinate widths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds \ell_j\le x_j\le u_j with w_j=u_j-\ell_j>0, define R_{\mathrm{var}}=\max_j w_j/\min_j w_j. The substitution z_j=(x_j-\ell_j)/w_j maps the represented intervals to [0,1] and makes this width ratio one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-domain imbalance compares the largest and smallest positive coordinate widths; unit-box scaling removes this particular disparity.
assumptions_latex: Every included coordinate has finite bounds and positive width.
The represented coordinate system is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\mathrm{var}}:=\frac{\max_j(u_j-\ell_j)}{\min_j(u_j-\ell_j)}\ge1.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Domain Scale Imbalance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-magnitude diagnostic after a declared row normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After fixing a row normalization, let c_j=\|A_{:j}\| for every nonzero coefficient column and define R_{\mathrm{col}}=\max_j c_j/\min_j c_j. Under x=Dz, column j is scaled by D_{jj}; hence the ratio depends on variable units and the row-normalization rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Column imbalance compares nonzero column magnitudes after row normalization and changes under variable rescaling.
assumptions_latex: A coefficient or linearized-coefficient array A is fixed.
Rows use a declared normalization.
Zero columns are omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\mathrm{col}}:=\frac{\max_j\|A_{:j}\|}{\min_j\|A_{:j}\|}\ge1.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Coefficient-Column Imbalance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Declared Objective and Constraint-Function Scale Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless profile of represented function variation over a declared reference region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D be a fixed reference region and F_0=f,F_1,\ldots,F_m the represented objective and nonlinear constraint functions. For each included nonconstant F_i with finite positive oscillation a_i=\sup_DF_i-\inf_DF_i, choose a dimensionally compatible reference scale \tau_i>0 and set r_i=a_i/\tau_i. The profile (r_i) and ratio R_{\mathrm{fun}}=\max_i r_i/\min_i r_i are meaningful only together with D and the declared scales; there is no canonical cross-unit ratio without those choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective and nonlinear-constraint magnitudes can be compared using declared dimensionless scales, but the comparison is normalization-dependent.
assumptions_latex: Each included function has finite positive oscillation on D.
Every \tau_i is positive and dimensionally compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\mathrm{fun}}:=\frac{\max_i(a_i/\tau_i)}{\min_i(a_i/\tau_i)}\ge1.

notation.meaning: Oscillation of function i on D.
Declared reference scale for function i.

knowledge_statements.title: Declared Objective and Constraint-Function Scale Profile

assumptions_latex: The formulation has nonzero coefficient rows \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
Row magnitude is measured in a fixed norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row-scaling imbalance is \(R:=\max_i s_i/\min_i s_i\ge1\), where \(s_i:=\|(a_i,b_i)\|\).

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the coefficient and right-hand-side row.
Coefficient vector and right-hand side of row i.
